units.title: How to solve interview problems
units.blurb: The method the whole course builds on: complexity and Big-O in practice, what the constraints let you afford, the cost of .NET collections, allocations and recursion in C# and Unity, how to reason out loud, and the usual mistakes.

lessons.title: Complexity in practice
lessons.sub: Big-O as growth of work, amortization, and what the constraints let you afford

cards.title: Big-O: how the work grows
cards.body:
The complexity of an algorithm is not its time in seconds. It answers the question “how many times more work is there when the data grows”. We count simple operations — a comparison, an addition, reading an array element — as a function of the input size n and keep the leading term without constants: 3n + 5 is O(n), n²/2 + n is O(n²).

Constants are dropped because for large n the leading term swamps the rest, and the constant itself depends on the CPU and the compiler. The growth does not: for O(n), 10 times more data means 10 times more work; for O(n²), 100 times.

How to read code: loops one after another add up (O(n) + O(n) = O(n)), nested loops multiply. With two inputs, each gets its own letter: a loop over b inside a loop over a is O(n·m), not O(n²). Collapsing n and m into one letter is a common interview mistake.

cards.q: What is the complexity of this function? a has length n, b has length m.
options: O(n·m)
O(n²)
O(n + m)
O(n·m + m), it cannot be simplified
cards.explain: Nested loops multiply: for each of the n elements of a there are m steps over b, n·m in total. The second loop adds m, and n·m + m = m·(n + 1), which is O(n·m): the lower-order term is dropped.

wrong.1: There are two inputs and their lengths are unrelated: with n = 10 and m = 10⁶ the work is 10⁷, not 100. Each input gets its own letter.
wrong.2: Loops one after another add up. Here the loop over b is nested inside the loop over a, so they multiply.
wrong.3: It can be simplified: m ≤ n·m for n ≥ 1, so the lower-order term is dropped — O(n·m).

cards.title: Best, average and worst case. Memory
cards.body:
The same function runs for different times on different inputs. Linear search for a value (Array.IndexOf, List<T>.Contains): the best case is the value at the front, one comparison; the worst is the value missing, n comparisons; the average, if the value is equally likely to be anywhere, is about n/2. Both average and worst are O(n).

Unless stated otherwise, interviews talk about the worst case: it is a guarantee. “On average” is said explicitly, along with what the average is over. A hash table lookup is O(1) on average over the distribution of keys and O(n) in the worst case; how that happens is in the next lesson.

Memory is part of complexity too. You count extra memory beyond the input: a dictionary of n elements is O(n), a couple of variables is O(1). Recursion depth is memory as well: every nested call takes a frame on the thread stack, and recursion of depth n costs O(n) memory even without a single array.

cards.title: Logarithm: how many times you can halve
cards.body:
log₂ n is how many times you can halve n before 1 is left. It is also the number of doublings it takes to get from 1 to n. It grows very slowly: log₂ 10³ ≈ 10, log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20, log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30. The base is not written inside O: log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ by a constant factor.

O(log n) is an algorithm that discards half of the candidates at every step. The example is binary search in a sorted array: look at the middle; if it is less than the target, the answer is to the right and the left half is thrown away; if greater, the other way round. A million elements take at most 20 comparisons. In .NET this is Array.BinarySearch and List<T>.BinarySearch.

O(n log n) is doing a log n operation n times, or splitting the problem in half and merging the halves in O(n). That is how sorting works: Array.Sort is O(n log n), about 2·10⁷ comparisons for n = 10⁶. A common shape of a solution is “sort, then one pass”: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n).

cards.q: What is the complexity of this code?
options: O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n)
O(log n)
cards.explain: The outer loop runs n times. The inner one doubles j: 1, 2, 4, … — it reaches n in about log₂ n steps. Nested loops multiply: n · log n.

wrong.1: The inner loop does not step through j one by one — j doubles, so it runs log₂ n times, not n.
wrong.2: The inner loop is not O(1): its iteration count grows with n, if slowly.
wrong.3: log n is just the inner loop, and it runs n times.

cards.title: Amortization: why List<T>.Add is O(1)
cards.body:
List<T> stores its elements in an array. While there is room, Add writes into the next slot — O(1). When the array is full, the list allocates a new one twice as large (the first holds 4 elements), copies everything over and only then adds. That insertion costs O(n).

Count n additions as a whole. Copies happen at sizes 4, 8, 16, …, and in total 4 + 8 + … + n/2 < n elements are copied. Together with the writes themselves that is fewer than 2n operations for n calls, so O(1) per call. This is amortized complexity: expensive operations are rare, and their cost is spread over the cheap ones. It is a guarantee for any sequence of operations, not a probability — do not confuse it with “on average” for a hash table, where the average is over the keys.

It is the geometric growth that makes it work: if the list grew by 10 elements at a time, there would be on the order of n²/20 copies — O(n) per call. If n is known in advance, set the capacity: new List<int>(n) — no reallocations at all. In Unity every reallocation is a new array, and the old one becomes garbage for the collector; in code that runs every frame, that shows.

cards.q: You add 1000 elements one by one to an empty List<int>. How many elements are copied in total during reallocations?
options: 1020: 4 + 8 + … + 512 — on the order of n
About 500,000: every Add copies the whole list
8: one copy per doubling
0: List<T> appends at the end without copying
cards.explain: Capacity grows 4 → 8 → … → 1024, and every doubling copies the whole old array: 4 + 8 + … + 512 = 1020. That is less than 2n, which is why Add is amortized O(1).

wrong.1: That would be the case if Add copied everything every time. A copy only happens when the array is full, and that gets rarer and rarer: capacity doubles.
wrong.2: There are indeed 8 doublings (from 4 to 1024), but each one copies not one element but the whole old array.
wrong.3: While there is room, yes. But when the array is full, a new one is needed and the old elements move into it.

cards.title: Constraints → affordable complexity
cards.body:
The constraints in a problem statement are not a formality: they hint at which solution is expected. The rule of thumb is about 10⁸ simple operations per second. Where it comes from: a CPU runs on the order of 3·10⁹ cycles per second; a simple operation in a loop — a comparison, an addition, an array read — is a few instructions, and cache misses and branches cost more. In C# that comes out at 10⁸–10⁹ such operations per second, and 10⁸ is the safe estimate. With a 1–2 second limit, a solution has to fit into ~10⁸ operations.

Plug the maximum n into the complexity and compare with 10⁸:

n ≤ 10–11 → O(n!) — all permutations (10! ≈ 3.6·10⁶)
n ≤ 20 → O(2ⁿ) or O(2ⁿ·n) — all subsets (2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶)
n ≤ 500 → O(n³) (500³ ≈ 1.25·10⁸)
n ≤ 10⁴ → O(n²) (10⁸)
n ≤ 10⁶ → O(n log n) (≈ 2·10⁷)
n ≤ 10⁸ → O(n)
larger → O(log n) or O(1): such an n is no longer an array length but a number, and you need a formula or a binary search over values

The estimate is rough, but being off by 2–3× changes nothing: neighbouring rows differ by hundreds of times. If the statement has no constraints, ask: the answer “n up to a million” rules out O(n²) on the spot.

In a game the budget is tighter: a frame at 60 FPS is 16.7 ms, about 1.7·10⁶ simple operations for everything, the engine included. Checking all pairs of 1000 units — 5·10⁵ pairs — eats a noticeable share of the frame.

cards.q: The limit is 1 second. Which solutions fit? Select all.
options: n ≤ 3000, an O(n²) solution
n ≤ 10⁵, an O(n²) solution
n ≤ 18, trying all subsets in O(2ⁿ·n)
n ≤ 10⁶, an O(n log n) solution
n ≤ 300, an O(n⁴) solution
cards.explain: 3000² ≈ 9·10⁶ — plenty of headroom. 2¹⁸ · 18 ≈ 4.7·10⁶ — same. 10⁶ · 20 = 2·10⁷ — fits. But 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰, a hundred times over budget, and 300⁴ ≈ 8·10⁹ is eighty times over. The rule: plug in the maximum, compare with 10⁸.

cards.title: Two Sum: O(n²) versus O(n)
cards.body:
The running example is Two Sum (LeetCode #1): find the indices of two numbers in nums that add up to target. Checking all pairs is n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²). But the inner loop looks for one specific value, target − x, from scratch every time. Remember everything seen so far in a Dictionary<int, int> “number → index”, and that lookup is O(1) on average, so one pass is enough: O(n) time, O(n) memory.

Why it is correct is explained by an invariant — a statement that holds before every iteration of the loop. Here: before step i the dictionary holds exactly nums[0..i−1]. If a pair (j, i) with j < i exists, then at step i its left element is already in the dictionary, so the pair is found. And so that a number does not find itself, we check first and insert after. The invariant is the main tool of this course: it proves the code correct, and it is what you say out loud in an interview.

The hash table unit covers this problem in detail. Here we care about cost: how many steps each solution takes.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [7, 3, 12, 1, 8, 4, 2, 6, 9, 15], target = 24. The pair sits at the very end — the worst case. Every step after the first is one dictionary lookup; count them. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.

options: seen[12] = 2
return new[] { 2, 2 }
asks.q: The next x is 12, and the value to look for is 12 as well. What does the code do?
asks.explain: By the invariant the dictionary holds only what is to the left: 7 and 3. There is no 12 in it, so the code stores 12 → 2 and moves on. Had the insert come before the check, the number would have found itself and returned [2, 2].

options: return new[] { 8, 9 }
seen[15] = 9
return new[] { 9, 8 }
asks.q: x = 15, looking for 9. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The 9 is in the dictionary at index 8: TryGetValue hands back j = 8, and the answer is { j, i } = { 8, 9 }. Ten lookups in total — one per element.

cards.q: The trace made 10 dictionary lookups. How many comparisons does checking all pairs i < j make on the same array before it reaches the pair (8, 9)?
options: 45: it is the last pair, so it goes through all 10 · 9 / 2
10: one per element
cards.explain: The pair (8, 9) comes last in the order of the loops, so all n(n − 1)/2 = 45 pairs get checked. 45 versus 10 is not much yet. But for n = 10⁵ it is 5·10⁹ comparisons versus 10⁵ lookups: a gap of tens of thousands of times, even if a dictionary lookup costs 20–50 times more than a single comparison.

wrong.1: 10 is the dictionary: one lookup per element. The brute force checks pairs, and there are on the order of n²/2 of them.
wrong.2: n² includes the pairs (i, i) and both orientations of every pair. The loop with j = i + 1 checks each pair once: n(n − 1)/2.
wrong.3: 10 · 9 counts (i, j) and (j, i) separately. The loop with j = i + 1 checks each pair once.

cards.title: When O(n²) beats O(n): constants and the cache
cards.body:
Big-O is about growth, not about the time at a particular n. A Dictionary lookup is a hash, a modulo, a walk along a chain and an Equals: tens of nanoseconds versus a fraction of a nanosecond to compare neighbouring array elements. So for 8–16 elements a linear scan of an array often beats a dictionary, and O(n log n) with a small constant can outrun O(n) with a large one.

The second constant is memory. An array is contiguous, and the CPU pulls it into the cache in blocks. Nodes of a list or a tree are scattered across the managed heap, and every hop can cost a cache miss — on the order of a hundred nanoseconds. The same O(n) traversal of an array and of a LinkedList<T> differs several times over.

In an interview you name the asymptotics first and, if asked about real speed, the constants: “for small n the linear scan wins, but at n = 10⁵ the dictionary is orders of magnitude faster”.
cards.deep:
Formally. f(n) = O(g(n)) if f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀ for some constant c: it is an upper bound. Θ is a tight bound (from above and below), Ω a lower one. In interviews “O” is usually meant as Θ: “checking all pairs is O(n²)” means “grows like n²”. Formally O(n²) is also true of a linear algorithm, but nobody answers that way.

Amortization and the spike of a single operation. Amortized O(1) for List<T>.Add does not stop an individual call from costing O(n): with 10⁶ int elements one doubling copies 4 MB. On a server nobody notices; in a game it is a spike in the frame graph. Hence the rule for hot code: capacity up front (new List<T>(n), the Capacity property), collections in fields and Clear() instead of new.

Why doubling. Any factor greater than 1 works: growing by a factor of k gives fewer than n/(k − 1) copies for n inserts. In .NET List<T>, Stack<T> and Queue<T> double, and Dictionary grows to a prime no smaller than twice its size. Collections never shrink on their own: Clear() keeps the capacity, and TrimExcess() gives the memory back.

Several parameters. A graph is O(V + E), two strings are O(n·m), “the best k out of n” is O(n log k). Do not reduce everything to one letter: “O(n log k), with k ≪ n” is a senior answer.

cards.q: Match the constraint with the affordable complexity (a 1–2 second limit).

lessons.title: .NET collections and their cost
lessons.sub: What is inside List, Queue, Dictionary, PriorityQueue, SortedSet and LinkedList, what each operation costs, and what Unity lacks

cards.title: The cost of an operation is part of the solution
cards.body:
The complexity of a solution is the number of operations times the cost of each. The same algorithm with a different collection has a different complexity. Removing duplicates while keeping the order: with List<T>.Contains every check is a linear scan, O(n), and the whole solution is O(n²); with HashSet<T> a check is O(1) on average, and the solution is O(n). For n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ operations versus 10⁵.

That is why interviewers ask about every collection you use: “why this one, and what does the operation cost”. The answer is not “it is fast” but a bound and the structure: “HashSet is a hash table, Add and Contains are O(1) on average”. This lesson is the price list of .NET collections and which of them Unity has.

cards.title: List<T>: an array and a counter
cards.body:
List<T> is an array plus a Count. Every price follows from that.

O(1): the indexer list[i], Add (amortized — from the previous lesson), RemoveAt(Count − 1) — removing the last element.
O(n): Insert(i, x) and RemoveAt(i) at the front or in the middle — every element to the right is shifted with Array.Copy; Contains, IndexOf, Remove(x) — a linear scan.
O(n log n): Sort; once sorted, BinarySearch is O(log n).

A trick worth knowing: when order does not matter, an element in the middle is removed in O(1) — move the last element into its place and remove the last. In a game this is how you clean up a list of live enemies or bullets: their order means nothing.

cards.title: Stack<T> and Queue<T>
cards.body:
Stack<T> is an array whose end is the top: Push (amortized), Pop and Peek are O(1). The order is “last in, first out” (LIFO): depth-first search, brackets, undo.

Queue<T> is a circular buffer over an array: two indices, head (where you take from) and tail (where you put to), and each wraps to the start when it reaches the end of the array. So Enqueue (amortized) and Dequeue are O(1), and nothing is ever shifted. When the buffer is full, the queue doubles the array and copies the elements over in order. The order is “first in, first out” (FIFO): breadth-first search, event queues.

Neither gives access by index (LINQ ElementAt is a linear scan here), and neither shrinks on its own. There are TryPop and TryDequeue — no exception on an empty collection.

cards.q: A job queue is built on a List<int>: Add at the end, RemoveAt(0) from the front. Up to 10⁵ jobs sit in it at once, and all of them pass through it. What is wrong?
options: RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list: O(n) per removal, on the order of 10⁹–10¹⁰ shifts in total. You need a Queue<T>
Nothing: List<T> is an array, and removing from it is O(1)
Add becomes O(n) because the list keeps growing
The only problem is memory: List<T> does not release space after RemoveAt
cards.explain: Removing from the front of an array shifts every element to its right by one slot. 10⁵ removals, each shifting tens of thousands of elements, is billions of operations. Queue<T> is a circular buffer: Dequeue just moves head, O(1).

wrong.1: Only removing the last element is O(1). RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole tail with Array.Copy.
wrong.2: Add stays amortized O(1): the capacity doubles. It is removal from the front that is expensive.
wrong.3: The capacity indeed does not shrink, but that is minor. The real trouble is O(n) for every RemoveAt(0).

cards.title: Dictionary and HashSet: O(1) on average
cards.body:
A hash table: key → GetHashCode() → bucket number; the bucket holds a short chain of entries compared with Equals. If the hashes are spread evenly, a bucket holds one or two entries, and TryGetValue, ContainsKey, Add, Remove are O(1) on average. The average here is over the keys: if the keys land in one bucket (a bad GetHashCode or deliberately crafted data), a lookup turns into a walk along the chain — O(n) in the worst case.

When there are more entries than buckets, the table grows to roughly twice the size (a prime) and redistributes every entry — O(n), but rarely: insertion is amortized O(1). If n is known, pass the capacity to the constructor.

Habits: TryGetValue is one lookup instead of the two of ContainsKey + indexer; the indexer d[k] = v overwrites, while Add throws on a duplicate key; HashSet.Add returns false if the element was already there. The enumeration order is not guaranteed — do not rely on it.

cards.title: The heap and PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>
cards.body:
A heap (binary) is a tree laid out in an array with no pointers: element i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the invariant is that a parent is no greater than its children. So the minimum is always at the root, a[0]. Insert: put the element at the end and move it up, swapping with the parent while the parent is greater. Remove the minimum: put the last element in place of the root and move it down towards the smaller child. The tree height is log n, so both operations are O(log n), and looking at the minimum is O(1). Do not confuse it with the managed heap where objects live: it is one word for two different things.

.NET 6+ has one ready-made — PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>: a min-heap by priority, Enqueue and Dequeue are O(log n), Peek is O(1). Inside it is a 4-ary heap: each node has four children, so the tree is shallower. What it lacks:

1. Changing a priority (decrease-key). The workaround is lazy deletion: enqueue the element again with the new priority and skip the stale copy when it comes out.
2. Order among equals: elements with the same priority come out in arbitrary order — the queue is not stable. If you need an order, add the insertion number to the priority.
3. Search: there is no Contains, and Remove only arrived in .NET 9 and costs O(n).

A max-heap is made with a reversed comparer. In Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) there is no PriorityQueue: you write your own binary heap over an array or use a SortedSet — more on it below.
cards.deep:
The 4-ary heap. Node i has its parent at (i − 1) / 4 and children at 4i + 1 … 4i + 4. There are log₄ n levels — half as many as in a binary heap — so moving up during Enqueue is shorter. Moving down during Dequeue compares up to four children per level, but they sit next to each other in memory — fewer cache misses. The asymptotics are the same, O(log n).

Building in O(n). The constructor from a collection and EnqueueRange into an empty queue do not insert one by one (O(n log n)); they build the heap bottom-up in O(n): most nodes are near the bottom and do not have far to sink. EnqueueDequeue (.NET 6) pushes and pops the minimum in a single sift — handy for “the best k”: keep a min-heap of k elements, and the worst of the best is always at the root.

Enumeration. UnorderedItems yields the elements in array order, not by priority. Sorted output only comes from successive Dequeue calls, O(n log n).

Your own heap in Unity. A binary heap over T[] with manual growth is about 40 lines and allocates nothing after warm-up. SortedSet<(int priority, int id)> is shorter to write and supports decrease-key (remove and insert again), but every Add is a new tree node on the heap, that is, garbage for the GC.

cards.q: What is true about PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>? Select all.
options: Peek is O(1), Dequeue is O(log n)
Unity has it out of the box since 2021.2
You cannot change the priority of an element in the queue: you enqueue a copy and skip the stale one
Elements with equal priority come out in insertion order
To get the maximum out, you pass a reversed comparer
cards.explain: The minimum sits at the root — Peek is O(1), and Dequeue sinks the new root through the height of the tree — O(log n). There is no decrease-key, hence lazy deletion. A max-heap is a Comparer with b.CompareTo(a). Unity does not have the class: it arrived in .NET 6, and Unity is .NET Standard 2.1. Equal priorities come out in arbitrary order: a heap is not stable.

cards.title: SortedSet, SortedDictionary, SortedList
cards.body:
SortedSet<T> is a red-black tree: a binary search tree (smaller to the left, larger to the right) that recolours and rotates nodes on inserts and deletes so that the height stays at most 2·log₂(n + 1). So Add, Remove, Contains are O(log n) in the worst case, not just on average. Min and Max are O(log n): a walk down to the outermost node. Enumeration goes in ascending order. GetViewBetween(lo, hi) returns the range [lo, hi] as a view without copying — that is how you find “the smallest element not less than x”.

The price: every node is an object on the managed heap, so every Add allocates, and the walk down causes cache misses. The set stores no duplicates: Add returns false, and elements with CompareTo == 0 count as the same. .NET has no multiset — you build one as a SortedDictionary<T, int> “value → how many times” or attach a unique id to each value.

SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> is the same tree over keys, O(log n). SortedList<TKey, TValue> is the opposite: two sorted arrays. Lookup is a binary search, O(log n), but inserting and removing in the middle is O(n), a shift. In return it is compact and offers access by position, Keys[i]. It suits data loaded once and then only read.
cards.deep:
Why the height is logarithmic. The red-black rules: a red node has no red children, and every path from the root to an empty leaf has the same number of black nodes. So the longest path (alternating black and red) is at most twice as long as the shortest (black only), hence height ≤ 2·log₂(n + 1). An insert repairs the rules by recolouring and at most two rotations, a delete with at most three. An AVL tree is balanced more strictly: lookups are slightly faster, rotations more frequent.

The GetViewBetween view. A view is a window onto the same tree: changes to the set show up in it, and adding a value outside the range to the view throws. Min and Max of a view are O(log n). The view's Count may be recomputed by a walk — O(k), so do not call it in a loop. If lo is greater than hi, you get an ArgumentException.

An empty set. Min and Max on an empty SortedSet do not throw; they return default(T): for int that is 0, which is easy to mistake for an answer.

The comparer decides what “equal” means. new SortedSet<Enemy>(Comparer<Enemy>.Create((a, b) => a.Hp.CompareTo(b.Hp))) silently refuses a second enemy with the same health. Hence the trick with an (Hp, Id) tuple: tuples compare field by field, left to right.

cards.q: A Unity project. Ability timers: every frame you need the one that fires next, and when a unit dies its timer is cancelled by id. Up to 10⁴ timers. What do you use?
options: SortedSet<(float time, int id)> plus a dictionary id → time: Min, Add and Remove are O(log n), and Unity has all of it
PriorityQueue<int, float>
A List<(float time, int id)> sorted after every insert
A Dictionary<int, float> id → time and a scan over all values to find the minimum
cards.explain: Three operations are needed: the minimum, an insert, and removing an arbitrary element. A red-black tree does all three in O(log n). The dictionary tells you the time a timer is stored with, so that you remove exactly the (time, id) tuple; the id in the tuple tells apart timers with the same time.

wrong.1: Unity does not have it (.NET 6+), and even in .NET a timer can only be cancelled by a scan — Remove arrived in .NET 9 and costs O(n).
wrong.2: Sorting after every insert is O(n log n) per operation. Even inserting in the right place with BinarySearch and Insert is O(n) because of the shift.
wrong.3: Insert and cancel are O(1), but finding the minimum scans every timer, O(n) every frame.

cards.title: LinkedList<T>, BitArray, and what .NET does not have
cards.body:
LinkedList<T> is a circular doubly linked list: every LinkedListNode<T> knows its neighbours, and inside the list the head’s previous node is the tail (from the outside, First.Previous still returns null). Inserting and removing by node — AddFirst, AddLast, AddAfter, Remove(node) — is O(1). But finding a node is a scan: Find and Remove(value) are O(n), and there is no index. Every node is a separate heap object: about 48 bytes per int versus 4 in an array, an allocation per insert and cache misses on traversal. The list pays off when the nodes are kept elsewhere, for example in a dictionary: that is how an LRU cache works.

BitArray is bits packed into an int[]: n/8 bytes versus n for a bool[]; Get and Set are O(1), and And, Or, Xor work on the whole array at once.

What the .NET standard library does not have: a deque — a double-ended queue, Deque<T> (replaced by LinkedList<T> at the cost of allocations, or by your own circular buffer); a multiset or a multimap; a direct “nearest above or below” on SortedSet — only via GetViewBetween; a trie and a disjoint-set union. In an interview you write these by hand — and that is fine.

cards.title: Unity: what .NET Standard 2.1 has and what it lacks
cards.body:
Unity 2021.2 and later compiles scripts as C# 9 against the .NET Standard 2.1 profile (or .NET Framework 4.x). Available: List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue, Stack, LinkedList, SortedSet, SortedDictionary, SortedList, BitArray, (int, int) tuples, HashCode, Span<T>, ArrayPool<T>, the dictionary’s TryAdd, TryDequeue and TryPop.

Missing is whatever came later: PriorityQueue (.NET 6), BitOperations (.NET Core 3.0; in Unity use math.countbits, math.lzcnt, math.tzcnt from Unity.Mathematics), CollectionsMarshal (.NET 5), Random.Shared and List<T>.EnsureCapacity (.NET 6). If you reach for PriorityQueue in a Unity interview, say that Unity lacks it and what you will use instead.

Jobs and Burst have their own collections from the com.unity.collections package: NativeArray, NativeList, NativeHashMap, NativeHashSet, NativeQueue. The memory lives outside the managed heap, elements must be unmanaged types, and you free it with Dispose(). More in the next lesson.
cards.code:
#if NET6_0_OR_GREATER
var open = new PriorityQueue<int, int>();           // .NET 6+
#else
var open = new SortedSet<(int priority, int id)>(); // Unity: .NET Standard 2.1
#endif

pairs: O(log n): the new root sinks
O(log n): a walk to the outermost node
O(1): the node is already known
