cards.title: struct or class: nodes and pairs
cards.body:
A class is a reference type: an object on the managed heap (on 64-bit, a 16-byte header plus the fields), the variable holds a reference, and assignment copies the reference. A struct is a value type: the data lives right in the variable, field or array slot, and assignment or passing to a method copies the whole value.

Hence the rule for interview problems. Small data — a cell, a “distance and vertex” pair, a segment — should be a readonly struct: a Cell[] array is contiguous in memory, with no separate object per element and no work for the GC. Nodes that point at each other (a tree, a list, a graph) are a class: a struct cannot hold a field of its own type. Or skip objects altogether and use indices into arrays: int[] left, right instead of references.

The copy trap: var c = cells[i]; c.X++; changes a copy, and the array element stays as it was. With a List<Cell>, list[i].X = 5 does not even compile: the indexer returns a copy. That is why structs in solutions are made immutable.

cards.title: Dictionary keys: IEquatable, tuples and boxing
cards.body:
Dictionary and HashSet compare keys through EqualityComparer<T>.Default. If the struct implements IEquatable<T>, its Equals(T) is called directly. If not, it is Equals(object), and the key gets boxed: a copy of the struct goes to the heap as an object, on every comparison. On top of that, the default ValueType.Equals and GetHashCode are slow and may not hash every field. The result is garbage on every lookup and a poor spread across buckets.

Three good keys for a grid cell:

1. The tuple (int x, int y): ValueTuple already implements IEquatable and a decent GetHashCode. The shortest option with no boxing.
2. Your own struct with IEquatable<Cell> and GetHashCode via HashCode.Combine.
3. A single number: y * width + x as an int or ((long)x << 32) | (uint)y as a long. This is the fastest, and if the grid size is known you need no dictionary at all — a bool[width * height] will do.

Bad keys: Tuple<int, int> (a class — an object per key) and the string $"{x},{y}" (a new string and format parsing on every lookup).

cards.q: Which keys for a HashSet of visited cells create no garbage on every lookup? Select all.
options: (int x, int y)
struct Cell without IEquatable<Cell>
y * width + x
Tuple.Create(x, y)
readonly struct Cell : IEquatable<Cell>
cards.explain: A tuple and a struct with IEquatable are compared through Equals(T) without boxing, and an int is just a number. A struct without IEquatable goes through Equals(object) and is boxed on every comparison. Tuple<int, int> is a class: an object for every key you create. A string is a new string on every lookup.

cards.title: Span<T> and stackalloc: counters off the heap
cards.body:
stackalloc allocates an array on the stack of the current method: the memory is released on return, the GC does not know about it, and nothing is allocated on the heap. With Span<T> it is safe code, no unsafe needed: Span<int> counts = stackalloc int[26]; is a letter counter for zero bytes of garbage.

Span<T> is a window onto contiguous memory: an array, a slice of one, a string (ReadOnlySpan<char>), the stack. Slice and AsSpan do not copy: s.AsSpan(1, 3) instead of s.Substring(1, 3) — no new string.

Limits. The stack is small (typically 1 MB per thread), so stackalloc is only for small sizes known in advance: 26 letters, 256 bytes, 64 neighbours; for an n that comes from the input, use a pool, covered next. Span is a ref struct: it cannot go into a class field, be captured by a lambda, or live across await or yield. The documentation treats the contents of stackalloc memory as undefined: if you need zeros, call Clear(). Unity has Span since 2021.2.

cards.title: ArrayPool<T>: a large buffer without garbage
cards.body:
When you need a buffer of input size n (10⁵–10⁶ elements), and often at that — once a frame or per request — new int[n] every time produces a lot of garbage. ArrayPool<T>.Shared hands arrays out again and again, and it comes with three rules:

1. Rent(n) returns an array of length at least n (usually rounded up to a power of two) — work with the first n elements, not with Length.
2. The array is not cleared: it holds the previous owner’s data. If you need zeros, use Array.Clear or Fill.
3. Return goes in finally; after returning, do not touch the array and never return it twice.

A common pairing: small size — stackalloc, large — the pool. Unity has ArrayPool (.NET Standard 2.1), but in an interview the simpler answer is often “a buffer in a class field, reused every frame” — also zero allocations, and no rental rules.

cards.title: Hidden allocations
cards.body:
Code without a single new can still produce garbage. What allocates on the heap:

LINQ. Where, Select, OrderBy create iterator objects, ToList and ToArray create new collections, and OrderBy also copies the data and costs O(n log n) where a single pass would do.
Closures. A lambda that captures a local variable or this creates an object for the captured state and a new delegate on every call of the method. A lambda without captures is cached by the compiler and does not allocate.
params. Log(params object[] args) is a new array per call, and every number in it is boxed as well.
Strings. +, Substring, ToString, interpolation — a new string; s += x in a loop is O(n²) copying, use a StringBuilder instead. In C# 9 (Unity), $"{hp}" with a number goes through string.Format and boxes hp.
Boxing. A struct converted to object or to an interface is copied to the heap. The sneakiest case is foreach over an interface. The enumerator of List<T> is a struct, and foreach over the List<T> itself creates no garbage. But foreach over a variable of type IEnumerable<T> gets the enumerator through the interface — boxed.
Iterators. A method with yield return is an object per call.
cards.code:
var alive = enemies.Where(e => e.Hp > 0).ToList(); // an iterator and a new list
int limit = 10;
enemies.Find(e => e.Hp < limit);    // captures limit: an object and a delegate per call
string s = "HP: " + hp;             // a new string
Debug.LogFormat("{0} {1}", x, y);   // params object[] and boxing of x, y
IEnumerable<Enemy> seq = enemies;
foreach (var e in seq) { }          // enumerator through the interface — boxed
foreach (var e in enemies) { }      // List<T>.Enumerator is a struct, 0 B
cards.deep:
Delegates from methods. Before C# 11, list.Find(IsAlive) creates a new delegate on every method group conversion, even for a static method. C# 11 caches the delegate for a static method, but Unity is C# 9: keep the delegate in a static readonly field. The static modifier on a lambda (C# 9) forbids captures at compile time — a handy safety net.

Unity APIs that return new arrays. Physics.RaycastAll and OverlapSphere return a new array on every call; RaycastNonAlloc and OverlapSphereNonAlloc write into your buffer. GetComponents<T>() is a new array, while the GetComponents(List<T>) overload fills the list you pass. gameObject.tag == "Enemy" creates a string, CompareTag("Enemy") does not.

How to find them. The Profiler’s GC Alloc column, plus Deep Profile mode to see the call that allocates. In .NET, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() before and after a piece of code, and BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser] in performance tests.

cards.q: This Update runs every frame; seen is a HashSet<(int, int)> field, enemies is a List<Enemy>. One line creates heap garbage on every call. Tap it.
cards.explain: foreach over a variable of type IEnumerable<Enemy> calls GetEnumerator through the interface, and the List<Enemy>.Enumerator struct gets boxed — an object every frame. Everything else is clean: Clear keeps the capacity, stackalloc is the stack, the tuple is a value, and foreach over the List<T> itself uses the struct enumerator. HashSet.Add allocates only when the set runs out of capacity — after the first few frames it has enough.

cards.title: Recursion and the thread stack
cards.body:
Every method call pushes a frame onto the thread stack: the return address, arguments, local variables — tens or hundreds of bytes. The stack is small: typically 1 MB per thread on Windows, sometimes more on other platforms, but of the same order. A depth of thousands or tens of thousands of calls is fine; a million is not.

Where it bites: a recursive depth-first search over a 1000×1000 grid. If the whole map is solid land or one long snaking corridor, the depth reaches 10⁶. That is a StackOverflowException, and in .NET it cannot be caught: try/catch will not help, the process terminates. In Unity the game or the editor crashes. C# does not promise to turn tail recursion into a loop.

The cure is an explicit stack: a Stack<T> on the heap instead of the call stack. The memory is the same, O(n) in the worst case, but the heap is large, and the traversal order stays depth-first. If order does not matter (flood fill, counting islands), a Queue<T> works too — breadth-first search. In an interview, say it out loud: “recursion is shorter, but for 10⁶ cells I would use an explicit stack”.

cards.q: A Unity game counts islands on a 2000×2000 map with a recursive depth-first search. On a 100×100 test map everything worked. What happens on the big map, where almost everything is land?
options: A stack overflow: the game crashes, and a try/catch around the call does not save it
It will be slower but finish: the traversal is still O(n)
A StackOverflowException is thrown — we catch it and switch to breadth-first search
The GC frees old stack frames, and the traversal carries on
cards.explain: On solid land the recursion depth reaches 4·10⁶ calls, while the stack is on the order of a megabyte. A StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET: the process terminates. Time has nothing to do with it — the stack memory runs out. The way out is an explicit Stack<T> or a breadth-first search with a Queue<T>.

wrong.1: O(n) is indeed fine for time, but it is not time that breaks, it is stack memory: a depth of 4·10⁶ calls.
wrong.2: This exception cannot be caught in .NET: the process terminates before control reaches the catch.
wrong.3: The thread stack is not the managed heap, and the GC does not manage it. Frames live until their call returns.

cards.title: GC in Unity: Boehm and “0 B per frame”
cards.body:
Unity runs the Boehm–Demers–Weiser collector on both Mono and IL2CPP. How it differs from the .NET (CoreCLR) collector:

No generations. In .NET short-lived garbage is cheap: the young generation is collected quickly and often. Boehm marks the entire managed heap every time, so the cost of a collection grows with the heap size, not with the amount of garbage.
No compaction. Objects do not move: the heap fragments, grows, and rarely gives memory back to the OS.
Stops the world. While marking runs, scripts wait. Incremental mode (on by default in Player Settings) slices the marking across frames: the spike is smaller, but the total work is the same, plus the cost of write barriers.

Hence the norm: code that runs every frame allocates 0 bytes — the GC Alloc column in the Profiler. How to get there: collections and buffers in fields, Clear() instead of new, capacity up front, object pools, structs, no LINQ and no closures in Update. One-off allocations while a level loads are fine.
cards.deep:
Conservativeness. Boehm scans stacks conservatively: any machine word that looks like an object’s address keeps that object alive. So a “dead” object sometimes survives a collection — correctness is unaffected, but memory can be held longer than you expect.

Control from code. UnityEngine.Scripting.GarbageCollector.GCMode lets you switch collection off during a fight and back on at a loading screen — only if the fight allocates almost nothing, otherwise the heap grows without bound. GarbageCollector.incrementalTimeSliceNanoseconds sets the per-frame slice of incremental collection. An explicit GC.Collect() belongs to pauses and scene changes, not to the game loop.

Compared with .NET. In CoreCLR an object in generation 0 that dies before a collection costs almost nothing: the collector copies only the survivors. So “do not allocate” on a server is about throughput, while in Unity it is about frame spikes. In an interview it is worth saying why the rule is stricter in Unity.

cards.title: NativeArray, Jobs and Burst: when they fit
cards.body:
When there really is a lot of data — thousands of agents, a direction field on a 512×512 grid (262,144 cells), hundreds of path searches per frame — Unity has a route around the managed heap. NativeArray<T> is memory outside the GC, and its elements must be unmanaged structs. Jobs spread work across cores (IJobParallelFor splits a range of indices). Burst compiles such a job into vectorized machine code and gives a several-fold speed-up.

The price: manual Dispose() (or a leak that the editor will warn about), allocators (Temp — within a frame, TempJob — up to four frames, Persistent — as long as needed), and no classes, strings or managed arrays inside a job.

In an interview you write the algorithm on plain arrays first. Jobs and Burst answer the question “what if there are 10,000 units?”: “the data goes into a NativeArray, the traversal into a Burst job, and I read the result next frame”. Dragging them into a whiteboard solution when nobody asked is overkill.

cards.title: C# 9 in Unity: what is missing
cards.body:
Unity compiles scripts as C# 9. Newer syntax that feels natural after .NET 8 will not compile in a Unity interview:

C# 10: record struct, file-scoped namespace X;, global using, interpolated strings without boxing.
C# 11: the unsigned shift >>> (in C# 9, (int)((uint)x >> k)), list patterns is [var first, ..], raw strings """, required, generic math (static abstract in interfaces), cached delegates for static methods.
C# 12: collection expressions int[] a = [1, 2, 3]; (in C# 9, new[] { 1, 2, 3 }), primary constructors on classes.

What C# 9 does have: target-typed new(), is not null, and and or in patterns, switch expressions, static lambdas, tuples, local functions. init properties and positional record types only work if you declare an empty System.Runtime.CompilerServices.IsExternalInit class in the project — the Unity profile does not have it.

cards.q: Match the situation with the technique.
pairs: An array in a field, or ArrayPool
A grid cell key in a HashSet
An explicit Stack<T> instead of recursion
A tree node with references to children
A class, or indices into arrays

lessons.title: Reasoning out loud
lessons.sub: Seven steps on one problem: from clarifying the statement to complexity, what to say when stuck, and how game dev interviews differ

cards.title: What an algorithm interview assesses
cards.body:
The interviewer assesses not only the answer but the line of thought: how you clarify the problem, whether you see the naive solution and its cost, whether you find where it does extra work, whether you write clean code and check it yourself. A silent correct solution is worth less than one talked through: nobody can tell whether you understand it or remembered it. And while you reason out loud, the interviewer hears where you are and can nudge you in time.

One seven-step script fits any problem:

cards.title: Steps 1–2: clarify the statement, come up with examples
cards.body:
From here on every step uses the problem in the code above: does the array contain two equal numbers at most k apart. The first two or three minutes are questions. Not out of politeness: the answers shape the solution.

Sizes. What are n and k? That decides whether O(n·k) passes — by the 10⁸ operations per second rule from the first lesson.
Values. The range of numbers, negatives, duplicates, whether you need long.
Edges. An empty array, one element, k = 0, k ≥ n.
Output. What to return when there is no answer; one answer or all; may the input be modified.
Mode. All the data at once or a stream; how much memory is allowed.

Then 2–3 examples on the board: an ordinary one, an edge case, and one where it is easy to slip, such as a distance of exactly k. The examples are your future tests: in step 6 you dry-run the code on them. Out loud it sounds like this: “Do I understand correctly that the indices differ and k can be zero? Then for k = 0 the answer is always false.”

cards.q: Which questions about problem 219 are worth asking before you write code? Select all.
options: What the maximum n and k are
Whether k can be zero or larger than the array length
What to return for an empty array
Which IDE we will use
What the problem is called on LeetCode
cards.explain: n and k decide whether the O(n·k) brute force passes. k = 0 and k ≥ n are edge cases that change the answer and the loop bounds. What to return for an empty array is agreed on up front. The IDE and the problem’s name have no bearing on the solution.

cards.title: Steps 3–4: the naive solution, then the idea
cards.body:
Always name the naive solution out loud, even if you see a better one right away: it is your baseline and a guarantee that you will have something. You do not have to code it — the idea and the cost are enough: “for each i I check the next k elements — O(n·k); for n = k = 10⁵ that is 10¹⁰, it will not pass”. And ask: “should I write it, or go straight for something better?”

The idea comes from the question “what work am I repeating?”. For every i the brute force searches again for the same value nums[i] among the last k. But of all past occurrences of a value only the last one matters: if even it is more than k away, the earlier ones are further still. So a dictionary “value → last index” answers in O(1) on average.

State the invariant in advance — it is half the proof: “before step i, last holds, for each value, its last index within nums[0..i−1]”.

cards.title: Steps 5–6: code with the invariant, then a dry run
cards.body:
Write the code and comment out loud on meaning, not syntax: “here I check whether the same number was at most k back”, “here I update the last index — the invariant holds”. Names carry meaning: last, not d.

Then the dry run: take an example from the board and step through the code like a debugger, writing down the state after each step. That catches boundary and ordering mistakes better than rereading. On [1, 0, 1, 1], k = 1: i = 0 — store 1 → 0; i = 1 — store 0 → 1; i = 2 — the 1 was at 0, distance 2 > 1, update 1 → 2; i = 3 — the 1 was at 2, distance 1 ≤ 1 → true.

cards.q: A candidate dry-ran their code on [1, 0, 1, 1], k = 1 and got false, although indices 2 and 3 qualify. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The statement allows a distance of exactly k (|i − j| ≤ k), but the code demands strictly less. At i = 3: j = 2, i − j = 1, and 1 < 1 is false. That is exactly why the examples need a boundary case: a dry run on it catches the bug in half a minute.

cards.title: Step 7: complexity and improvements. When you are stuck
cards.body:
Give the complexity together with memory and caveats: “O(n) time on average — because of the dictionary; O(n) memory in the worst case, when all numbers differ”. Then say what can be improved: here memory can be capped at O(min(n, k)) by keeping only the last k numbers in a HashSet — a sliding window.

When you are stuck, do not go quiet — say what you are trying: “I see the brute force, I am looking for what it repeats”. Go back to the examples and work them by hand: the idea is often visible on paper. Simplify the problem: k = 1, a sorted array, a small n. Run through the signals of known techniques: lookup by exact value → hash table, sorted array → binary search. If nothing moves for several minutes, say honestly where you are stuck: asking for a hint beats silence.

Take the interviewer’s hint: restate it in your own words, check it on an example, build it into the solution, and say what changed in the complexity. If you disagree, do not argue — check it out loud on an example.
cards.deep:
Time. For 45 minutes a rough split is: 5 for the statement and examples, 5 for the naive solution and the idea, 15–20 for code, 5–10 for the dry run and fixes, and the rest for follow-up questions. If there is no code by the halfway mark, say that you are writing a simplified version and finish it: a working O(n²) beats an unfinished O(n).

What is expected of a senior or a lead. Trade-offs with numbers: “the dictionary is O(n) memory, the window is O(k); if k is small, the window wins”. Production follow-ups: the data does not fit in memory, arrives as a stream, the code is called from several threads, the team needs an API. And tests: which cases you would cover and why — empty, the k boundary, all equal, all different, maximum sizes.

Code as in a team. Clear names, early returns, no magic numbers, argument checks if they were agreed on. The interviewer is silently answering the question “would I want to review this code every day?”

cards.q: You have been staring at the problem silently for three minutes and cannot see an O(n) solution. What is the best thing to do?
options: Say the naive solution and its cost out loud, offer to start with it, and keep looking for what it repeats
Keep thinking silently until you find the optimal one
Start writing some code without explaining it
Ask for a different problem
cards.explain: The naive solution is a guaranteed result and a baseline. While you reason out loud, the interviewer sees your thinking and can help, and the question “what does the brute force repeat?” often leads to the idea by itself.

wrong.1: Silence is the worst option: the interviewer cannot see that you are thinking and cannot help. Every quiet minute looks like having no ideas.
wrong.2: Code without a plan usually gets erased. First the idea and its cost out loud, then code.
wrong.3: That is not how problems get solved — it counts against you right away. Better to show your thinking on this one.

cards.q: The interviewer hints: “What if you kept only the last k numbers instead of all of them?” What is the best response?
options: Restate the idea in your own words, check it on an example, and say that memory becomes O(min(n, k))
Say that the dictionary is already O(1) and carry on with your own approach
Silently rewrite the code to follow the hint
Agree and ask the interviewer whether the answer is right now
cards.explain: A hint is part of the conversation. Restating it shows you understood it, checking it on an example shows you do not take it on faith, and the new memory cost closes the question the hint was about.

wrong.1: The hint is about memory, not time: the dictionary holds all n values. Brushing it off means not hearing the question.
wrong.2: Rewriting is right, but not silently: the interviewer will not know whether you understood why.
wrong.3: Checking your code is your job. Dry-run an example yourself and say what you got.

cards.title: Game dev interviews
cards.body:
In game dev the problems often come “from the engine”: a path on a grid, the nearest enemies, an object pool, a ring buffer, layer masks. And behind them there is almost always a question about the frame: 16.7 ms at 60 FPS, 8.3 ms at 120, and your system gets only a part of it.

What it sounds like: “we check collisions between all pairs of bullets”. Checking all pairs for n = 2000 is 2·10⁶ checks per frame — more than the whole frame budget (~1.7·10⁶ simple operations, from the first lesson). The answer is a spatial grid: divide the world into cells the size of the check radius, drop the objects into cells in O(n), and compare each one only with objects in its own and the eight neighbouring cells. With an even distribution that is about O(n).

Other common topics: 0 B allocations in Update (the previous lesson); spreading work across frames — recompute paths not for all 1000 agents at once but 50 per frame; determinism for network games (float on different platforms); and the inevitable “what about a real game?” — name the profiler, the budget in milliseconds, and what you would measure.

cards.q: A Unity interview: “2000 bullets and 500 enemies; every frame you need to find the hits”. What do you answer?
options: Bullets × enemies is 10⁶ checks per frame, almost the whole budget. I will put the enemies into a spatial grid and check each bullet only against neighbouring cells
10⁶ is less than 10⁸, so the brute force is fine
For each bullet I will sort the enemies by distance and take the nearest
I will move the check into a coroutine so that Update does not slow down
cards.explain: The frame budget is about 1.7·10⁶ simple operations for everything, and the brute force alone eats 10⁶. The grid places the enemies in O(m) and leaves each bullet a few candidates from neighbouring cells: about O(n + m) in total.

wrong.1: 10⁸ is per second. Per frame at 60 FPS it is 60 times less, about 1.7·10⁶, and it is shared with the whole game.
wrong.2: Sorting for every bullet is O(n·m log m), even worse than the brute force.
wrong.3: A coroutine runs on the same main thread: the work is the same, only split across frames — and hits are needed every frame.

cards.q: You are solving problem 219 out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: what n and k are, whether k can be zero, what to return for an empty array
Write examples: [1, 2, 3, 1] with k = 3 and k = 2, plus a case with a distance of exactly k
Name the brute force: for each i check the next k — O(n·k), 10¹⁰ at 10⁵
Idea: of a number’s past occurrences only the last one matters — a dictionary “value → last index”
Write the code, stating the invariant: last holds each value’s last index to the left of i
Dry-run [1, 0, 1, 1], k = 1 step by step
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memory; improvement — a HashSet window of k elements
cards.explain: First agree on the statement and the examples, then the baseline and the idea, then the code with its invariant, a check on an example, and only at the end the complexity and improvements. The example with a distance of exactly k guards against the boundary bug in advance.

lessons.title: Common mistakes
lessons.sub: Overflow, boundaries, modifying a collection in a loop, strings and char, comparers — and how to check code by hand in a minute

cards.title: int overflow
cards.body:
int runs from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, about ±2.1·10⁹. By default C# computes unchecked: when a value crosses the limit it silently wraps around, int.MaxValue + 1 == int.MinValue. No exception — just a wrong answer.

Where it bites in interviews:

Sums. 10⁵ numbers up to 10⁹ add up to 10¹⁴ — sum in a long.
Products. long x = a * b; still overflows: the multiplication happens in int, and widening comes after. You need (long)a * b.
The middle. (lo + hi) / 2 overflows when lo + hi > int.MaxValue: on arrays larger than 2³⁰ elements or in a binary search over values up to 2·10⁹. The safe form is lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
Absolute value. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException, and -int.MinValue equals int.MinValue again.

checked { … } turns overflow into an exception — handy in tests, so the bug does not hide.
cards.code:
int a = 100_000, b = 100_000;
long wrong = a * b;              // 1410065408: multiplied in int, widened afterwards
long right = (long)a * b;        // 10000000000

int lo = 1_500_000_000, hi = 2_000_000_000;
int bad = (lo + hi) / 2;         // a negative number
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;    // 1750000000

checked { int boom = int.MaxValue + a; }  // OverflowException instead of a silent bug
cards.deep:
“Infinity” in distances. dist[v] = int.MaxValue as “not reached yet” — and dist[v] + w wraps into a negative number that looks like the best path. Either check dist[v] != int.MaxValue before adding, use int.MaxValue / 2, or use long.

Checking across the project. The CheckForOverflowUnderflow property in the .csproj makes checked the default — useful in debug builds and tests. Then, where overflow is intended (hashes, random number generators), write unchecked.

Where to get more width. long goes up to 9.2·10¹⁸, ulong up to 1.8·10¹⁹. Beyond that there is System.Numerics.BigInteger (Unity has it too), but in an interview you are usually expected to notice the overflow and avoid it with a formula or by working modulo something.

cards.q: a[i] and b[i] are up to 10⁶, the length is up to 10⁵. On large inputs the sum sometimes comes out negative. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: a[i] * b[i] is up to 10¹², and the multiplication happens in int: the result wraps before it is ever added to the long. You need (long)a[i] * b[i]. The sum itself is up to 10¹⁷, which fits in a long.

cards.title: Off-by-one and half-open intervals
cards.body:
The off-by-one error is the most common one in interviews. The cure is to pick one convention for boundaries and stick to it across the whole solution.

Half-open [lo, hi): lo is included, hi is not. The length is hi − lo, an empty range is lo == hi, and halving gives [lo, mid) and [mid, hi) with no gaps or overlaps. This is how for (i = 0; i < n; i++), Span.Slice and most APIs work.
Closed [lo, hi]: both ends are included — hi = n − 1, a while (lo <= hi) loop, moves to mid + 1 and mid − 1, as in the binary search from the first lesson. A closed range [a, b] holds b − a + 1 elements, not b − a: that is how you count windows and iterations too.

Mixing conventions gives an infinite loop or a lost element. Another C# trap: the second argument of Substring(start, length), Slice, Array.Copy and GetRange is a length, not an end index as in Java or Python. The check is the boundary iterations: what happens on the first, on the last, and with n = 0.

cards.q: You need to go through every substring of length k in a string of length n. Which loop condition on the start i is right, and how many windows are there?
options: i <= n - k; n − k + 1 windows
i < n - k; n − k windows
i < n; n windows
i <= n - k + 1; n − k + 2 windows
cards.explain: The last window starts at n − k and ends at n − 1. The starts run from 0 to n − k inclusive, n − k + 1 of them. Check the edge case k = n: there is exactly one window, i = 0, and the condition 0 <= 0 lets it through.

wrong.1: It loses the last window, the one that starts at n − k. With k = n the loop does not run at all, although there is one window.
wrong.2: Windows that start after n − k run past the end of the string, and Substring throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
wrong.3: With i = n − k + 1 the window ends at index n — past the end of the string.

cards.title: Modifying a collection during foreach
cards.body:
The enumerators of List<T>, HashSet<T> and Dictionary remember the collection’s version number. Add and Remove change it, and the next step of foreach throws InvalidOperationException: “Collection was modified”. How to remove correctly:

1. list.RemoveAll(e => e.Hp <= 0) — one pass, O(n), order preserved.
2. A for loop from the end with RemoveAt(i): the indices of elements not yet visited do not shift. But every removal from the middle is a shift, O(n²) in the worst case.
3. From the end, swapping with the last element (the trick from the collections lesson) — O(1) per removal, order changes.
4. For a dictionary, collect the keys into a separate list, then remove them.

A forward for loop with RemoveAt(i) throws nothing but skips the next element: it moved into the removed one’s place while i moved on. “Then and now”: since .NET Core 3.0 you may call Remove and Clear on a Dictionary during foreach, but do not rely on it in .NET Framework or in Unity.

cards.q: How do you correctly remove dead enemies from a List<Enemy>? Select every correct way.
options: A for loop from the end with RemoveAt(i)
enemies.RemoveAll(e => e.Hp <= 0)
foreach over enemies with enemies.Remove(e) inside
A forward for loop with RemoveAt(i), without adjusting i
A loop from the end: put the last element in place of i and remove the last
cards.explain: Removing from the end does not shift what is still ahead. RemoveAll makes one pass and keeps the order. Swapping with the last element is O(1) per removal when order does not matter. foreach with Remove throws InvalidOperationException on the next step, and a forward loop without adjusting i skips the element that moved into the removed one’s place.

cards.title: Strings: ordinal comparison and culture
cards.body:
Some .NET string operations are culture-sensitive by default — they compare by the language rules of the current machine: CompareTo, string.Compare(a, b), StartsWith(string), EndsWith(string), IndexOf(string), and also Array.Sort and List.Sort on strings and OrderBy(s => s). Whereas ==, Equals, Contains(string) and IndexOf(char) are ordinal: they compare character codes.

Why that is a bug in an algorithm: the sort order depends on the machine, in the Turkish culture “I” and “i” are not an upper/lower case pair, and linguistic comparison is several times slower. Since .NET 5, Windows too uses the ICU library for culture, and, for example, "\r\n".IndexOf("\n") started returning −1 even though the character is there. In string problems, pass StringComparison.Ordinal or StringComparer.Ordinal explicitly.

cards.title: char and int
cards.body:
A char in C# is a 16-bit number, a UTF-16 code unit. That gives both tricks and traps.

Letter index: c - 'a' is an int from 0 to 25 if c is a lowercase Latin letter. Digit: '7' - '0' == 7. Back again: (char)('a' + k) — without the cast you get a number.
Arithmetic yields int: 'a' + 1 is 98, and Console.Write('a' + 1) prints 98. The expression is evaluated left to right, so "" + 'a' + 1 is "a1": the string comes first and everything is appended to it.
Not just Latin: char.IsLetter lets “é” through, and counts[c - 'a'] goes out of the bounds of an int[26]. Emoji and some CJK characters are two chars (a surrogate pair), so s.Length counts code units, not characters.

That is why “lowercase Latin only?” is a mandatory question at the clarification step. If not, use a Dictionary<char, int> or a dictionary keyed by code points.
cards.code:
int idx = 'k' - 'a';             // 10
int digit = '7' - '0';           // 7
char next = (char)('a' + 1);     // 'b'
Console.Write('a' + 1);          // 98 — the addition produced an int
Console.Write("" + 'a' + 1);     // a1 — the string comes first
Console.Write("😀".Length);      // 2: a surrogate pair

cards.q: What does Console.WriteLine('a' + 1 + "b") print?
options: a1b
bb
A compile error
cards.explain: The expression is evaluated left to right: 'a' + 1 adds a char and an int, giving the int 98. Then 98 + "b" is concatenation with a string: "98b". To get "bb" you need (char)('a' + 1) + "b".

wrong.1: "a1" would come out if the string were first. Here 'a' + 1 comes first, and that is arithmetic, not concatenation.
wrong.2: 'a' + 1 is the int 98, not the char 'b': without a (char) cast there is no letter.
wrong.3: It all compiles: char + int gives an int, and int + string gives a string.

cards.title: Sorting: comparers and stability
cards.body:
The a - b comparer is a classic bug. While the numbers are small it works, but the difference of numbers with large magnitudes overflows: 2·10⁹ − (−2·10⁹) does not fit in an int and turns negative, and the comparer lies about the order. The result is a wrong sort, and sometimes an exception saying “IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results”. The right way is a.CompareTo(b): it only compares, no subtraction.

Stability. Array.Sort and List<T>.Sort in .NET are an introspective sort: O(n log n) in the worst case, but unstable — elements with equal keys may swap places. If the original order of equals matters (events at the same time, players with the same score), there are two ways: LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy — stable, but they allocate; or add the original index to the key.

Several keys: compare by the first and, on a tie, by the second. Tuples do it for you: (a.Time, a.Id).CompareTo((b.Time, b.Id)).
cards.deep:
Introspective sort. It starts as a quicksort with a median-of-three pivot; ranges of up to 16 elements are finished with insertion sort; if the recursion depth exceeds about 2·log₂ n (bad pivots), it switches to heapsort. That is why the worst case is O(n log n) rather than the O(n²) of plain quicksort. .NET Framework has done this since 4.5; before that Array.Sort was a quicksort with a quadratic worst case.

API variants. Array.Sort(keys, items) sorts two arrays in parallel — keys and the data attached to them, with no tuples. Span<T>.Sort exists since .NET 5; Unity does not have it. Unity.Collections provides NativeArray<T>.Sort() for Jobs and Burst data.

Why LINQ is stable. OrderBy first computes the keys into a separate array and, on equal keys, compares the original positions. The price is arrays of keys and indices, an iterator and a delegate: hot code in Unity does not use it.

cards.q: Merging intervals. On tests with large-magnitude coordinates the result is sometimes wrong. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: x[0] − y[0] with x[0] = 2·10⁹ and y[0] = −2·10⁹ is 4·10⁹, which overflows into a negative: the comparer calls the larger number smaller, and the sort breaks. The rest of the code is right as long as the intervals are sorted by start. You need x[0].CompareTo(y[0]).

cards.title: Empty input, one element, recursion depth: a one-minute check
cards.body:
Before you say “done”, walk the code through a short list. It takes a minute and catches most interview bugs.

1. Empty input and a single element — will a[0], a[n − 1], res[res.Count − 1] blow up?
2. Two equal, all equal, all different.
3. Boundaries: the answer at the first and at the last position, a distance of exactly k, a condition like i <= n − k.
4. Signs and sizes: negatives, zero, maximum values — is int enough?
5. “Not found”: what is returned when the loop ends.
6. Recursion depth on the maximum input: up to 10⁶ on a 1000×1000 grid, and then you need an explicit stack (the C# and Unity lesson).

Do the dry run on the smallest non-trivial example and write the variables down in a column after each iteration — that shows both the boundaries and the order of operations. Tests in code are short checks for these cases.

cards.q: Match the bug with its fix.
pairs: RemoveAll or a loop from the end

lessons.title: Unit final: the method
lessons.sub: Estimate from constraints, pick a collection, find the bug and the allocation, explain out loud

cards.q: The statement: 1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵, values up to 10⁹, a 1 second limit. What complexity do you aim for before you even know the idea?
options: O(n log n) or better
O(n²): the loops are simple, it will fit
O(n · 10⁹): try every value
O(2ⁿ)
cards.explain: n log n ≈ 2·10⁵ · 18 ≈ 3.6·10⁶ — far below 10⁸. n² = 4·10¹⁰ — 400 times over budget. So you look for sorting, a hash table, one or two passes, or a binary search.

wrong.1: Simple loops win a few times over, but you are short by hundreds of times: 4·10¹⁰ versus 10⁸.
wrong.2: Trying values up to 10⁹ for every element is 2·10¹⁴ operations. The value range is not a size you can iterate over.
wrong.3: 2ⁿ works up to n ≈ 20, and here n is two hundred thousand.

cards.q: The limit is 1 second. Which solutions fit? Select all.
options: n ≤ 15, trying all permutations in O(n!)
n ≤ 22, trying all subsets in O(2ⁿ)
n ≤ 2000, an O(n²) solution
n, m ≤ 5000, an O(n·m) table
n ≤ 10⁵, an O(n²) solution
cards.explain: 2²² ≈ 4·10⁶, 2000² = 4·10⁶, 5000 · 5000 = 2.5·10⁷ — all under 10⁸. But 15! ≈ 1.3·10¹² — permutations only work up to n ≈ 10–11, and 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰.

cards.q: A matchmaking queue: take the player who has waited longest, and any player can leave the queue by id. Both operations must be O(1). What do you use?
options: A LinkedList<Player> and a Dictionary<int, LinkedListNode<Player>> id → node
Queue<Player>
A List<Player> with Add at the end and RemoveAt(0)
A PriorityQueue<Player, float> by join time
cards.explain: The longest-waiting player is the head of the list, First, O(1). Leaving by id: the dictionary hands over the node, and Remove(node) is O(1). New players go in with AddLast, also O(1). The price is a node object per player, which is justified here.

wrong.1: Taking the first is O(1), but you cannot remove a player from the middle of the queue except by rebuilding it, O(n).
wrong.2: RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list — O(n), and leaving by id is a linear search, O(n) as well.
wrong.3: Dequeue is O(log n), not O(1), removing by id is only possible by a scan (Remove in .NET 9 is O(n)), and Unity does not have this class.

cards.q: Update runs every frame, and units is a List<Unit>. One line creates heap garbage on every call. Tap it.
cards.explain: The lambda captures the local variable team: every Update call creates an object for the captured state and a new delegate. The for loop over a List<T> and the Vector3 arithmetic (a struct) produce no garbage. The fix is a loop instead of Exists, or team in a field and a delegate created once.

cards.task: Binary search for 66 in a sorted array of 12 elements. Step through the trace: the rig will stop twice and ask what the next check will be. Count how many comparisons it takes.

options: mid = 9 → 66 == 66 → return 9
asks.q: The candidates are [9..11]. What will the next check be?
asks.explain: mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 = 9 + 1 = 10: the middle of [9..11] is index 10, not 9. a[10] = 71 is greater than 66, so the answer is to the left, and the right part goes together with mid: hi = mid − 1 = 9.

options: mid = 9 → return 9
lo > hi → return -1
asks.q: One candidate is left, [9..9]. What next?
asks.explain: The while (lo <= hi) loop also runs when lo == hi: mid = 9, a[9] = 66 — found. Four comparisons in total, where a left-to-right scan would have made 10.

cards.q: How many comparisons does a binary search make in the worst case on a sorted array of 10⁶ elements — and how many does a linear scan make?
options: About 20 versus 10⁶
About 1000 versus 10⁶
About 500,000 versus 10⁶
About 20 versus 20
cards.explain: Every comparison discards half of the candidates, and 10⁶ can be halved about 20 times: log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20. In the worst case a linear scan looks at all 10⁶ elements.

wrong.1: 1000 is the square root of 10⁶. Binary search halves; it does not split into blocks of √n.
wrong.2: n/2 is the average case of a linear scan. Binary search discards half at every step, so it takes log₂ n steps.
wrong.3: Order does not help a linear scan: in the worst case it looks at all n elements.

cards.q: The function counts pairs i < j that sum to target; count maps a number to how many times it was seen. On [3, 3], target = 6 it returned 3, but there is one pair. Tap the line that is in the wrong place.
cards.explain: The invariant “the dictionary holds only elements to the left of the current one” is broken: x enters the counter before it looks for a partner, and with target = 2x it finds itself. On [3, 3] the first 3 pairs with itself (1), the second with both 3s (2), 3 in total instead of 1. Check first, insert after: the count[x] = c + 1 write has to move below the partner lookup.

cards.q: First Unique Character in a String (LeetCode #387): the index of the first character that occurs in the string exactly once. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: lowercase Latin only? What to return if there is none? How long is the string?
Examples: "leetcode" → 0, "loveleetcode" → 2, "aabb" → −1
Naive: for each character, recount it over the whole string — O(n²)
Idea: the brute force counts the same letters again and again — count them all once in an int[26]
Code: the first pass builds the counters, the second finds the first index with a count of 1
Dry-run "loveleetcode": l and o occur twice, v once
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory for 26 counters; in Unity — stackalloc and zero allocations
cards.explain: The same seven-step script. The question “Latin only?” decides everything here: it determines whether an int[26] is enough or a dictionary is needed.

cards.q: Code from .NET 8 is being ported to Unity (C# 9, .NET Standard 2.1). What will not compile? Select all.
options: var pq = new PriorityQueue<int, int>();
int h = x >>> 1;
Span<int> c = stackalloc int[26];
int hash = HashCode.Combine(x, y);
var seen = new HashSet<(int, int)>();
cards.explain: PriorityQueue arrived in .NET 6, the unsigned shift >>> in C# 11, collection expressions in C# 12. Span and stackalloc, HashCode and tuple keys are available in Unity: they are all part of .NET Standard 2.1 and C# 9.

cards.q: What is the complexity of this code?
options: O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n log² n)
O(n)
cards.explain: Sorting is O(n log n), then n binary searches at O(log n) each — another O(n log n). The steps come one after another and add up: O(n log n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).

wrong.1: There is no second loop over the array inside the loop: BinarySearch is O(log n), not O(n).
wrong.2: The logarithms would multiply if the binary search were nested inside the sort. Here the sort and the loop come one after another and add up.
wrong.3: One pass is O(n), but every step does a log n binary search, and the sort itself costs n log n.

units.title: Hash tables and prefix sums
units.blurb: Trade memory for time: Two Sum, duplicates, anagrams, prefix sums in a dictionary, a set as an accelerator and an array as a hash table. How Dictionary works in .NET and what GetHashCode costs on a struct.

lessons.title: Two Sum and the hash map reflex
lessons.sub: Trade memory for time: from O(n²) to a single pass

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Two Sum (LeetCode #1). Given an integer array nums and a number target, find two elements at different indices that add up to target and return their indices. On LeetCode there is exactly one answer, 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, and the numbers and target are at most 10⁹ in absolute value.

In an interview this problem tests a reflex, not whether you remember Two Sum. Signals that a hash map will help:

1. For each element you look for a “partner” by exact value: the complement of a sum, the same number, the same anagram.
2. The question sounds like “have I seen this before?” or “how many times?”.
3. The array is unsorted, and sorting is expensive or not allowed: you need the original indices.

All three are here: the partner of x is exactly target − x, the question is “have I seen it?”, and the answer is indices.

cards.q: Which problems call for the same “have I seen this?” → hash map reflex? Select all.
options: Does the array contain a number that appears at least twice
Does the array contain two numbers whose difference is k
The first non-repeating character of a string
The largest sum of consecutive elements
The k-th largest number in the array
cards.explain: A duplicate is “have I seen it before?” (signal 2). Difference k is a partner by exact value: for x look up x − k and x + k (signal 1). The first non-repeating character is “how many times?”: counters, then a second pass. The largest consecutive sum and the k-th largest are not about finding a partner by value: other techniques work there (a greedy pass, a heap, quickselect), covered in later units.

cards.title: The naive solution and its cost
cards.body:
The brute-force solution checks every pair i < j. There are n(n − 1)/2 pairs, so the time is O(n²) and the extra memory is O(1).

Put numbers on it. For n = 10⁵ there are 10⁵ · (10⁵ − 1) / 2 ≈ 5·10⁹ pairs. By the rule from the first unit, ~10⁸ simple operations per second, that is about 50 seconds against a 1–2 second limit: 25–50 times too slow.

A square grows fast: 10 times more data means 100 times more work. In an interview, always name the naive solution and its cost — it is your baseline.

cards.q: On LeetCode, Two Sum has n ≤ 10⁴. How many comparisons does the naive solution make in the worst case, and what follows from that?
options: ≈ 5·10⁷ — fits the time limit, but the interviewer will ask for something faster than O(n²)
≈ 5·10⁹ — too slow, a different solution is required
≈ 10⁴ — instant, nothing to improve
cards.explain: n(n − 1)/2 for n = 10⁴ is about 5·10⁷: by the same rule (~10⁸ operations per second) that is a fraction of a second. That is why brute force passes on LeetCode, and the problem statement asks: can you do better than O(n²)? That step is exactly what the interview is waiting for.

wrong.1: 5·10⁹ is for n = 10⁵. With 10 times smaller n the work is 100 times smaller: it is a square.
wrong.2: 10⁴ is the number of elements, but we compare pairs. There are about n²/2 of them.

cards.title: What work am I repeating?
cards.body:
Look at the inner loop: for each nums[i] it searches for one specific value, target − nums[i] — and it starts over every time, scanning. Finding a value in an unsorted array is O(n). In a hash map it is O(1) on average.

Turn the problem around: walk left to right and for the current x ask “have I met target − x?”. Keep everything seen so far in a Dictionary<int, int>. The dictionary stores not “what was there” but “where it was”: the key is the number, the value is its index.

Invariant: before step i the dictionary holds exactly the elements nums[0..i−1]. So check first, then insert — otherwise x finds itself. Time O(n), memory O(n): we trade memory for time.

In a game: the same trade-off applies when an object is looked up by id with List.Find every frame — a Dictionary<int, Enemy> keyed by id answers in O(1).

cards.q: Assemble the single-pass solution.
cards.explain: We look for the complement need = target − nums[i]. TryGetValue answers “is it there?” and hands over the index j in a single lookup — j comes before i, so the answer is { j, i }. Then we remember the current number: seen[nums[i]] = i. The indexer, not Add: Add throws ArgumentException on a repeated key, for example on [1, 1, 5] with target = 10.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 8, 2, 11, 7, 5], target = 9. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the dictionary on screen, not from the whole array.

options: seen[2] = 2
return new[] { 2, 4 }
return new[] { 0, 2 }
asks.q: x = 2, looking for 7. The array does contain a 7. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The code only sees the dictionary, and so far it holds 3 and 8. The 7 is further right and not visited yet, so we store 2 → 2. The 7 will find the pair itself when we reach it: by then its partner 2 is already in the dictionary.

options: seen[7] = 4
return new[] { 2, 4 }
return new[] { 1, 4 }
asks.q: x = 7, looking for 2. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 2 is in the dictionary at index 2 — TryGetValue finds it and returns j = 2. We return { j, i } = { 2, 4 }: the partner index first, then the current one. No need to store 7 any more.

cards.q: On nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 this code returns [0, 0]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The number goes into the dictionary before the check, which breaks the invariant “the map holds only what is left of i”. At i = 0: seen[3] = 0, we look up 6 − 3 = 3 — and find the element itself, answer [0, 0]. This is the classic target = 2x trap. The fix is the order: TryGetValue first, then seen[nums[i]] = i.

cards.q: The dictionary solution (check first, then insert). What is true? Select all.
options: On [3, 3], target = 6 it returns [0, 1]
Negative numbers and zero need no changes at all
On a repeat, seen[x] = i overwrites the index, and the answer can get lost because of it
With |nums[i]|, |target| ≤ 10⁹ the difference target − nums[i] overflows int
If there is no pair, the loop ends and you return what was agreed on: an empty array or an exception
cards.explain: Duplicates: at i = 1 we look up 3, and 3 → 0 is already there — answer [0, 1]. The dictionary does not care what the keys are: negatives and zero just work. Overwriting is safe: any index of that value makes a valid pair, and a pair of two equal numbers is caught before the overwrite. No overflow: |target − x| ≤ 2·10⁹, and int.MaxValue = 2 147 483 647. If the numbers in the statement are wider, compute in long. What to return without a pair is a question for the interviewer at the very start.

cards.title: Variations: what changes in the statement
cards.body:
The array is sorted, memory O(1) (Two Sum II, #167; indices there are 1-based). No dictionary needed — two pointers moving towards each other: if the sum is too small, move the left one; if too large, the right one. A move loses nothing: if nums[lo] + nums[hi] < target, then nums[lo] gives a too-small sum with any smaller right element as well. O(n) time, O(1) memory. Details are in the two pointers unit.

How many pairs sum to target. A dictionary “value → how many times seen”: at each x first add count[target − x] to the answer, then increment count[x]. Still O(n).

A stream: add(x) and find(value) (Two Sum III, #170). If add is frequent and find is rare, keep counters: add is O(1), find walks the distinct keys, O(n); for x == value − x you need a count ≥ 2. If it is the other way round, keep a set of all pairwise sums: add is O(n), find is O(1), but memory is O(n²). Which operation is more frequent — ask the interviewer.

No index needed, only the fact (Contains Duplicate, #217): a HashSet<int>, and Add returns false if the number was already there.

cards.q: You solve Two Sum out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is there always an answer, can one element be used twice, what to return, what are n and the values
Name the brute force over pairs: O(n²), about 5·10⁹ comparisons for n = 10⁵
Idea: the brute force keeps searching for target − x; a “value → index” dictionary answers in O(1)
Write the code while stating the invariant: the map holds everything left of i
Run a small example out loud, such as [3, 2, 4] with target = 6
State the complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memory
Edge cases: no pair, duplicates, target = 2x, negative numbers
cards.explain: First agree on the statement, then the baseline (brute force and its cost), then the idea and the code, a check on an example, and only then complexity and edge cases. The [3, 2, 4] example also checks the 3 + 3 trap.

cards.title: Why a dictionary is O(1), and when it is not
cards.body:
The O(1) of a Dictionary is on average. A key lands in a bucket by its hash, and if keys are spread evenly, a bucket holds one or two entries.

Growth. When it runs out of room, the dictionary allocates arrays roughly twice as large and re-places every entry — that insert costs O(n). It happens rarely, so overall it is amortized O(1) per insert. If n is known in advance, set the capacity and there will be no re-placing.

The worst case is every key in one bucket: lookup is O(n), and Two Sum degrades to O(n²). For struct keys implement IEquatable<T> and GetHashCode, otherwise comparisons are slow and hashes are worse.
cards.code:
// n is known in advance: capacity up front, no re-placing
var seen = new Dictionary<int, int>(nums.Length);
cards.deep:
Internals. Dictionary<TKey,TValue> in .NET is two arrays: buckets (the number of the first entry in a chain) and entries (structs: hash, next, key, value). Lookup: key hash → bucket hash % buckets.Length → walk the next chain comparing the hash and Equals. The size is a prime; when full, the new size is a prime at least twice as large, and every entry is rehashed. The constructor without a capacity allocates no arrays — they appear on the first insert.

Collisions. The hash of an int is the number itself, so keys that all land in one bucket for a known table size can be picked on purpose. String hashing in .NET Core and .NET 5+ is randomized per process — a defence against collision attacks (hash flooding). So string.GetHashCode() must not be saved to disk, sent over the network, or used for determinism. In .NET Framework it is deterministic by default — code that relied on that breaks after migrating. The documentation does not guarantee the enumeration order of a dictionary either.

Struct keys. Without IEquatable<T> the default comparer calls Equals(object) — boxing on every comparison, and the default ValueType.Equals and GetHashCode may use reflection and may not take every field into account. Implement IEquatable<T> and GetHashCode; HashCode.Combine exists since .NET Core 2.1 and .NET Standard 2.1 (in Unity since 2021.2), but it is randomized per process too. The tuple (int, int) already implements IEquatable.

Allocations. new Dictionary is an object plus two arrays on the heap, and every re-placing means new arrays while the old ones become garbage. In hot code keep the dictionary in a field and call Clear(): the capacity stays, no new allocations.

Unity. The garbage collector is Boehm: no generations and no compaction, a collection walks the whole managed heap. Incremental mode spreads it across frames but does not cancel it. A new dictionary in Update is garbage every frame, so reuse it. Managed collections are unavailable in Jobs and Burst: NativeHashMap<TKey,TValue> from the com.unity.collections package — key and value are unmanaged, the key implements IEquatable<TKey>, memory lives outside the managed heap (Allocator.Temp, TempJob, Persistent) and is released with Dispose(). For writing from a parallel job use NativeParallelHashMap and its AsParallelWriter().

cards.q: Match the condition with the technique.
pairs: Two pointers moving towards each other
How many pairs sum to target
A stream: add often, find rarely

lessons.title: Counters and group keys
lessons.sub: Valid Anagram and Group Anagrams: int[26] instead of a dictionary, a group key and the Unicode trap

cards.title: Valid Anagram: the problem and its signals
cards.body:
Valid Anagram (LeetCode #242). Given strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s: the same letters in the same quantities, in any order. On LeetCode the length is up to 5·10⁴ and only lowercase English letters appear; the follow-up asks: what if the input contains Unicode characters?

The signal from the previous lesson is the question “how many times?”. An anagram is equality of multisets: “aab” and “abb” are built from the same letters a and b, yet they are not anagrams. So a HashSet (“seen or not”) is not enough here — you need a counter, “character → how many times”.

The first solution that comes to mind is to sort both strings and compare them: anagrams have the same sorted letters. Time is O(k log k) for strings of length k, memory is O(k): two character arrays plus two more strings.

cards.q: In which problems is a set not enough, so you need a “how many times” counter? Select all.
options: Can a ransom note be built from the letters of a magazine, each magazine letter used at most once
Does the array contain at least one duplicate
Do two words have the same set of distinct letters
Does every number in the array appear exactly twice
The first non-repeating character of a string
cards.explain: The note needs each letter as many times as it appears in the note — that is a quantity, not a fact. “Exactly twice” and “non-repeating” are about quantities too: a counter, and for the first non-repeating character a second pass over the string as well. A duplicate and a set of distinct letters are “seen or not” questions: a HashSet is enough, and it reports the duplicate by itself — Add returns false.

cards.title: A counter: int[26] instead of a dictionary
cards.body:
A counter in one pass: add 1 for every character of s, subtract 1 for every character of t. Invariant: after the pass, counts[c] = (how many times c occurs in s) − (how many times in t). The strings are anagrams exactly when all counters are zero. Time is O(k) instead of O(k log k).

The key here is a character, and the alphabet is small and dense: 'a'..'z'. Then no hash table is needed — an array indexed by c - 'a' replaces it: 26 counters, 104 bytes, no hashing and no buckets. A Dictionary<char, int> gives the same O(k), but every counts[c]++ is a hash plus two lookups (read and write), and the dictionary itself is an object and two arrays on the heap. On the same strings the array is several times faster.

No heap at all: Span<int> counts = stackalloc int[26] is an array on the method's stack — zero allocations, nothing for the garbage collector to collect. This is the trick from the first unit: no unsafe, and in Unity since 2021.2 (.NET Standard 2.1). The documentation does not guarantee the contents of stackalloc memory, so clear it before counting: counts.Clear(). The price is a set of restrictions: stackalloc memory lives only until the method returns, and the Span itself cannot be stored in a class field or captured in a lambda.

In a game: the same trick works whenever the key is a small dense number: items by (int)ItemType, units by team number — an array instead of a dictionary.

cards.q: Assemble Valid Anagram with a counter in a single pass.
cards.explain: Different lengths mean false right away; it also allows a single loop over a shared index i. A character of s adds, a character of t subtracts, and the index c − 'a' maps 'a'..'z' to 0..25. Any non-zero counter at the end is a difference in quantity. Without subtracting 'a' the index would be 97..122 — outside an array of 26. c > 0 would also do: with equal lengths the counters sum to 0, so if any is non-zero, some is positive.

cards.title: Group Anagrams: invent a group key
cards.body:
Group Anagrams (LeetCode #49). Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together: ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"] → [[eat,tea,ate],[tan,nat],[bat]]. Up to 10⁴ strings of length up to 100, lowercase English letters.

Comparing every pair of strings is O(n²·k). Instead, invent a group key: a value that is the same for all anagrams and different for non-anagrams. Then a “key → list of strings” dictionary does the job: each string lands in its bucket with a single lookup. The whole difficulty of the problem is inventing the key.

Key 1 — the sorted letters: “eat”, “tea”, “ate” → “aet”. O(k log k) per string, O(n·k log k) in total. Key 2 — a counter: 26 numbers with a separator, “eat” → “1#0#0#0#1#…”. O(k + 26) per string — better when strings are long. For k ≤ 100 the difference is small, and the sorted key is easier to write without bugs. Memory is O(n·k) either way: the dictionary holds every string and key.

An int[26] itself does not work as a dictionary key: arrays are compared by reference, so every word would get its own group. That is why the counter is turned into a string (or into your own struct with IEquatable).

In a game: this is how objects are grouped for instanced rendering — the key is (Mesh, Material), the value is a list of matrices, and each group is drawn in batches with Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced (Unity 2021.2+; earlier, DrawMeshInstanced), up to 1023 instances per call.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [tea, eat, aab, bab, aba, ate]. The rig stops twice and asks where a word goes: decide by the key, not by the set of letters.

options.label: Into the “aab” group: same letters, a and b
A new group with the key “abb”
A new group with the key “bab”

asks.q: The next word is “bab”. Its letters are the same as in “aab”: a and b. Where does it go?
asks.explain: The key is all the letters, repeats included, in order: “bab” → “abb”. “aab” has two a’s and one b, “bab” has one a and two b’s: they are not anagrams, and the keys differ. A key made of distinct letters ({a, b}) would glue them into one group — a common mistake.

options: groups["aab"].Add("aba")
groups["aba"] = new List<string>()
groups["abb"].Add("aba")
asks.q: Now “aba”. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Sorting gives a canonical form: all permutations of the same letters share one. “aba” → “aab”, that key already exists, TryGetValue hands over the group’s list, and the word is added to it. A new list is created only for a new key.

cards.q: A counter key for Group Anagrams. It puts “aaaaaaaaaaab” and “abbbbbbbbbbb” into one group, yet they are not anagrams. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Without a separator the numbers run together: 11 and 1 give “111”, and so do 1 and 11. The key is no longer unambiguous, and different strings land in one group. The fix is a separator: sb.Append(n).Append('#') — then “11#1#…” and “1#11#…” differ. While every counter is below 10 the bug stays invisible: only words with a letter repeated 10 times or more expose it.

cards.title: Unicode: “only English letters?”
cards.body:
The first question to the interviewer: which characters can appear. The solution depends on the answer.

Only a–z — int[26]. But for 'A' the index 'A' - 'a' is −32, for 'é' it is 136: IndexOutOfRangeException. Case is normalized up front, and with ToLowerInvariant(), not ToLower(): the latter depends on the thread’s culture, and in the Turkish locale "I".ToLower() is the dotless “ı”.

Any characters — a counter in a dictionary. But a char in .NET is not a character, it is a UTF-16 code unit: emoji and rare CJK characters take two chars (a surrogate pair). They must be counted as one code point — char.ConvertToUtf32 joins the pair into one number.

Normalization. “é” can be the single character U+00E9 or the pair “e” + U+0301 (a combining accent). They look the same on screen, but the counters differ. Before comparing, bring both strings to one form: s.Normalize() (form NFC by default).

In a game: player names, chat, localization into Japanese or Chinese — exactly the case where int[26] crashes.

cards.q: The strings may contain any Unicode characters. What is true? Select all.
options: int[26] indexed by c - 'a' throws IndexOutOfRangeException on 'A' or 'é'
A Dictionary<char, int> counts an emoji as one character
A single-character “é” and “e” with a combining accent give different counters without Normalize()
ToLower() returns the same result on every machine
char.ConvertToUtf32 turns a surrogate pair into one code point
cards.explain: 'A' − 'a' = −32 and 'é' − 'a' = 136 — both indices are outside 0..25. An emoji is two chars, and a dictionary over char counts the two halves separately. The two spellings of “é” differ until normalized. ToLower() uses the thread’s culture: in Turkish “I” becomes “ı”, so keys need ToLowerInvariant(). ConvertToUtf32 is exactly what joins the pair into one code point.

cards.title: Variations: the same counter, a different key
cards.body:
Ransom Note (#383): can the note be built from the magazine’s letters. Count the magazine’s letters, then subtract the note’s; if a counter goes negative, it cannot. O(m + n), memory O(1).

All anagrams of a pattern in a string (Find All Anagrams, #438): a window of length |p| slides along the string, +1 for the character entering, −1 for the one leaving, and the window’s counter is compared with the pattern’s. The same counter, an O(1) update per step — details are in the sliding window unit.

Shifted strings (Group Shifted Strings, #249): “abc”, “bcd”, “xyz” form one group because neighbouring letters are the same distance apart. The key is the string shifted so that it starts with 'a'. This is the main skill of the lesson: ask what the members of a group have in common, and make that the key.

Long strings, few words (k = 10⁴, n = 100): a counter key in O(k) instead of sorting in O(k log k).

cards.q: You solve Group Anagrams out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: which characters, any uppercase, does the group order matter, what are n and the lengths
Name the brute force: compare every pair of strings — O(n²·k)
Idea: anagrams share a key — the sorted letters; a “key → list” dictionary
Write the code while stating: the key is equal for anagrams and different for everything else
Run an example: eat, tea, tan — two groups
State the complexity: O(n·k log k) time, O(n·k) memory
Edge cases: an empty string, a single word, Unicode, long strings — a counter key
cards.explain: The statement, the baseline, the key idea, the code, an example, the complexity, edge cases. Ask about Unicode at the very first step — the answer decides whether int[26] and sorting chars are enough.

cards.title: The cost of a string key
cards.body:
A string key is not free. For every word ToCharArray allocates an array and new string allocates one more string: for 10⁴ words that is 2·10⁴ heap objects. And a lookup by a string key is not “O(1)” but O(k): .NET computes a string’s hash over every character on every call (the string does not store it), and when hashes match, Equals walks the string once more.

The easiest thing to remove is the character array: one buffer for all the words, sort its prefix and build the string from a slice of the buffer. One allocation per word remains — the key itself.
cards.deep:
A key without intermediate copies. string.Create(length, state, (span, st) => …) (.NET Core 2.1+, .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2) hands you a Span<char> over the new string’s own memory: copy the letters into it and sort in place. Sorting a Span<T> — MemoryExtensions.Sort — exists only since .NET 5; in Unity sort the buffer with Array.Sort, as above.

A lookup with no string at all (.NET 9+). groups.GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>() searches a Dictionary<string, …> by a ReadOnlySpan<char>: sort the letters in a stackalloc buffer and look up by it. The string key is created only for a new group — when writing through the same lookup. It needs a comparer that can compare a span with a string: the default one for string, StringComparer.Ordinal and OrdinalIgnoreCase can.

String hashing in a dictionary. In modern .NET a Dictionary<string, …> with the default comparer (or with StringComparer.Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase) first hashes strings without randomization — it is faster. If an insert has to walk a chain of more than 100 entries, the dictionary switches to the randomized hash and rehashes everything. The protection against collision attacks stays, and in the normal case it costs nothing.

stackalloc in a loop. stackalloc memory is released only when the method returns. Inside a loop over 10⁴ words every iteration bites off a new chunk of the stack — all the way to a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught (the analyzer warns about it with rule CA2014). Allocate the buffer once before the loop and zero it with counts.Clear() before every word. Code without Clear() usually works: by default the C# compiler asks the runtime to zero a method’s locals (the localsinit flag). But with the [SkipLocalsInit] attribute (.NET 5+) there is no zeroing, and the counters start with leftover stack garbage.

Surrogates and sorting. Sorting by char tears surrogate pairs apart, and a key of sorted UTF-16 code units can glue different strings together: the code point pairs U+1F600 + U+1F900 and U+1F500 + U+1FA00 consist of the same units D83D, D83E, DD00, DE00. For a Unicode key sort code points (int), not chars. .NET Core 3.0+ has System.Text.Rune and s.EnumerateRunes() for this; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no Rune — char.ConvertToUtf32 remains. And a “character” as the player sees it is bigger still — a grapheme cluster (a letter with accents, an emoji with a skin tone modifier); StringInfo.GetTextElementEnumerator walks those.
