lessons.title: Prefix sums
lessons.sub: Subarray Sum Equals K and Product of Array Except Self: a prefix in a dictionary, a prefix and a suffix without division

cards.title: Subarray Sum Equals K: the problem and its signals
cards.body:
Subarray Sum Equals K (LeetCode #560). Given an integer array nums and a number k, how many contiguous subarrays sum to exactly k? n ≤ 2·10⁴, elements from −1000 to 1000 — negatives occur. Example: [1, 1, 1], k = 2 → 2.

Signals: “contiguous subarray” and “sum” mean sums of segments, and those are conveniently obtained as a difference of prefix sums. “How many” means a counter.

Why not a window. A sliding window works in O(n) by moving the right edge while the sum is below k and the left edge when it is above. That is only valid if widening the window never decreases the sum, that is, if the numbers are non-negative. With a −7 in the array the sum can drop after widening, and the rule “the sum is too big — shrink” throws away segments that would still reach k.

The naive solution: for every start i, extend the end j and keep a running sum. There are about n²/2 pairs (i, j) — for n = 2·10⁴ that is 2·10⁸ additions, right at the edge of the time limit.

cards.q: What breaks the sliding window in this problem?
options: Negative numbers: after widening, the sum can decrease, and shrinking on “sum above k” loses answers
Speed: the window runs in O(n²), and O(n) is required
A window can find only one subarray, it cannot count them all
cards.explain: A window relies on monotonicity: wider means a bigger sum, narrower a smaller one. Then once the sum exceeds k, widening further is pointless and the left edge can move. A negative number breaks that monotonicity: [5, −3, 1] with k = 3 gives a sum of 5, above 3, already at the first element; the window drops the 5 — and loses [5, −3, 1] = 3.

wrong.1: A window is O(n): each edge crosses the array once. The problem is correctness, not speed.
wrong.2: A window can count — with positive numbers it would cope. It is the sign of the numbers that breaks it.

cards.title: A prefix in a dictionary: Two Sum on sums
cards.body:
Let sum be the sum of the elements from the start up to and including the current j — the prefix sum. The sum of the segment nums[i..j] is the prefix up to j minus the prefix up to i − 1. So a segment ending at j sums to k exactly when a prefix equal to sum − k has occurred before.

This is Two Sum from the first lesson, only on prefixes: for the current sum look up the partner sum − k by exact value. The one difference is that we need not an index but how many times that prefix occurred: each occurrence is a separate segment start. A “prefix → how many times” dictionary. The counter is incremented like this: seen[sum] = seen.GetValueOrDefault(sum) + 1 — GetValueOrDefault returns 0 for a new key (available since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity too).

The empty prefix. Before the first element the sum is 0 — it has already “occurred” once, so the dictionary starts as {0: 1}. Without it, segments starting at index 0 are lost.

Invariant: before step j the dictionary holds every prefix ending left of j, plus the empty one. So, as in Two Sum, check first, then insert. Time O(n), memory O(n). Negative numbers no longer matter: the dictionary does not care whether the sum rises or falls. No overflow: |sum| ≤ 2·10⁴ · 1000 = 2·10⁷; with larger values keep prefixes in long.

In a game: prefix sums are the path length to every waypoint (the point “at distance d along the path” is found through the prefixes) and the cumulative weights of a loot table.

cards.q: Assemble the single-pass solution.
cards.explain: The {0: 1} start is the empty prefix, the start for segments beginning at index 0. The partner of the current prefix is sum − k. We add times, not 1: every earlier occurrence of the prefix is a separate segment. And we increment the current prefix’s counter rather than write 1: otherwise repeated prefixes (plentiful with negative numbers) would lose their past occurrences.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 4, −7, 1, 3, 3, 1, −4], k = 7. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the prefix dictionary on screen.

options.label: count += 1: prefix 0 is already in the dictionary
count stays, seen[0] stays 1: the key already exists

asks.q: x = −7: sum becomes 0, need = 0 − 7 = −7. What does the code do?
asks.explain: We look up need = −7, and no such prefix occurred — count does not grow. But prefix 0 has occurred before (the empty one) and now occurs a second time: its counter becomes 2. That is the difference from Two Sum: we do not overwrite, we count — both zeros will later serve as segment starts.

options: count += 2
count += 1
count += 0
asks.q: x = 3: sum = 7, need = 7 − 7 = 0. By how much does count grow?
asks.explain: Prefix 0 occurred twice: the empty one (before index 0) and the one after −7 (index 2). Each is its own segment start: [3, 4, −7, 1, 3, 3] and [1, 3, 3], both summing to 7. count = 1 + 2 = 3.

cards.q: On nums = [1, 2], k = 0 this code returns 2, although no subarray sums to 0. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The prefix goes in before the check, which breaks the invariant “the map holds only what is left of j”. With k = 0 we look up sum − 0 = sum — and find the prefix just stored: an empty segment. With k ≠ 0 the order happens not to matter (sum − k ≠ sum), so the bug survives until the first test with k = 0. The same trap as target = 2x in Two Sum: TryGetValue first, then seen[sum].

cards.title: Product of Array Except Self: a prefix and a suffix
cards.body:
Product of Array Except Self (LeetCode #238). Return an array ans where ans[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i], in O(n) and without division. n ≤ 10⁵, elements from −30 to 30, and the product of any prefix and suffix is guaranteed to fit in an int. Follow-up: O(1) extra memory, the output array does not count.

Why not division. “Multiply everything and divide by nums[i]” is forbidden by the statement, and for good reason: one zero, and at its position we divide 0 by 0 (DivideByZeroException), while the right answer there is the product of the rest. Zeros can be handled separately, but that is three code branches instead of one idea.

Idea: ans[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i). The first pass, left to right, carries prefix and writes it into ans. The second pass, right to left, carries suffix and multiplies it in. Invariant: before step i, prefix is the product strictly left of i and suffix strictly right of it. So in both passes we write into ans[i] first and multiply by nums[i] afterwards — otherwise the element ends up in its own product.

Time O(n), extra memory O(1): two variables besides the answer. The same “prefix + suffix” trick shows up in Trapping Rain Water (the two pointers unit), only with a maximum instead of a product.

cards.q: Assemble Product of Array Except Self: two passes, no division.
cards.explain: There is nothing left of element zero — the empty product is 1, not 0. ans[i] gets prefix as it is: it does not contain nums[i] yet, while prefix * nums[i] would include the element itself. The backward pass starts at the last index n − 1 (starting at n is out of bounds). And suffix is multiplied by nums[i] only after the write — for the next step to the left.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [2, 3, 0, 4] — with the zero that breaks division. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from prefix and suffix on screen.

options.label: ans[2] = 6, and prefix stays 6: the zero is skipped

asks.q: i = 2, nums[2] = 0, prefix = 6. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Write first, multiply after: ans[2] gets the product strictly to the left — 2 · 3 = 6, the zero is not in it. Then prefix × 0 = 0, and everything to the right gets a zero from the left — as it should: for them the zero is among “the rest”.

asks.q: Backward pass, i = 2: ans[2] = 6, suffix = 4. What is written into ans[2]?
asks.explain: suffix is the product strictly right of i, that is, just 4: the zero joins suffix on the next line. ans[2] = 6 · 4 = 24 — the product of everything but the zero. The rest get 0: for i = 3 the zero sits in prefix, for i = 1 and i = 0 in suffix. Answer [0, 0, 24, 0].

cards.title: Variations: where else prefixes lead
cards.body:
Many range sum queries (Range Sum Query, #303): build an array of prefixes P of length n + 1 once, with P[0] = 0; after that the sum of [l..r] = P[r + 1] − P[l] in O(1).

The longest subarray summing to k (#325): a “prefix → first index” dictionary. The segment length is j minus the index of prefix sum − k, and the further left that index, the longer the segment. So the index is written on the prefix’s first occurrence and never overwritten. Contiguous Array (#525) belongs here too: the longest segment with equal numbers of 0s and 1s — replace 0 with −1, and the problem becomes “the longest subarray summing to 0”.

A sum divisible by k (#974): a segment is divisible by k when two prefixes have the same remainder. The key is the remainder, the start is remainder 0 once. A C# trap: % keeps the sign of the dividend, -7 % 5 == -2, so normalize: ((sum % k) + k) % k. There are only k remainders — an int[k] array is enough instead of a dictionary.

A sum over a rectangle (#304): two-dimensional prefixes. S[y, x] is the sum of all cells above and to the left; a rectangle is assembled from four corners (inclusion–exclusion) in O(1). In a game: “how many walls or units are in this area of the tile map”, “is a 5×5 plot free for a building” — O(1) per query after O(w·h) preparation.

cards.q: You solve Subarray Sum Equals K out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: can numbers be negative, what are n, k and the values, does an empty subarray count
Name the brute force over starts and ends with a running sum: O(n²), about 2·10⁸ additions for n = 2·10⁴
Explain why not a window: negative numbers break the monotonicity of the sum
Idea: the segment ending at j sums to k if prefix sum − k occurred before; a “prefix → how many times” dictionary starting at {0: 1}
Write the code: first add seen[sum − k], then increment seen[sum]
Run [1, 1, 1] with k = 2 and state the complexity: O(n) time and memory
Edge cases: k = 0, a segment starting at index 0, sum overflow
cards.explain: The statement, the baseline, why the obvious optimization (a window) fails, the idea, the code, an example and the complexity, edge cases. Interviewers expect the window point: it shows you know where a technique stops applying.

cards.title: A counter in a dictionary: one lookup instead of two
cards.body:
seen[sum] = seen.GetValueOrDefault(sum) + 1 is two lookups by key: a read and a write. Together with TryGetValue for sum − k, that is three hash computations per element. In .NET 6+ the increment takes a single lookup: CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault finds the entry or creates it with the default value and returns a ref to the value right inside the dictionary.

Capacity. There are at most n + 1 distinct prefixes — set the capacity up front, and the dictionary will not grow along the way.

Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no CollectionsMarshal — there you keep GetValueOrDefault and the indexer, or an array instead of a dictionary if the keys fall in a narrow range.
cards.deep:
Why a ref into a dictionary is dangerous. GetValueRefOrAddDefault returns a reference straight into the entries array. While it is alive you must not add or remove keys: on growth the entries move to a new array, while the ref keeps pointing into the old one — the write “gets lost” without any exception. For reading without inserting there is CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef (also .NET 6+); a missing key is checked with Unsafe.IsNullRef. The same trick in Group Anagrams: ref var list = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(groups, key, out bool exists); if (!exists) list = new List<string>(); — one lookup, and for a string key that means one hashing pass over the string instead of two.

EnsureCapacity and TrimExcess (.NET Core 2.1+, .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2). EnsureCapacity(n) grows in advance a dictionary that lives in a field and is reused via Clear() — before a batch of inserts, with no re-placing along the way. TrimExcess() gives memory back after a peak: a dictionary that ballooned to 10⁶ entries during level loading keeps the same arrays after Clear() until you shrink it. And Clear() costs O(capacity), not O(number of entries): the whole bucket array is zeroed. A huge dictionary cleared every frame for a dozen entries wastes time.

An array instead of a dictionary. If prefixes fall in a narrow range — in Contiguous Array, for instance, after replacing 0 with −1 the sum lies in [−n, n] — an int[2n + 1] with the index shifted by sum + n replaces the dictionary: no hashes, no collisions, and in Jobs such a counter is a NativeArray<int>, which Burst handles with no restrictions.

Overflow and float. In #560 the sum is at most 2·10⁷ in absolute value — int is enough; in general keep prefixes in long. Prefixes in float — path length, accumulated time — lose precision: the difference of two large, close numbers eats the significant digits. For long routes use double, or measure distances from the nearest reference point rather than from the start.

The longest subarray summing to k

lessons.title: A set, and an array as a hash table
lessons.sub: Longest Consecutive Sequence and First Missing Positive: O(n) without sorting and without extra memory

cards.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence: the problem and its signals
cards.body:
Longest Consecutive Sequence (LeetCode #128). Given an unsorted integer array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers — values x, x + 1, x + 2, …, wherever they sit in the array. [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] → 4 (the run 1, 2, 3, 4). n ≤ 10⁵, values up to 10⁹ in absolute value, and the statement demands O(n).

Signals: neighbours in a run are partners by exact value (for x they are x − 1 and x + 1), and the question “is that number present?” means a set. And “O(n)” in the statement explicitly rules out sorting.

Without that constraint the honest answer is sorting plus one pass that skips duplicates: O(n log n). It is worth naming as the baseline.

A set, head-on: put everything into a HashSet and from every number count upwards while the next one is in the set.

cards.q: How many Contains checks does the head-on set approach make on the array [1, 2, 3, …, n]?
options: ≈ n²/2 — from every number we walk to the end of the run
≈ n — every number is checked once
≈ n log n — like sorting
cards.explain: From 1 the loop walks the whole run, from 2 one number less, … from n just one. The sum n(n + 1)/2 ≈ n²/2: for n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ checks. The work repeats: every number of a run walks its tail again.

wrong.1: Each number would be checked once if we counted only from the start of a run. Here counting starts from every number.
wrong.2: There is nowhere for a logarithm to come from: no halving, no sorting. Every start walks the run linearly.

cards.title: Count only from the start of a run
cards.body:
The repeated work is the tail of a run: every number of the run walks it again. But a run only needs counting once — from its first number. And the first number is recognized in O(1): x starts a run if x − 1 is not in the set.

Why O(n). The inner while starts only from run starts and walks each run once; runs do not overlap, so all the while loops together make at most n steps. Plus one x − 1 check per number. O(n) time in total: a nested loop does not by itself mean O(n²) — count how many times the body runs in total. Memory is O(n) for the set.

Iterate over the set, not the original array: each number is in the set once, so each run start is counted once as well.

cards.q: Assemble the O(n) solution.
cards.explain: Iterate over set: each number once. A run start is a number without x − 1; the rest are skipped with continue. Then grow len while x + len is in the set. With x + 1 in the while the loop would never end: the condition does not change from step to step.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [5, 2, 99, 3, 1, 4, 100]. The rig walks the set in insertion order: 5, 2, 99, 3, 1, 4, 100 (in .NET without removals this is what usually happens, but HashSet enumeration order is not guaranteed). The rig stops twice and asks what the code does with the next number.

options.label: Skip it: 4 is in the set

asks.q: The first number of the set is 5. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 5 − 1 = 4 is in the set, so 5 is not a run start: continue. The run that contains 5 will be counted by its first number — we will get there.

options.label: Skip it: 2 is in the set

asks.q: x = 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 0 is not in the set — 1 starts a run. The while walks 2, 3, 4, 5 and stops at 6: length 5. Skipping 5 earlier removed nothing from the set — continue only declined to count from it. The record was 2 (99…100), now it is 5. We check x − 1, not x + 1: almost every number has a successor.

cards.q: This code gives the right answer, but on an array of 1, 2, …, 50 000 plus another 50 000 ones it exceeds the time limit. Tap the line responsible.
cards.explain: The loop walks nums, which holds 50 001 ones — and each of them starts a run, since there is no 0 in the set. Every one walks the run 1…50 000 again: about 2.5·10⁹ checks. The set holds a single 1, and the run is counted once. The fix is foreach (int x in set).

cards.title: First Missing Positive: an array instead of a set
cards.body:
First Missing Positive (LeetCode #41, hard). Given an unsorted integer array, find the smallest positive number that is not in it, in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. [3, 4, −1, 1] → 2, [1, 2, 0] → 3, [7, 8, 9] → 1.

Observation: n numbers can occupy at most n of the values 1, 2, …, n. So the answer lies in 1..n + 1, and numbers ≤ 0 or > n can be ignored. With a HashSet it is easy: put everything in and check 1, 2, … — O(n), but O(n) memory too. Sorting is O(n log n).

Idea: a set over the keys 1..n is a bool[n] array, and we already have an array of length n — the input itself. Let value v live in slot v − 1. For every i, while a[i] is a number from 1..n that is not in its place, swap it with the contents of slot a[i] − 1. A new number arrives at position i, and it needs placing too — hence while, not if. Then the first slot i without “its own” number i + 1 gives the answer; if everything is in place, the answer is n + 1.

Why O(n): every swap puts one number into its place for good, and there are n places — so there are at most n swaps in total. The condition a[a[i] − 1] != a[i] (“the target slot does not hold this number yet”) protects against duplicates: on [1, 1] with the check a[i] != i + 1 the two ones would swap forever.

In a game: the smallest free save slot number or id is the same problem.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 4, −1, 1, 6, 2]. The slots are labelled #1…#6: slot #v must hold v (index v − 1 in the code). The rig stops twice and asks what happens next.

options.label: Move on to the next i: this i already had a swap

asks.q: The pointer is on slot #2: 4 has just left for slot #4, and 1 arrived here. What next?
asks.explain: The while checks this slot again: 1 is within 1..6, and slot #1 holds −1, not a one. Swap: 1 takes its place, −1 arrives in slot #2 and stays — it is outside 1..n. With an if the 1 would stay in someone else’s slot, and the answer would come out wrong. The answer is searched for only after the placement, in a second pass.

options: return 5;
return 7;
return 1;
asks.q: The placement is done: [1, 2, 3, 4, −1, 6]. What does the method return?
asks.explain: The second pass looks for the first slot without its own number: #1…#4 are in place, #5 holds −1. The answer is 5. n + 1 = 7 would be the answer only if all of 1..6 were in their places.

cards.q: On [3, 4, −1, 1] this code returns 1, while the right answer is 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The if makes one swap and moves on, while the number that arrived at position i stays unplaced. At i = 1: 4 leaves for slot #4, 1 arrives — and stays in slot #2, while #1 holds −1. The second pass sees −1 in #1 and answers 1. A while places the arriving number too.

cards.title: Variations: indices as a set
cards.body:
Missing Number (#268): numbers 0..n, one is missing. Placement would work, but arithmetic is simpler: n(n + 1)/2 minus the array’s sum (keep the sum in a long) — or XOR, covered in the bits unit.

Find All Duplicates (#442): values 1..n, each appears once or twice. Marking by sign: for each v make slot |v| − 1 negative; if it is already negative, v has been seen. The sign is a spare bit in the slot, no second array needed.

The array must not be modified. Placement and marks spoil the input. Ask the interviewer; in production code a method that silently reorders someone else’s array is a bug. Then be honest: a HashSet or a copy of the array, O(n) memory.

Keys are dense and bounded — tile ids 0..10⁴, slot numbers, enemy indices in a pool: a bool[] instead of a HashSet<int>. No hashes, no buckets, one byte per key (or one bit in a BitArray).

cards.q: You solve First Missing Positive out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: can the array be modified, what values occur, how much memory is allowed
Observation: the answer lies in 1..n + 1, other numbers do not matter
Name the simple solutions: HashSet — O(n) memory, sorting — O(n log n)
Idea: the array is its own set — value v goes into slot v − 1
Write the code: a while with a swap, the condition via the target slot a[a[i] − 1] != a[i]
Run [3, 4, −1, 1] and state the complexity: at most n swaps, O(n) time and O(1) memory
Edge cases: duplicates, all of 1..n in place (answer n + 1), negative and huge values
cards.explain: First agree on whether the input may be spoiled — that decides whether placement is allowed at all. The 1..n + 1 observation is the key to the whole problem: without it, it is not obvious that an array of length n is enough. Explain the complexity through the number of swaps, not through nested loops.

cards.title: The cost of a set, and when an array is enough
cards.body:
A HashSet<int> of 10⁵ numbers is a bucket array plus an entry array (hash, next, value): about 16 bytes per element plus headroom up to a prime size, around 1.6 MB. Every Contains is a jump to a random place in memory, and for large n the cache misses show more than O(1) promises. Hence an honest conclusion: O(n) with a set is not always faster than O(n log n) with sorting — sorting an int array walks memory sequentially. In an interview name both options and their cost; in a project, measure.

When keys are dense and the range is known, no set is needed at all: an array of flags by index is the same “hash table” where the hash is the number itself.
cards.deep:
HashSet internals. In modern .NET HashSet<T> is built like a Dictionary without values: the same buckets and entries, prime sizes. The constructor from a collection, new HashSet<int>(nums), takes its capacity from the collection’s Count right away, and if duplicates left the arrays 4 or more times larger than the number of entries, it calls TrimExcess() itself. HashSet has EnsureCapacity since .NET Core 2.1 and .NET Standard 2.1 (in Unity since 2021.2).

Sparse set. When you need O(1) add, remove and contains as well as a fast walk over the occupied keys only (active entities, selected units), use a pair of arrays: dense holds the keys contiguously, sparse[key] is the key’s position in dense. Contains: sparse[k] < count && dense[sparse[k]] == k; remove: move the last element of dense into the removed one’s place and fix its sparse. No hashes, no allocations, iteration over a dense array. Component storage in a number of ECS libraries is built on this structure, EnTT for one. Unity Entities stores components differently: in chunks grouped by archetype.

Unity: Jobs and Burst. The com.unity.collections package has NativeHashSet<T> and NativeBitArray — a set and a bit array outside the managed heap, usable from Burst; release them with Dispose(). For dense keys the bit array beats the hash set there too.

Proof for First Missing Positive. Let P be the number of slots holding “their own” value. A swap in the while puts a[i] into slot a[i] − 1, which did not hold its own value yet, and touches no slot that already does (slot i does not hold its own, otherwise the condition is false). So every swap increases P by 1, and P ≤ n — there are at most n swaps over the whole algorithm, and at most 2n checks of the while condition.

The sign-marking variant of #41: first replace every number ≤ 0 or > n with n + 1, then for every v in 1..n make slot v − 1 negative; the first positive slot i gives the answer i + 1. Also O(n) and O(1), with no swaps — easier to prove.

If the input must stay untouched and memory counts: take the copy from ArrayPool<int>.Shared.Rent(n) (available in .NET Standard 2.1 and in Unity). The array may be longer than n — work with the first n elements — and give it back with Return in a finally. In hot code, after warm-up, that is zero new allocations.

cards.q: Match the condition with the technique.
pairs: Length of a run of consecutive numbers in O(n)
HashSet, count only from x without x − 1
Value v goes into slot v − 1
Keys are dense ids from 0 to 10⁴

lessons.title: Final: hash tables and prefixes
lessons.sub: Recognize the technique from the statement, predict a trace, find a bug, explain out loud

cards.q: A playlist: song durations in seconds, up to 6·10⁴ songs. How many pairs of songs i < j have a total duration divisible by 60? Which technique?
options: A remainder counter: for each song add count[(60 − t % 60) % 60], then count[t % 60]++
Sort and walk with two pointers moving towards each other
A “prefix → how many times” dictionary of prefix sums
cards.explain: This is pair counting from Two Sum, only on remainders: the partner of song t is a song with remainder (60 − t % 60) % 60. The outer % 60 is for t divisible by 60: their partner is remainder 0, not 60. There are 60 remainders — an int[60] is enough. Add first, then store, so a song does not find itself. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

wrong.1: Converging pointers look for an exact sum in a sorted array. Here any sum divisible by 60 will do — 60, 120, 180…, and the pairs are scattered across the whole array.
wrong.2: Prefixes are for contiguous segments. Here it is any pair of two songs, not a segment.

cards.q: A string of lowercase English letters. Can its letters be rearranged into a palindrome?
options: int[26]: count the letters; at most one counter may be odd
Sort it and compare with its reverse
A HashSet of distinct letters: there must be at most half the length of them
cards.explain: In a palindrome letters stand in symmetric pairs — except perhaps one in the centre. That is a “how many times?” question → an int[26] counter, then a parity check. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

wrong.1: A sorted string is not necessarily a palindrome: “aab” sorted is “aab”, reversed “baa”, yet these letters do make the palindrome “aba”.
wrong.2: A set loses the quantities. “aabbc” makes the palindrome “abcba”, yet it has 3 distinct letters — more than half the length.

cards.q: New statements from games. Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: Thousands of queries “total damage over frames l..r”
An array of prefixes: P[r + 1] − P[l]
The longest stretch of a match with equal wins and losses
Can a word be built from the letters in the inventory
int[26]: plus the inventory, minus the word
Are there 5 consecutive values among the item ids
HashSet, count from the start of a run
The smallest free slot number with no extra memory
Value v goes into slot v − 1

cards.task: A new problem: how many segments of [2, −2, 3, 0, −3, 1] sum to zero (k = 0). The rig stops once — predict how much count grows.

options: count += 2
count += 1
count += 3
asks.q: x = −3: sum is 0 again, need = 0 − 0 = 0. By how much does count grow?
asks.explain: Prefix 0 occurred twice — the empty one and the one after [2, −2] — so two new zero-sum segments end here: [2, −2, 3, 0, −3] and [3, 0, −3]. count = 2 + 2 = 4. +3 would come out if the current prefix were stored before the check: with k = 0 it would find itself.

cards.q: Product of Array Except Self. On [1, 2, 3, 4] this code returns [24, 24, 24, 24] instead of [24, 12, 8, 6]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: ans[i] must get the product strictly left of i — prefix as it is. prefix * nums[i] includes the element itself: after the first pass ans = [1, 2, 6, 24], and every number ends up in its own product. The invariant: write first, then prefix *= nums[i].

cards.q: What is true about the complexity? Select all.
options: Group Anagrams with a sorted-letters key is O(n·k log k), k being the word length
First Missing Positive is O(n²): there is a while inside the for
Longest Consecutive Sequence counting only from run starts is O(n)
Subarray Sum Equals K with a prefix dictionary is O(n log n)
A lookup by a string key of length k costs O(k): the hash is computed over every character
cards.explain: Sorting each word is k log k, and there are n words. In First Missing Positive every swap puts a number in place for good — at most n swaps, O(n) overall. In Longest Consecutive all the while loops together visit each number once. The prefix dictionary is one pass with O(1) on average per step, so O(n). And a string key is hashed in full on every lookup.

cards.q: A Unity project (C# 9, .NET Standard 2.1). How do you increment a counter in a Dictionary<int, int> for a key that may not exist yet?
options: counts[key] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(key) + 1;
CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(counts, key, out _)++;
counts.Add(key, counts[key] + 1);
cards.explain: GetValueOrDefault exists in .NET Standard 2.1 and returns 0 for a new key. That is two lookups, but in Unity it is the honest option. A single lookup via CollectionsMarshal is .NET 6+ only.

wrong.1: CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault arrived in .NET 6; the .NET Standard 2.1 profile does not have it — it will not compile in Unity.
wrong.2: For a new key counts[key] throws KeyNotFoundException, and for an existing one Add throws ArgumentException: the key is already there.

cards.q: A new problem: how many contiguous segments have a sum divisible by k (numbers can be negative). Put the steps of the out-loud explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is k > 0? can numbers be negative, what are n and the values
Name the brute force over segments with a running sum — O(n²)
Idea: a segment is divisible by k when two prefixes have the same remainder
Structure: an int[k] remainder counter, starting with count[0] = 1 for the empty prefix
Code: remainder ((sum % k) + k) % k, first add count[r], then count[r]++
A run on a small example and the complexity: O(n) time, O(k) memory
Edge cases: negative sums, k = 1, sum overflow
cards.explain: The same frame as Subarray Sum Equals K: a prefix, a partner by exact value, a counter that starts with the empty prefix. Only the key changes — a remainder, and with it a C# trap: % keeps the sign, hence the normalization.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: A prefix dictionary starts at {0: 1}, otherwise segments starting at index 0 are lost
An int[26] can be a Dictionary key — anagrams will find each other
Longest Consecutive Sequence iterates over the set, not the original array
For the longest segment summing to k, the prefix index is overwritten on every occurrence
A Span<int> from stackalloc cannot be stored in a class field
cards.explain: The empty prefix is the start for segments beginning at index 0. An array as a key is compared by reference: every word gets its own group, which is why the counter is turned into a string. Iterating over the set guarantees each run start is counted once. The longest segment needs the leftmost prefix index — write it on first occurrence and never overwrite. A Span lives only inside the method.

units.title: Two pointers and in-place arrays
units.blurb: Compacting an array without allocations, converging pointers and why they lose nothing, trapping rain water, rotating and spiralling a matrix, a tile grid in memory and an in-place cellular automaton.

lessons.title: In-place compaction
lessons.sub: Read and write pointers: Move Zeroes, squares from both ends, palindromes and dead enemies without allocations

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Move Zeroes (LeetCode #283). Given an array nums, move all zeroes to the end while keeping the relative order of the other elements. Do it in place — no copy of the array; 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴.

This belongs to the family of compaction problems: drop some elements and pack the rest at the front of the array. Signals:

1. The statement says “in place”, “O(1) extra memory” or “return the new length”.
2. Every element is either “keep” or “drop”, and you can tell by looking at the element itself (sometimes at it and the last kept one).
3. The order of the kept elements matters. If it explicitly does not, there is an even faster trick — it comes at the end of the lesson.

The solution is two pointers moving in the same direction: read visits every element, write marks where the next kept element goes.

cards.q: Which problems are solved by the same single-pass read/write compaction? Select all.
options: Remove every occurrence of val from an array in place and return the new length
Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, keeping one copy of each value
Keep only the live bullets in an array; order does not matter
Find two elements that add up to target in an unsorted array
Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters
cards.explain: Removing val — “drop” is decided by the element itself, and the new length is write. Duplicates in a sorted array — keep an element if it differs from the last kept one (nums[write − 1]). Live bullets — the same compaction, and since order does not matter, the trick from the end of the lesson works too. A sum equal to target is a partner lookup by value — the dictionary from the hash map unit. The longest substring without repeats is a sliding window, the next unit.

cards.title: The naive solution and its cost
cards.body:
There are two brute-force routes, and both are bad.

Copy. Write the non-zeroes into a new array, append the zeroes, copy back. O(n) time, but O(n) memory, and the problem asks for in place. In a game it is also an allocation: a new array every frame is work for the garbage collector.

Remove one at a time. Found a zero — shift the tail one position left and put the zero at the end. That is exactly what List<T>.RemoveAt(i) does: it copies the tail with Array.Copy, which is O(n − i). With k zeroes the work is O(k · n); with half of the array zeroes it is O(n²). There are n/2 zeroes and the tail averages about n/2 elements — roughly n²/4 moves: 2.5·10⁷ for n = 10⁴ and 2.5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵.

The repeated work is easy to see: every non-zero is shifted as many times as there are zeroes to its left. Instead, each one can be moved exactly once — straight to its final place.

cards.q: n = 2·10⁴, half of the elements are zeroes, spread across the whole array. How many moves does “remove one at a time” make, and what follows?
options: ≈ 10⁸ — on the order of a second at 10⁸ operations per second; you need a single pass
≈ 2·10⁴ — RemoveAt and Array.Copy are O(1), it is instant
≈ 4·10⁸ — every zero shifts all n elements
cards.explain: There are n/2 = 10⁴ zeroes, and each shifts a tail of about n/2 = 10⁴ elements on average: 10⁴ · 10⁴ = 10⁸. Array.Copy is a fast memmove, so in practice it is more like tens of milliseconds than a second, but it is still 10⁸ moves (400 MB copied) for a problem that takes 2·10⁴ steps. In a 16 ms frame that is unacceptable.

wrong.1: RemoveAt and Array.Copy shift the tail: O(n − i), not O(1).
wrong.2: Only the tail to the right of the zero moves — half the array on average. And there are n/2 zeroes, not n: that gives n²/4.

cards.title: Key idea: read and write
cards.body:
Move every non-zero once, straight to its place. read visits every element; write is the cell where the next non-zero goes. On a non-zero, swap nums[read] and nums[write] and advance write. On a zero, just move on.

Invariant: left of write are all the non-zeroes read so far, in their original order, and between write and read there are only zeroes. So the swap puts the non-zero in place and the zero into the “zero zone”. Every element is read once: O(n) time, O(1) memory.

Why swap instead of assign: nums[write] = nums[read] also works, but then a second pass has to fill the tail with zeroes. The swap does that along the way. If the dropped elements are not needed at all (Remove Element, #27), assignment is enough and the answer is the new length write.

In a game: this is how you compact an array of enemies or particles after some of them died — no new array, no garbage.

cards.q: Assemble Move Zeroes in a single pass.
cards.explain: Skip a zero — only read moves. The tuple (a, b) = (b, a) swaps without a temporary (C# 7+, works in Unity). After the swap the non-zero sits at write, so write++. The for loop does read++ itself: an extra read++ would skip an element.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [2, 0, 0, 7, 0, 4, 9]. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does: answer from the invariant — left of write are the non-zeroes in order, between write and read only zeroes.

asks.q: read = 3, nums[3] = 7, write = 1. What value ends up in nums[3] after this step?
asks.explain: Between write and read there are only zeroes, so nums[write] = nums[1] = 0. The swap puts 7 at position 1 and the zero at position 3, in the zero zone. Nothing is lost: the zero just moved to the right.

asks.q: read = 5, nums[5] = 4, write = 2. What is left of write after this step?
asks.explain: 4 goes to position write = 2, right after the 2 and 7 already there, and write becomes 3. The order of the non-zeroes is preserved: each new one lands at the end of the part collected so far — that is why the compaction is stable.

cards.title: Squares of a sorted array: merging from both ends
cards.body:
Squares of a Sorted Array (#977). The array is sorted in non-decreasing order and contains negatives. Return the squares, also in non-decreasing order. n ≤ 10⁴, |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴ — a square is at most 10⁸ and fits in an int.

Brute force: square everything and sort — O(n log n). But the order is almost there already: the squares decrease from the left down to zero and increase to the right of it. The largest square is always at one of the ends. Put l and r at the ends, compare absolute values, write the larger square at the end of the answer and move its pointer inward. It is a merge of two sorted halves, just from the ends toward the middle.

Invariant: the tail of the answer right of w holds the largest squares in order, and all numbers not taken yet are in [l, r]. O(n) time. The memory is the answer itself, O(1) extra. You cannot fill from the front: the smallest square is somewhere in the middle, and you do not know where in advance.

cards.q: Assemble Squares of a Sorted Array: the answer is filled from the end.
cards.explain: Write from the end: w goes from n − 1 down to 0. The larger absolute value gives the larger square, and its pointer moves inward: the left one right (l++), the right one left (r--). The loop over w makes exactly n steps — one per number — so a separate l <= r check is not needed.

cards.title: Valid Palindrome: opposite pointers, no new strings
cards.body:
Valid Palindrome (#125). A string is a palindrome if, after removing everything except letters and digits and lowercasing, it reads the same both ways: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true. The string consists of printable ASCII characters, n ≤ 2·10⁵.

Brute force: build the cleaned string (Where, ToLower, new string) and compare it with its reverse. O(n) time, but two or three new strings and O(n) memory — garbage on a hot path.

Without allocations — opposite pointers: l from the start, r from the end. Each one skips characters that are not letters or digits (char.IsLetterOrDigit); then we compare the two characters via char.ToLowerInvariant and move inward. The inner skip loops also check l < r, otherwise on a string of pure punctuation a pointer runs off the end. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

ToLowerInvariant, not ToLower: char.ToLower(c) uses the current thread culture, and in the Turkish culture 'I' becomes a dotless 'ı'. IsLetterOrDigit understands all of Unicode; on ASCII it is exactly Latin letters and digits.

cards.q: On the string ".," this code throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The left skip loop does not check l < r. On ".," neither character is a letter: l passes 0 and 1 and reaches 2, and s[2] is past the end of the string. The right loop is guarded, the left one is not. The fix is the same condition: while (l < r && !char.IsLetterOrDigit(s[l])) l++.

cards.title: Unity: removing dead enemies in one pass
cards.body:
A common Unity interview question: some enemies in a List<Enemy> died — how do you remove them in Update? Three answers, from bad to good.

Remove in a loop. foreach + Remove throws InvalidOperationException: the list changed during enumeration. A forward for + RemoveAt(i) skips the neighbor: it slid into position i, and i++ stepped over it. Even a correct backward loop is O(n²) in the worst case: every RemoveAt shifts the tail.

RemoveAll(e => e.IsDead) is exactly the read/write compaction inside List<T>: one pass, O(n), the order of the survivors is preserved. A lambda that captures neither locals nor this is created once by the compiler (Roslyn) and cached in a static field — no allocation, and RemoveAll itself allocates nothing. With a capture (e => e.Hp < minHp, where minHp is a local) you get a new closure and delegate on every call.

Swap-remove, if order does not matter: put the last element in the dead one’s place and remove the last. RemoveAt(Count − 1) shifts nothing — O(1) per removal. Walk from the end: the element you move has already been checked and is alive.
cards.deep:
How RemoveAll works. In dotnet/runtime, List<T>.RemoveAll first finds the first element to remove, then walks with two indices — freeIndex writes, current reads — which is Move Zeroes without the swap. At the end it clears the tail with Array.Clear if T is a reference type or contains references (otherwise the array would keep dead objects alive for the GC), shrinks _size and returns the number of removed items. The predicate is called exactly once per element.

Destroyed Unity objects. After Destroy (the object is destroyed at the end of the frame, DestroyImmediate does it right away) a reference to a MonoBehaviour does not become null, but the overloaded == on UnityEngine.Object treats it as equal to null. RemoveAll(e => e == null) works, while e is null and ?. bypass the overload and will not see the destroyed object.

Cost and order. Swap-remove is O(1) per removal and O(n) per pass, but it shuffles the list. If anything depends on the order (update order, draw order, a target queue), use RemoveAll. For 10⁴ particles both take microseconds; Remove in a loop during a mass death is already quadratic.

Jobs and Burst. In com.unity.collections, NativeList<T> has RemoveAtSwapBack — the same swap-remove. For a particle array inside a job you usually compact in one pass over a NativeArray with a live counter — the same read and write.

cards.q: In Update, burnt-out bullets are removed from a List<Bullet> of 5000; the list order affects nothing. What is true? Select all.
options: Swap-remove from the end of the list is O(n) for the whole pass, with no allocations
bullets.RemoveAll(b => b.Dead) is also O(n), and a non-capturing lambda does not allocate every frame
for (int i = 0; i < bullets.Count; i++) if (bullets[i].Dead) bullets.RemoveAt(i); is correct, just slow
foreach (var b in bullets) if (b.Dead) bullets.Remove(b); throws InvalidOperationException
Swap-remove works the same way walking from the start of the list, with no changes to the loop
cards.explain: Swap-remove from the end: each removal is O(1), the pass is O(n). RemoveAll is the read/write compaction, O(n); a non-capturing lambda is cached by the compiler. The forward loop with RemoveAt is not just slow, it is wrong: after a removal the neighbor slides into position i and i++ skips it — two burnt-out bullets in a row, and the second one stays. foreach with Remove breaks the enumeration with an exception. Swap-remove from the start moves the not-yet-checked last element into position i — it must be checked again (no i++), otherwise a dead bullet stays.

cards.q: You are solving Move Zeroes out loud in an interview. Put the steps of your explanation in order.
items: Clarify: in place or not, does the order of non-zeroes matter, what about an empty array
Name the naive options: a new array costs O(n) memory, shifting the tail for every zero costs O(n²)
Idea: read visits everything, write is where the next non-zero goes
Write the code while stating the invariant: non-zeroes in order left of write, zeroes between write and read
Walk through [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] out loud
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: no zeroes, all zeroes, a single element
cards.explain: The statement, the baseline and its cost, the idea with its invariant, the code, a walkthrough, complexity, edge cases. On an array with no zeroes read and write move together, and every swap is an element with itself: that is correct, so there is no need to check read != write.

lessons.title: Opposite pointers
lessons.sub: Two Sum II, Container With Most Water, 3Sum — and the proof that a move loses nothing

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Two Sum II (LeetCode #167). The array numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order; find two numbers that add up to target and return their indices starting from one. There is exactly one answer, 2 ≤ n ≤ 3·10⁴, and extra memory must be O(1).

The dictionary from Two Sum would solve it in O(n) but take O(n) memory — the problem forbids that. Signals of opposite pointers:

1. The array is sorted — or can be sorted, because the original indices are not needed.
2. You look for a pair by a quantity that the two ends move in opposite directions: moving the left end right increases the sum, moving the right end left decreases it. Then the sign of the error tells you which one to move.
3. Memory must be O(1).

lo and hi start at the ends. Sum too small — lo++, too large — hi--. Each step shrinks the range by one, so there are at most n − 1 steps. You already saw the same opposite pointers in Valid Palindrome — there they just compared characters.

cards.q: Where do opposite pointers work? Select all.
options: How many pairs in a sorted array have a sum less than target
Does a sorted array contain two numbers whose difference is exactly k
Does a string read the same in both directions
The pair whose sum is closest to target in an unsorted array — you need the numbers, not the indices
A pair with sum target in an unsorted array — you need the original indices
cards.explain: Pairs with a sum below target: the two ends move the sum in opposite directions (how exactly to count comes at the end of the lesson). A palindrome uses the opposite pointers from the previous lesson. Closest sum: indices are not needed — sort and walk from the ends. The difference is the trap: moving either end inward decreases it, the moves have no opposite effect, and the sign of the error does not tell you which one to move; two pointers in the same direction work there. Original indices are lost by sorting — that is the dictionary.

cards.title: Why a move loses nothing
cards.body:
The interviewer’s key question: “What if the answer is a pair with the lo you just discarded?” Let us prove it by elimination.

Picture all pairs (i, j), i < j, as the upper triangle of a table. Suppose numbers[lo] + numbers[hi] < target. For any j ≤ hi: numbers[j] ≤ numbers[hi], so numbers[lo] + numbers[j] < target. None of the remaining pairs with numbers[lo] works — the whole row lo is discarded, and lo++ is safe. Symmetrically, if the sum is too large, numbers[hi] is too large even with the smallest remaining number — we discard the column hi.

Invariant: if an answer exists, it is a pair inside [lo, hi]. Each step discards a whole row or column, n − 1 pairs are checked instead of n(n − 1)/2 — and none that matters is lost.

The template “say we move this end; every pair with it is worse or impossible” proves the other problems of this lesson too.

cards.q: numbers = [2, 3, 5, 8, 11], target = 16. lo is on 2, hi is on 11: the sum 13 is less than 16. Why does lo++ lose nothing?
options: Every remaining pair with 2 is at most 2 + 11 = 13 — none of them reaches 16
2 is the smallest number, and the smallest numbers are never in the answer
The pointers must move in turns, otherwise they never meet
cards.explain: The largest partner of 2 is 11, and even with it the sum is 13 < 16. So the whole row “2 + anything” has no answer. The answer here is 5 + 11: lo will reach the 5, and hi stays on 11.

wrong.1: A small number can well be in the answer: with target = 5 the answer is 2 + 3. We drop 2 not because it is small, but because no remaining pair with it works.
wrong.2: There are no turns: we move the end that is proven exhausted. The pointers meet anyway — every step shrinks the range.

cards.title: Container With Most Water: move the shorter line
cards.body:
Container With Most Water (#11). The array h holds the heights of vertical lines at positions 0..n − 1. Two lines and the axis form a container holding min(h[l], h[r]) · (r − l) water. Find the maximum. n ≤ 10⁵, h ≤ 10⁴ — the area is at most 10⁹, an int is enough.

Checking all pairs is O(n²), 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵. Opposite pointers: start with the widest pair and move the shorter line.

Proof by elimination. Suppose h[l] < h[r]. All remaining pairs with l are (l, k), k < r: narrower, and their height min(h[l], h[k]) ≤ h[l]. None is better than the current one — line l is exhausted, l++. Moving the taller one is pointless: h[l] still limits the height while the width drops. With equal heights both are exhausted — either can move.

This is not a game problem, but it is exactly where interviewers check the proof: “how do you know you did not skip the best pair?”.

cards.q: Assemble Container With Most Water.
cards.explain: The shorter line holds the water — Math.Min. The width is the distance between the lines, r − l, not the number of positions. Move the shorter one: if the left is lower, l++. With h[l] > h[r] the code would move the taller line and skip better pairs.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]. The rig stops twice: name the area and which pointer the code moves.

options: best = 49; r--
best = 49; l++
best = 56; r--
asks.q: L = 1 (height 8), R = 8 (height 7). What does the code do?
asks.explain: min(8, 7) · (8 − 1) = 49 — a new record. The right line is lower: every remaining pair with it is narrower and no higher than 7, so it is exhausted — r--. 56 = 8 · 7 would use the taller line’s height, but the shorter one holds the water.

options: area = 40, best = 49; r--
area = 40, best = 49; l++
area = 48, best = 49; r--
asks.q: L = 1 (height 8), R = 6 (height 8): equal heights. What does the code do?
asks.explain: min(8, 8) · (6 − 1) = 40, the record 49 stays. With equal heights both lines are exhausted: any remaining pair with either of them is narrower and cannot get higher than 8. The code moves R because the condition h[l] < h[r] is strict and goes to else on a tie.

cards.title: 3Sum: sort, fix one element, skip duplicates
cards.body:
3Sum (#15). Find all unique triples [a, b, c] from the array that sum to 0. 3 ≤ n ≤ 3000. Checking all triples is n³/6 ≈ 4.5·10⁹ — far too many.

Reduce it to Two Sum II: sort (O(n log n)), fix nums[i] and use opposite pointers on [i + 1, n − 1] to find a pair summing to −nums[i]. Each i costs O(n), O(n²) in total: 9·10⁶ for n = 3000.

Duplicates. Triples are unique by value. If nums[i] == nums[i − 1], skip i: all triples with that first number are already found — the previous i had the whole range to its right, including this element. After a hit, move l and r past equal values. Compare with the previous element: the check nums[i] == nums[i + 1] skips the first of the equal ones — and with it triples like [−1, −1, 2], where it needs its twin as a partner.

A dictionary instead of pointers is also O(n²), but removing duplicates with it hurts more — you need a HashSet of triples. A small speed-up: if nums[i] > 0, only positives remain — you can stop.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]. The rig asks twice what the code does: watch i, L and R and where duplicates are skipped.

options.label: The sum is too small — L++

asks.q: We fixed −1 (i = 1). L = 2 points to another −1, R = 5 to 2. What happens next?
asks.explain: −1 + (−1) + 2 = 0 — a triple. Duplicates are skipped in two places: at i — the same value in the first-number slot — and at L and R, but only after a match. There has been no match yet, and the second −1 is a partner in the pair: that is a different triple, and it must not be lost.

asks.q: After two hits i = 2, and it is −1 again. What does the code do?
asks.explain: All triples with −1 as the first number were found at i = 1: it had the whole range to its right, including the second −1. So i = 2 is skipped — otherwise [-1, 0, 1] would come out twice.

cards.q: On [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] this code returns only [[-1, 0, 1]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: After sorting: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. At i = 1 the code sees that nums[2] is also −1 and skips — but only the first −1 has the second −1 in its range, which [-1, -1, 2] needs. Compare with the previous one: i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i − 1] skips a repeat after the first of the equal ones has done its work.

cards.title: Variations: k-Sum, closest sum, counting pairs
cards.body:
3Sum Closest (#16): the same scheme, but instead of “found” you keep the sum closest to target. O(n²).

4Sum (#18): two nested fixed indices plus opposite pointers — O(n³). In general, k-Sum is k − 2 nested loops with opposite pointers inside: O(nk−1). In 4Sum the numbers go up to 10⁹, and a sum of four overflows an int (maximum 2,147,483,647) — add in long.

How many pairs sum to less than target (sorted array): if a[lo] + a[hi] < target, then a[lo] works with every number to its right up to hi — that is hi − lo pairs at once, then lo++. Elimination here counts pairs by whole rows. With sorting, O(n log n).

Indices needed, array unsorted — sorting loses them: either a dictionary (O(n) memory) or sort an array of indices by value.
cards.deep:
Proof for counting. If a[lo] + a[hi] < target, then a[lo] + a[j] ≤ a[lo] + a[hi] for every j ≤ hi — all hi − lo pairs of the row qualify, and the row is closed. If the sum is ≥ target, column hi gives no pair with any remaining lo, and it is closed. Every pair is counted exactly once.

Sorting in .NET. Array.Sort is introsort: quicksort, switching to heapsort when recursion gets too deep and to insertion sort on short ranges. Worst case O(n log n), in place, O(log n) stack, not stable — irrelevant for plain numbers. Span<T>.Sort appeared in .NET 5; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have it — sort an array, or a NativeArray<T> via Sort() from com.unity.collections.

Faster than O(n²) for 3Sum. No algorithm noticeably faster than quadratic is known: the best ones only shave logarithmic factors. The bound is so well known that hardness proofs for other problems are built on it. In an interview, O(n²) is the optimal answer.

Allocations in 3Sum. Every triple is a new int[3], plus the List growing. On a hot path in a game you would return a flat buffer of triples or write into the caller’s Span, not a list of arrays.

cards.q: 4Sum via “sort + two fixed indices + opposite pointers”, numbers up to 10⁹ in absolute value. What is true?
options: O(n³) time, add the four numbers in long
O(n²) time, add the four numbers in long
O(n³) time, int is enough: four numbers up to 10⁹ sum to less than 4·10⁹
cards.explain: Two nested fixed indices give n² combinations, and each one runs an O(n) opposite-pointer pass: O(n³) in total, i.e. k-Sum with k = 4 is O(n^(k−1)). A sum up to 4·10⁹ does not fit in an int, whose maximum is about 2.1·10⁹.

wrong.1: The two fixed indices alone give n² pairs, and there is an O(n) pass inside.
wrong.2: int.MaxValue = 2,147,483,647 ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — a sum up to 4·10⁹ overflows.

cards.q: You are solving Container With Most Water out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: n, the range of heights, whether you need the area or the lines themselves
Brute force over pairs: O(n²), 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵
Idea: start with the widest pair and move the shorter line
Prove it: every remaining pair with the shorter line is narrower and no higher — it is exhausted
Code while narrating: best = max(best, min · width)
Complexity O(n), memory O(1); edge cases: two lines, equal heights
cards.explain: The proof comes before the code: on this problem it is exactly what the interviewer waits for. The example with two 8s also checks equal heights.

lessons.title: Water between the bars
lessons.sub: Trapping Rain Water: three solutions and the proof of why we move the lower side

cards.title: The problem and the water-over-one-bar formula
cards.body:
Trapping Rain Water (LeetCode #42, hard). The array h holds the heights of bars of width 1. How much water is trapped after the rain? n ≤ 2·10⁴, 0 ≤ h ≤ 10⁵. Example: [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6.

Do not think about whole “puddles” — count the water over each bar separately. The water over i rises to the lower of two “walls”: the highest bar on the left and the highest bar on the right.

water[i] = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) − h[i], where maxLeft[i] is the maximum of h[0..i] and maxRight[i] is the maximum of h[i..n − 1]. The bar itself is part of both maxima, so the difference is never negative: the highest bar holds no water.

Signals: the answer is a sum of per-position contributions, and each contribution depends on the maximum to the left and to the right. That invites prefix maxima — and two pointers, if memory must be O(1).

cards.q: h = [2, 0, 4, 1, 3]. How much water is over the bar at index 3 (height 1)?
cards.explain: The maximum to its left (itself included) is 4, to its right 3. The lower wall holds: min(4, 3) − 1 = 2. The array holds 4 in total: another 2 over index 1.

wrong.1: That is 4 − 1: it takes the left wall, but the water spills over the lower one — the right wall of height 3.
wrong.2: The bar’s neighbors (4 and 3) are higher than its 1 — there is water. What matters is not the neighbors but the maxima on each side.

cards.title: The naive solution: find the walls for every bar
cards.body:
Straight from the formula: for each i, scan left and right to find the maxima. That is O(n) per bar and O(n²) overall; O(1) memory. For n = 2·10⁴ it is about n · n = 4·10⁸ steps — several seconds at 10⁸ operations per second, while the limit is usually 1–2 seconds.

What work am I repeating? The left maximum for i + 1 is the maximum for i plus one more bar. Yet we recompute it from scratch every time. Same on the right.

cards.title: Solution 1: prefix maxima
cards.body:
Precompute all the maxima. A left pass: maxLeft[i] = max(maxLeft[i − 1], h[i]). A right pass: maxRight[i] = max(maxRight[i + 1], h[i]). A third pass adds up the water by the formula. Time O(n), memory O(n) — two arrays.

It is the same “remember the past instead of recomputing” as prefix sums from the hash map unit, just with max instead of +. An interviewer will accept this solution; the next question is “and with O(1) memory?”.

cards.title: Solution 2: two pointers, and why we move the lower side
cards.body:
For the water over a bar you do not need both maxima, only the smaller of the two. Pointers l and r walk toward each other from the ends; lmax is the maximum of what has been passed on the left, rmax on the right.

Rule: if h[l] < h[r], process l: lmax = max(lmax, h[l]), water lmax − h[l], l++. Otherwise do the same on the right with rmax.

Why the true right maximum is not needed. The left pointer only moves off the lower bar: every bar passed on the left was, at its moment, lower than h[r] for some r not to the left of the current one. So lmax is below the maximum to the right of l, and so is h[l], since h[l] < h[r]. The lower of the two walls over l is the left one, max(lmax, h[l]), however high the right side is. Meanwhile rmax may still be 0: nothing on the right was passed yet, but h[r] already guarantees a wall at least that high.

Invariant: the water over every bar outside [l, r] is counted correctly, and the lower of h[l], h[r] is bounded by its own side. On a tie either side works. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

cards.q: h = [5, 1, 2, 9]. Step one: 5 < 9, lmax = 5, l = 1. Step two: h[1] = 1 < h[3] = 9, rmax is still 0, and the code adds 5 − 1 = 4. Why is that correct?
options: There is guaranteed to be a wall of at least 9 on the right, and 5 on the left — the left side holds the water over l
The right pointer has not moved yet, so water on the right is not counted
It is a bug: it should be min(lmax, rmax) − h[l] = 0
cards.explain: rmax is the maximum of the bars passed on the right only, not of all of them. The true maximum to the right of l is at least h[r] = 9, the left one is 5. The lower wall holds: 5 − 1 = 4. The total for this array is 7: another 3 over the 2.

wrong.1: The water over l depends on both walls; the right one is simply proven higher than the left, so its exact value is not needed.
wrong.2: rmax = 0 is incomplete knowledge, not a wall of height 0. The formula with min(lmax, rmax) would give 0 and lose the water.

cards.q: Assemble the two-pointer solution.
cards.explain: Process the lower side: h[l] < h[r] means the left one. lmax already includes h[l], so lmax − h[l] is never negative. The right side is symmetric: rmax − h[r]. Math.Min(lmax, rmax) would lose water while rmax is still small, and h[r] − h[l] takes the right wall as the water level.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]. The rig stops twice: decide which side the code processes and how much water it records.

options.label: Processes R: rmax = 2, water 0, R moves
Processes L: lmax = 2, water 0, L moves

asks.q: L moved to index 3 (height 2), R is at index 10 (height 2). The heights are equal. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The condition h[l] < h[r] is strict: 2 < 2 is false, so the code goes to else and processes the right side. On a tie either side works: the wall on the other side is at least as high, and the proof holds for both.

asks.q: L = 5 (height 0), R = 7 (height 3), lmax = 2, rmax = 2. How much water does the code record over bar 5?
asks.explain: h[5] = 0 < h[R] = 3 — the left side is processed. The wall on the right is at least 3, on the left it is 2, and the lower one holds: 2 − 0 = 2. h[R] = 3 is only a guarantee that the right wall is no lower than lmax, not the water level.

cards.title: Solution 3: a monotonic stack — water in layers
cards.body:
A third view counts water not per bar but in horizontal layers. Keep a stack of indices whose heights do not increase from bottom to top. When h[i] is higher than the top, the top, bottom, has found its right wall. Pop it; the new top, left, is the left wall. The layer between them has width i − left − 1 and height min(h[left], h[i]) − h[bottom]. Repeat while h[i] is higher than the top, then push i.

The nested while does not make it quadratic: every index is pushed and popped once, at most 2n stack operations in total. Time O(n), O(n) memory for the stack. This is the “nearest greater to the left and right” template; the stacks unit is devoted to monotonic stacks.

The solution is useful when data arrives one value at a time, left to right: two pointers need the whole array at once, while the stack needs only the past.

cards.q: On [3, 0, 5] this code returns 7 instead of 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: A copy-paste from the right branch: lmax takes h[r] instead of h[l]. On the first step lmax = 5, so 5 − 3 = 2 water appears over the 3 and 5 over the 0. But h[r] is only a guarantee that the right wall is no lower; the water level over l is set by the maximum passed on the left. It should be lmax = Math.Max(lmax, h[l]).

cards.q: What is true about the three solutions? Select all.
options: Prefix maxima: O(n) time and O(n) memory
Two pointers need the whole array at once, while the stack walks left to right and only looks at the past
In the two-pointer solution rmax always equals the true maximum to the right of l
When h[l] == h[r], either side can be processed
The monotonic stack is O(n²) in the worst case because of the nested while
cards.explain: Prefixes are two arrays of size n. Two pointers start from the right end, the stack does not. rmax is the maximum of what has been passed on the right only and can be smaller than the true one; the whole proof is that it is not needed. On a tie the wall on the other side is no lower — either side works. The stack is O(n): every index is pushed and popped once.

cards.q: You are solving Trapping Rain Water out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: n, the range of heights, whether the array can be empty
The formula: water over i = min(max on the left, max on the right) − h[i]
Naively: find the walls for every i — O(n²)
Remove the repetition: maxLeft and maxRight arrays — O(n) time and memory
Two pointers: process the lower side, its own side sets the level — O(1) memory
Complexity and edge cases: n < 3, a monotonic array, a flat plateau
cards.explain: The single-bar formula is the key to all three solutions, so it comes right after clarifying. Then the ladder: O(n²) → O(n) with memory → O(n) without, and at every step — which repeated work was removed.

cards.title: Where this shows up in games, and what comes next
cards.body:
The 2D version (Trapping Rain Water II, #407): a height map with water in the pits. Pointers do not work there — the “lower side” is now the whole boundary of the region. The solution is a heap over the boundary: pop the lowest boundary cell, its unvisited neighbors fill up to its level and become boundary themselves. It is a Dijkstra-style traversal, O(wh · log(wh)); heaps and pathfinding come in later units.

In a game: filling lakes on procedural terrain, puddles on a height map, the water level in a tile simulator. A profile along one line is exactly problem #42.

Overflow: the water is less than n · max h = 2·10⁴ · 10⁵ = 2·10⁹ — that still fits in an int (2,147,483,647), but barely. With other constraints, accumulate in a long.
cards.deep:
Two pointers as a merge of prefixes. Solution 2 is solution 1 where, at any moment, only the array whose maximum is smaller is read. The left prefix only grows to the right, the right suffix only to the left, and the pointers simply walk them toward each other; nothing extra is stored.

Formally. Suppose at some step h[l] < h[r]. Every bar k < l was passed at a step where h[k] < h[r_k] and r_k ≥ r > l, so lmax < max(h[l + 1..n − 1]), and h[l] < h[r] too. Hence min(maxLeft[l], maxRight[l]) = max(lmax, h[l]). The right branch is symmetric with a non-strict inequality.

Performance. Prefix arrays are three linear passes: the CPU predicts such access well. Burst can vectorize the third pass (summing min − h, independent iterations), while the prefix maxima themselves are a dependency chain — each step waits for the previous one. Two pointers branch on every step, and the branch depends on the data. For n = 2·10⁴ all three solutions take tens of microseconds; argue about memory and clarity, not speed.

Allocations. new Stack<int>() and the arrays are garbage if the function runs every frame. In Unity keep the stack in a field and call Clear(), or for a small n use Span<int> st = stackalloc int[n] with a manual top (the thread stack is limited, usually 1 MB — not for large n).

cards.q: Match each solution with its cost.
pairs: Scanning for walls for every i
O(n), one left-to-right pass, stack up to n
Heap over the boundary, O(wh · log(wh))

lessons.title: Matrices in place
lessons.sub: Rotate Image, Spiral Matrix, Set Matrix Zeroes: reasoning with indices and O(1) memory

cards.title: Rotate Image: where a cell goes
cards.body:
Rotate Image (LeetCode #48). A square n×n matrix (n ≤ 20); rotate it 90° clockwise in place — no second matrix.

Start with indices, not the picture. In a clockwise rotation row i becomes column n − 1 − i, and column j becomes row j: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i). Check it on a corner: the top-left (0, 0) goes to the top-right (0, n − 1). Counterclockwise is the inverse mapping: (i, j) → (n − 1 − j, i).

Brute force: res[j][n − 1 − i] = m[i][j] into a second matrix — O(n²) time and O(n²) memory. The time cannot improve — every cell has to be touched — but the memory can go.

cards.q: n = 4. Where does cell (1, 3) go in a 90° clockwise rotation?
cards.explain: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i) = (3, 4 − 1 − 1) = (3, 2). Check with the picture: the cell at the right edge of the second row moves down, to the second-from-right position of the bottom row.

wrong.1: That is the counterclockwise rotation: (i, j) → (n − 1 − j, i) = (0, 1).
wrong.2: That is only the transpose (i, j) → (j, i). After it the row still has to be mirrored: column 1 → 4 − 1 − 1 = 2.

cards.title: The idea: transpose, then mirror
cards.body:
The rotation splits into two simple swaps, each done in place.

1. Transpose — mirror over the main diagonal: (i, j) ↔ (j, i). Swap only the pairs above the diagonal, j > i: if you go over every j, each pair is swapped twice and ends up back where it was.
2. Mirror every row: (j, i) → (j, n − 1 − i). Together: (i, j) → (j, i) → (j, n − 1 − i) — exactly the clockwise rotation.

Counterclockwise — transpose and reverse the order of the rows. 180° — reverse the order of the rows and each row. O(n²) time, O(1) memory, n(n − 1)/2 + n·⌊n/2⌋ swaps.

Unity: this is how you rotate a tetromino in an n×n mask and the data of a room prefab — the walkability grid, the door mask. Transform rotates the prefab itself; the grid data is your code. A non-square w×h room cannot be rotated in place: the result is h×w, you need a new array, res[x, h − 1 − y] = cells[y, x].
cards.deep:
Rotating in fours. The second classic solution goes ring by ring: within a ring a cell moves along a cycle of four positions (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i) → (n − 1 − i, n − 1 − j) → (n − 1 − j, i), and one temporary rotates the whole four. Same O(n²) and O(1), but every cell is written once instead of twice. Transposing is easier to write without bugs, the fours are easier to explain through indices; both are accepted.

Cache. Transposing reads along a row and writes along a column. For n = 20 it does not matter; on a 4096×4096 matrix of int nearly every write is a cache miss. Blocked transposition helps: walk in squares, say 32×32, so both blocks stay in cache.

int[][] versus int[,]. LeetCode gives a jagged array: rows are separate arrays, and Array.Reverse(m[i]) reverses a whole row. That does not work for int[,] — Array.Reverse on a multidimensional array throws RankException; write a swap loop or store the grid flat (next lesson).

A rectangle in place. Transposing a non-square matrix within the same buffer is possible by following the cycles of the index permutation, but that is a separate, tricky problem. In an interview the honest answer is a new h×w array.

Tetrominoes in Unity. A piece is often stored not as a matrix but as cell offsets from a pivot: a clockwise rotation with y pointing up is (x, y) → (y, −x). The SRS rotation system adds “wall kick” tables — which shifts to try if the rotated piece hits something.

cards.q: Assemble the in-place clockwise rotation.
cards.explain: Transpose only above the diagonal: j starts at i + 1. Swap with a tuple — (m[i][j], m[j][i]) = (m[j][i], m[i][j]). Then reverse every row. Array.Reverse(m) would reverse the order of the rows — together with the transpose that is a counterclockwise rotation.

cards.task: Step through the rotation of a 4×4 matrix of the numbers 1..16. The rig stops twice: name the next swap.

asks.q: Row 0 is transposed: (0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3) were swapped with their mirrors. Which swap starts row 1?
asks.explain: j starts at i + 1 = 2: only cells above the diagonal are taken. Swapping (1, 0) ↔ (0, 1) would put 2 and 5 back where they were, and (1, 1) lies on the diagonal and maps to itself.

asks.q: The transpose is done, row 0 is [1, 5, 9, 13]. What does the first mirroring step do?
asks.explain: Mirroring a row swaps columns a and n − 1 − a: first 0 and 3, then 1 and 2. The swap (0, 0) ↔ (3, 0) would reverse a column, i.e. the order of the rows — that gives a counterclockwise rotation.

cards.q: On [[1, 2], [3, 4]] this code produces [[2, 1], [4, 3]] — a mirror image, not a rotation. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: j from 0 visits every pair twice: at (0, 1) the cells swap, at (1, 0) they swap back. No transpose happened, only the row mirroring is left. It should be j = i + 1.

cards.title: Spiral Matrix: four boundaries
cards.body:
Spiral Matrix (#54). Return the elements of an m×n matrix (m, n ≤ 10) in clockwise spiral order, starting at the top-left corner.

No need to simulate “turns” with a visited array — keep four boundaries of the unvisited rectangle: top, bottom, left, right. One lap: the top row left to right, top++; the right column top to bottom, right--; the bottom row right to left, bottom--; the left column bottom to top, left++.

The trap: after the first two sides the rectangle may have degenerated — only one row or one column was left, and it has been walked already. So walk the bottom row only if top <= bottom, and the left column only if left <= right. Without these checks, matrices like 3×4 output elements twice.

Invariant: the unvisited cells are exactly the rectangle [top..bottom] × [left..right]. O(mn) time, memory is just the answer.

cards.q: Assemble the spiral traversal.
cards.explain: Going down follows the right column — a[i][right] — and starts from the already moved top so the corner is not read twice. The way back along the bottom row happens only if rows are left (top <= bottom), the way up the left column only if columns are left (left <= right). A finished left column moves left++.

cards.task: Step through the spiral over a 3×4 matrix. The rig stops twice: say what the code reads next.

asks.q: The right column was read: 8, 12, and right became 2. What does the code read next?
asks.explain: The bottom row right to left, from right = 2 to left = 0: 11, 10, 9. The 12 was already read with the column — that is why right-- comes before the way back.

options.label: Skips the way back: no rows are left

asks.q: Second lap: 6, 7 were read, top became 2 and bottom = 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: top = 2 > bottom = 1 — no unvisited rows remain, and the check top <= bottom keeps the code out of the way back. Without it row 1 would be read a second time, and 6 would come out twice.

cards.title: Set Matrix Zeroes: markers in the first row and column
cards.body:
Set Matrix Zeroes (#73). If a cell is 0, set its entire row and column to 0; in place. m, n ≤ 200.

The brute-force trap: zeroing immediately when you meet a 0 — the new zeroes start zeroing their own rows and columns too, and the zeroes spread over almost the whole matrix. So first mark, then fill.

Memory, step by step: a copy of the matrix — O(mn); two flag arrays rowZero[m] and colZero[n] — O(m + n); O(1) — keep the flags in the matrix itself: m[i][0] = 0 means “zero row i”, m[0][j] = 0 means “zero column j”. But the first row and first column may contain zeroes of their own — remember their fate in two bools before marking.

Order matters: 1) flags for the first row and column; 2) marking over cells [1.., 1..]; 3) zeroing cells [1.., 1..] by the markers; 4) at the very end — the first row and column by the flags. Zeroing the first row before step 3 erases the markers.

cards.task: Step through Set Matrix Zeroes on a 4×4 matrix with zeroes at (1, 1) and (3, 0). The rig asks twice what the code does.

options.label: Zeroes row 1 and column 1 right away

asks.q: The flags are stored: firstRowZero = false, firstColZero = true. Marking reached the zero at (1, 1). What does the code write?
asks.explain: Markers live in the first row and first column: m[1][0] = 0 means “zero row 1”, m[0][1] = 0 means “zero column 1”. Zeroing right away is not allowed — the new zeroes would start marking on their own. There are no separate arrays: O(1) memory.

options.label: Leaves the first row as is: [1, 0, 3, 4]
Zeroes the first row: it holds a 0 marker
Restores m[0][1] to its old value 2

asks.q: The inner cells are filled. firstRowZero = false, and the first row holds the marker m[0][1] = 0. What does the code do with the first row?
asks.explain: The fate of the first row is decided by the flag, not by the markers in it: it had no zero of its own. The marker m[0][1] = 0 sits in the cell of the zeroed column 1 — it has to be zero anyway. There is no need, and nothing, to restore the 2 from.

cards.q: On [[0, 1], [1, 1]] the code zeroes the whole matrix, though the answer is [[0, 0], [0, 1]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The first row is zeroed before the inner cells are filled. Its zeroes look like “zero this column” markers, and m[1][1] gets zeroed although neither row 1 nor column 1 had a zero. The first row and column go last, after the fill step.

cards.q: Room and piece data in Unity. What is true? Select all.
options: A 6×4 room cannot be rotated 90° within the same 6×4 array — you need a 4×6 array
A 180° rotation means reversing the order of the rows and each row
Transposing with j from 0 rotates the matrix by 180°
If the prefab is rotated via Transform, the door mask in the data must also be rotated by code
Set Matrix Zeroes in place takes a single pass: zero immediately when you meet a zero
cards.explain: A rotated room swaps its width and height — it does not fit a buffer of the old dimensions. 180° is two mirrors: the order of the rows and each row. Transposing with j from 0 swaps every pair twice and does nothing. Transform rotates only the visuals and colliders; the grid data is your array, and your code rotates it. Zeroing immediately is not allowed: new zeroes would spread over the whole matrix.

cards.q: You are solving Rotate Image out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: is the matrix square? clockwise? in place?
Indices: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i), check it on a corner
Naively: a second matrix — O(n²) memory
Idea: transpose only above the diagonal and mirror each row
Complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases and variations: n = 1, counterclockwise, a rectangular matrix
cards.explain: The index formula comes first — both the check and the proof that transpose plus mirror is exactly the rotation rest on it. For a rectangle the honest answer is “not in place, a new h×w array”.

lessons.title: A grid in memory
lessons.sub: T[,], jagged and flat arrays, neighbors by offsets, Island Perimeter and Game of Life in place

cards.title: Three ways to store a tile map
cards.body:
A w×h tile map — walkability, tile type, step cost. In C# you can store it in three ways.
