T[,] — a rectangular array. One object, one contiguous block, row-major order: [y, x] and [y, x + 1] sit next to each other. Indexing is convenient, but every access checks bounds in both dimensions, and the sizes come from GetLength(0) (rows) and GetLength(1) (columns) — easy to mix up.

T[][] — a jagged array. An array of references to h separate row arrays: h + 1 objects on the heap, rows wherever the allocator put them, an extra pointer hop on every access. In exchange you can take a whole row: grid[y] is a plain T[]. This is how LeetCode passes grids.

A flat T[] of length w * h, cell (x, y) at index y * w + x. One block, one bounds check, easy to hand to Span<T>, NativeArray<T>, Jobs and Burst. The price is doing the index math by hand.

Locality. The CPU reads memory in cache lines — 64 bytes on x86 and most ARM chips, i.e. 16 ints (128 bytes on Apple M). Walking memory sequentially costs one miss per 16 cells; jumping down a column of a 1024-wide grid misses on almost every cell. So the outer loop goes over y and the inner one over x.

cards.q: A 1024×1024 grid of int is stored flat: cells[y * w + x]. Which traversal is faster, and why?
options: Outer over y, inner over x — it walks memory in order, one cache miss per 16 cells
Outer over x, inner over y — also in order: the index keeps growing anyway
No difference: array access is O(1) in any order
cards.explain: Neighboring x are neighboring memory cells, and one 64-byte cache line brings in 16 cells. An inner loop over y jumps by w · 4 = 4096 bytes — every step lands in a new cache line.

wrong.1: The index grows, but in steps of w = 1024 elements, i.e. 4 KB: every access is a new cache line.
wrong.2: O(1) counts operations, not time: a cache miss costs tens of times more than a hit. Same asymptotics, different speed.

cards.title: Neighbors: an array of offsets
cards.body:
Four ifs for “up, down, left, right” get copied from problem to problem and break differently in each one. Instead use an array of offsets: one loop over directions and one bounds check.

The “inside the grid” test in one comparison: (uint)nx < (uint)w. A negative nx cast to uint becomes a huge number and fails too — two checks for the price of one.

Eight neighbors (with diagonals) — the same arrays with 8 entries. In Unity the same thing is written as an array of Vector2Int or Vector3Int — for Tilemap.GetTile.

cards.title: Island Perimeter: 4 · land − 2 · adjacencies
cards.body:
Island Perimeter (LeetCode #463). A grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land), up to 100×100; there is exactly one island and no lakes inside it. Find the length of its coastline.

Brute force: for every land cell count the sides that face water or the edge: 4 neighbors per cell, O(wh). That is already optimal in time, but there is a shorter formula.

Via adjacencies: every land cell has 4 sides; every pair of adjacent land cells hides two sides — one of each. Perimeter = 4 · land − 2 · adjacencies. To count each pair once, look only right and down.

In a game this is how you measure the border of a region — a fence, a coastline, a selection outline. And “only right and down” is a general trick for not counting a pair twice.

cards.q: Compute the island’s perimeter with the formula.

wrong.1: 16 − 3: one side per pair was subtracted, but a pair of neighbors hides two — one on each cell.
wrong.2: 4 · 4 = 16 — forgot to subtract the sides where land cells touch each other.

cards.q: The same count on int[,]. On a 3×5 grid (3 rows, 5 columns) with land in the bottom row the code throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The check for the neighbor below compares y + 1 with the width w = 5 instead of the height h = 3. On the bottom row y = 2: 3 < 5 passes, and g[3, x] is out of range. On a square grid the bug is invisible — so test on a rectangular one. It should be y + 1 < h.

cards.title: Game of Life: two state bits in one cell
cards.body:
Game of Life (#289). A cell is live (1) or dead (0). Next generation: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors (out of 8) survives, otherwise it dies; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbors comes alive. All cells change simultaneously, the grid is up to 25×25, solve it in place.

The in-place problem: if you write the new state immediately, the neighbors to the right and below will count the new value instead of the old one. Naively — a copy of the grid, O(wh) memory.

Two bits in one cell. A 0 or 1 takes one bit, the other 31 are free. Bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 the next one. The first pass counts neighbors by cell & 1 (the old state; the second bit does not interfere) and, if the cell will live, sets cell |= 2. The second pass shifts: cell >>= 1. Values between the passes: 0 — dead and stays dead, 1 — live, will die, 2 — dead, will come alive, 3 — live and stays live. Bit operations are covered in detail in the bits unit.

In a game a cellular automaton smooths procedural caves (the rule “become a wall if ≥ 5 walls around”). There you usually keep two buffers and swap them — simpler and parallelizable; the bit trick saves memory on huge grids.

cards.q: Assemble Game of Life in place.
cards.explain: Count a neighbor by its low bit — the old state, even if its “next” bit is already set. A cell will live with three neighbors (any cell) or if it is live with two. Write the future into the second bit, |= 2, leaving the current one alone. The second pass shifts the second bit into the first one’s place. b[y][x] &= 1 would keep the old generation.

cards.q: A cell is live and has 4 live neighbors. What value does it hold after the first pass, before the shift?
cards.explain: With 4 neighbors a live cell dies: the “next” bit is not set, and the “current” bit stays 1. The value is 0b01 = 1 — “live, will die”. After the shift it becomes 0.

wrong.1: 3 = 0b11 means “live and stays live”. But with 4 neighbors a live cell dies.
wrong.2: 2 = 0b10 means “dead now, will come alive”. A live cell’s current bit is 1, and the first pass does not change it.
wrong.3: The first pass does not touch the current bit — otherwise the neighbors to the right and below would already see it as dead.

cards.q: On three live cells in a row in the middle of a 3×3 board the code should produce a vertical triple, but it loses the bottom cell. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: After the first pass a surviving cell holds 3, not 1, and the == 1 comparison does not see it. The middle cell of the triple survives and becomes 3; when the code reaches the bottom middle, it sees only two of its three live neighbors — and it is not born. Count a neighbor by its low bit: live += b[ny][nx] & 1.

cards.title: A flat grid in a game: edges, padding, Jobs
cards.body:
In a flat array, neighbors are index offsets: right i + 1, left i − 1, the adjacent rows i ± w. The trap: for a cell on the right edge, i + 1 is the first cell of the next row. The array will not throw, and the bug will be silent. Check the edge by x, not by the index.

Padding: a (w + 2)×(h + 2) grid with a ring of “walls” around the edge. Inner cells never go out of bounds, the checks disappear, and the neighbor offsets are constants { +1, −1, +W, −W } with width W = w + 2.

Unity: a flat NativeArray<int> goes into an IJobParallelFor over cells, compiled with Burst. For an automaton like Game of Life use two buffers: the job reads the old one and writes the new one, because a parallel job must not write where its neighbors read. Tilemap is slow for logic: read a block via GetTilesBlock into an array, compute on the array, write back with SetTilesBlock.
cards.deep:
T[,] in .NET. Multidimensional array access has historically been slower than one-dimensional: the index is computed from each dimension’s lower bound and length, and the JIT is worse at removing the bounds checks. In newer .NET versions the JIT optimizes such access better and the gap has narrowed, but on Mono and IL2CPP in Unity the flat array is the most predictable option. Measure with the profiler, not by faith.

Bounds checks. In a loop for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) a[i] the JIT removes the check. For a row of a jagged array, put it in a local, var row = g[y];, and loop to row.Length. For a flat one — Span<int> row = cells.AsSpan(y * w, w) (available in Unity too).

Burst vectorizes simple loops over a NativeArray; branches and calls inside get in the way. In an IJobParallelFor a writable container may, by the rules, be accessed — read or written — only at the index passed to Execute. The safety system (active in the Editor and development builds) checks the range of the current batch and throws on any access outside it until the restriction is lifted with [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] — and then the races are your problem. A [ReadOnly] container can be read at any index — hence the scheme “old buffer read-only, new buffer written at your own cell”.

An infinite board is a common follow-up to #289: store only the live cells in a HashSet<(int, int)> and, for the next generation, count neighbors for the live cells and their neighbors — O(live) instead of O(wh). Games split an infinite world into chunks (say 32×32), each a flat array, and do not store empty chunks.

Two bits versus two buffers. Bits halve the memory, but one array is both read for neighbors and written: in a single-threaded loop that is safe, but a parallel job cannot do it — formally it is a race, and the safety system will not let you read other cells of a writable container. Two buffers cost twice the memory, but the old buffer is read-only, and traversal order does not matter.

cards.q: A flat w×h grid, cell i = y * w + x. What is true? Select all.
options: The right neighbor is i + 1, but only if x + 1 < w; otherwise it is a cell of the next row
The neighbor in the next row is i + w
The i + 1 bug on the right edge always ends in IndexOutOfRangeException
With a one-cell padding ring, inner cells are visited without bounds checks
In an IJobParallelFor the automaton can be updated in place: the jobs will agree on an order
cards.explain: i + 1 on the right edge is the first cell of the next row: the index is inside the array, there is no exception, the bug is silent (it only throws for the very last cell). The next row is +w. Padding makes every offset of an inner cell safe. Parallel jobs do not coordinate an order: an in-place update creates races — you need two buffers.

cards.q: You are solving Game of Life out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: the rules, simultaneous update, in place or not, what lies beyond the edge
Naively: a copy of the grid — O(wh) memory
Idea: bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 the next one
First pass: count neighbors by cell & 1, mark future life with cell |= 2
Second pass: cell >>= 1
Walk through three cells in a row: they become a vertical triple
Complexity O(wh) time, O(1) memory; the follow-up is an infinite board
cards.explain: The key word is “simultaneously”: it explains why writing immediately breaks the neighbors and why the second bit is needed. Three in a row is the best example: it also catches the == 1 instead of & 1 bug.

cards.q: Match each storage option or technique with its property.
pairs: One block, [y, x], sizes via GetLength
Rows are separate objects, grid[y] is a whole row
One bounds check, ready for NativeArray and Burst

lessons.title: Final: two pointers and in-place arrays
lessons.sub: New problems to recognize, a trace with a prediction, traps and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match each statement with a technique from this unit.
pairs: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place
read/write: write if not equal to the last written
Merge sorted nums2 into nums1, which has free space at the end
Fill from the end, comparing the tails
Reverse only the vowels in a string
Opposite pointers that skip everything but vowels
How many pairs in a sorted array sum to < target
Transpose and reverse the order of rows

cards.q: Merge Sorted Array (#88): nums1 has length m + n, holding m sorted numbers and n free cells at the end; merge the sorted nums2 of length n into it. Why write from the end?
options: The tail of nums1 is free: writing at position m + n − 1 and leftward never overwrites a number not yet read
From the end there are fewer comparisons: O(n) instead of O(m + n)
From the start also works without extra memory — the end is just the habit
cards.explain: Write the larger of the two tails at position w = i + j + 1, where i and j are the unread ends. While nums2 still has numbers, w > i: the write is always to the right of anything unread in nums1. It is the same trick as in squares of a sorted array: we know where the largest values are, so we start with them.

wrong.1: The number of comparisons is the same — O(m + n) either way. The gain is in memory, not in steps.
wrong.2: From the start, the very first write overwrites nums1[0] before it is compared; you would have to shift the tail or copy nums1 — O(m) memory or O(m · n) time.

cards.q: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (#26): keep one copy of each value at the front of the array and return how many there are.
cards.explain: Compare with the last kept value, nums[write − 1]: everything left of write is already the unique values in order, and in a sorted array equal values stand together. nums[read + 1] runs off the end on the last step. No swap is needed — dropped values are never needed again, plain assignment is enough. The answer is the new length, write.

cards.task: Step through Trapping Rain Water on [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]. The rig stops and asks how much water the code records: look at lmax, rmax and h[R].

asks.q: L = 2 (height 0), R = 5 (height 5), lmax = 4, rmax = 0 — nothing on the right has been passed yet. How much water does the code record over bar 2?
asks.explain: h[L] = 0 < h[R] = 5 — the left side is processed. There is guaranteed to be a wall of at least 5 on the right and 4 on the left, so the left one holds: 4 − 0 = 4. rmax = 0 only means “nothing passed on the right”, not “a wall of height 0”. h[R] = 5 is a guarantee, not the water level. On this array the right pointer never moves: the total is 9.

cards.q: The interviewer changes Two Sum II: there may be no answer, then return an empty array. On [2, 3, 4, 9], target = 8 the code returned [3, 3] — the same number twice. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: When lo == hi both pointers sit on the same 4, and 4 + 4 = 8 counts as a pair. While an answer is guaranteed it is found before the pointers meet — so the bug only shows on an input with no answer. A pair means two different indices: while (lo < hi).

cards.q: Valid Palindrome II (#680): you may delete at most one character. Opposite pointers; on the first mismatch, check whether s[l + 1..r] or s[l..r − 1] is a palindrome. Complexity?
options: O(n)
O(n²)
O(n log n)
cards.explain: There is only one mismatch where we branch: each of the two checks is a plain opposite-pointer pass with no deletions allowed, O(n). At most three linear passes in total — O(n), O(1) memory.

wrong.1: O(n²) would come from trying to delete every character in turn. Here there are only two candidates to delete — s[l] and s[r].
wrong.2: There is no sorting or halving — only linear passes.

cards.q: A colleague writes Squares of a Sorted Array: l and r at the ends, the smaller of the two squares goes to the front of the answer. What ends up in res[0] on [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]?
cards.explain: The ends are 16 and 100, the smaller is 16, and it goes to res[0], even though the smallest square is the 0 in the middle. The ends only guarantee the maximum; nobody knows where the minimum is. That is why the answer is filled from the end, taking the larger one.

wrong.1: 0 is the correct answer to the problem, but this code only looks at the ends and has not reached the zero in the middle.
wrong.2: 1 = (−1)² is not at an end either; the code picks the smaller of 16 and 100.

cards.q: Game code. What is true? Select all.
options: Removing dead units from a List<Unit> when order does not matter: swap-remove from the end, O(1) per removal
Rotating the data of a 5×3 room by 90°: you need a new 3×5 array
The right neighbor in a flat grid is always i + 1
Game of Life in an IJobParallelFor: read the old buffer, write the new one
Container With Most Water: move the taller line so as not to lose height
cards.explain: Swap-remove from the end shifts no tail and moves an element that has already been checked. A rotated room swaps width and height. i + 1 on the right edge is the first cell of the next row; the edge is checked by x. Parallel jobs must not write where neighbors read — two buffers. In Container you move the shorter line: it is exhausted, the taller one is not.

cards.q: You are solving 3Sum out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: values or indices, must triples be unique, the range of n
Brute force over triples: O(n³), about 4.5·10⁹ for n = 3000
Idea: sort, fix nums[i], find the pair with opposite pointers
Duplicates: skip i if nums[i] == nums[i − 1], and move l and r past equal values after a hit
Complexity: O(n²) time, memory is the in-place sort plus the answer
Variations: 3Sum Closest, 4Sum in O(n³) with the sum in long
cards.explain: Sorting is allowed because values, not indices, are needed — worth saying out loud while clarifying. The example with two −1s checks the duplicate skipping.

units.blurb: Fixed and variable windows, a window with a counter, Minimum Window Substring and the sliding window maximum on a monotonic deque. Why .NET has no Deque<T> and what to use instead.

lessons.title: Fixed-size window
lessons.sub: Add the one coming in, subtract the one leaving: from O(n·k) to O(n), plus an FPS counter on a ring buffer

cards.title: The problem and the window signals
cards.body:
Maximum Average Subarray I (LeetCode #643). Given an integer array nums and a number k, find the contiguous subarray of length exactly k with the largest average and return that average. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴.

Signals of a sliding window:

1. The problem is about a contiguous piece: “subarray”, “substring”, “k in a row”, “the last N frames”. A subsequence — elements with gaps — is no longer a window.
2. You need the best piece or an answer for every position of the piece: the largest sum, the longest, the shortest.
3. Whatever you compute over the piece can be updated when one element enters on the right and one leaves on the left: a sum, a count, letter counters.

Here the length is given, so this is a fixed-size window: the left edge follows the right one at exactly distance k. The average is the sum divided by k, and k is the same for every window. So it is enough to find the largest sum and divide once at the end.

cards.q: Where does a fixed-size window work? Select all.
options: The largest sum of k consecutive elements
Does string s contain a substring of length |p| made of the same letters as p
The average frame time over the last 60 frames, updated every frame
The largest sum of any k elements of the array, not necessarily consecutive
The longest increasing subsequence
cards.explain: A sum of k in a row is the template itself. A permutation of p inside s is a window of length |p| with letter counters: a letter enters — plus one, a letter leaves — minus one. The last 60 frames is a window over a stream of values. Any k elements with gaps is not a window: you need the k largest, not a piece — that is sorting or a heap. A subsequence has gaps too, so no window.

cards.title: The naive solution and its cost
cards.body:
Brute force: for every start i from 0 to n − k, add up k elements from scratch. There are n − k + 1 windows with k additions each — (n − k + 1)·k in total, that is O(n·k) time and O(1) memory.

The cost depends on k. With k = 1 there are n windows, but one addition each. With k = n there is one window, but of length n. The middle is the worst: with k ≈ n/2 the work is ≈ n²/4. For n = 10⁵ that is 2.5·10⁹ additions — at the rule of thumb of 10⁸ simple operations per second, about 25 seconds instead of a fraction of a second.

So O(n·k) must not be called “almost linear”: when k is comparable to n, it is a square.

cards.q: n = 10⁵. For which k does the naive solution do the most additions?
options: k ≈ n / 2, that is about 5·10⁴
k = n
cards.explain: The work is (n − k + 1)·k: the number of windows times the window length. For k = 1 it is n, for k = n it is n as well. The factors always add up to n + 1, and a product of two numbers with a fixed sum peaks when they are equal: k ≈ n/2 gives ≈ n²/4 = 2.5·10⁹.

wrong.0: With k = 1 there are n windows, but one addition each — n in total.
wrong.2: With k = n there is a single window: n additions. A long window, but only one.

cards.title: What work am I repeating?
cards.body:
Neighbouring windows [i..i+k−1] and [i+1..i+k] share k − 1 elements. The naive solution adds them up again. Yet the windows differ in just two elements: nums[r] entered on the right and nums[r − k] left on the left.

So we don’t recompute the sum, we patch it: sum += nums[r] − nums[r − k]. One step is O(1), the whole pass is O(n), memory O(1).

Invariant: after the slide at step r, sum holds the sum of exactly the last k elements, nums[r − k + 1..r]. The element that leaves has index r − k — the one k positions to the left of the incoming one.

No overflow: |sum| ≤ k·10⁴ ≤ 10⁹, and int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹. Compare sums and divide once, at the end, and make sure it is in double.

In a game: the same window smooths noisy input — the average of the last k samples of a stick, a mouse or an accelerometer.

cards.q: Assemble the single-pass solution.
cards.explain: The starting window is the first k elements, and best starts from its sum, not from zero: if every number is negative, zero beats every window and the answer is wrong. The leaving element is nums[r − k], k positions left of the incoming one; r − k + 1 is the first element that stays. best / k is integer division: 51 / 4 gives 12, not 12.75, so cast to double before dividing.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 8, 2, 6, 1, 9, 4, 7], k = 3. The rig stops twice: first it asks which element leaves the window, then what the method returns.

asks.q: Window [8, 2, 6], sum = 16. nums[4] = 1 comes in. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The leaving element is nums[r − k] = nums[1] = 8, the leftmost element of the current window. The 3 already left on the previous step, and the 2 stays: the new window is [2, 6, 1] with sum 9. best stays 16.

asks.q: The best sum is 20, for the window [9, 4, 7]. What does return (double)best / k return?
asks.explain: The cast to double comes before the division, so 20.0 is divided by 3: the answer is 6.666…. Without the cast, best / k is integer division and gives 6. And 20 is the sum, not the average.

cards.title: Unity: an FPS counter on a ring buffer
cards.body:
FPS shown as 1 / Time.deltaTime jumps every frame. What you want on screen is the average over the last N frames — a fixed-size window, except the numbers arrive as a stream, and there is no point in keeping the whole history.

Keep the last N values in an array plus an index head — the slot of the oldest value. Every frame: subtract the leaving frames[head], add the new value, write the new value in its place and move head around the circle. That is a ring buffer: O(1) per frame and zero allocations. A Queue<float> would also do — internally it is the same circular array — but your own array is clearer and never grows.

Details you will be asked about:
— Use Time.unscaledDeltaTime. Time.deltaTime is multiplied by Time.timeScale — on a pause with timeScale = 0 it is zero — and capped by Time.maximumDeltaTime.
— Average FPS is N / the sum of frame times, not the average of 1/dt. Frames of 10 and 30 ms: the average of 100 and 33.3 FPS is 66.7, but in fact 2 frames took 40 ms, which is 50 FPS. Averaging instantaneous FPS is skewed upward by the fast frames.
— Until the buffer is full, divide by the number of frames recorded, not by N.
— A float accumulates rounding error over millions of additions and subtractions, and the sum slowly drifts. Recompute it every N frames or keep it in a double.

Ring buffers in detail, with mask indexing, come in the last unit of the course, in the lesson on pools and ring buffers.

cards.q: In this counter the sum stays zero forever: two neighbouring lines are in the wrong order. Tap the one that runs too early.
cards.explain: The new value is written into the slot before the old one is subtracted from the sum. The next line then subtracts not the leaving frame but the one just written: sum += dt − dt, and the sum never changes. As with check-before-insert in Two Sum, order matters: first sum += dt − frames[head], then frames[head] = dt.

cards.q: An FPS counter on a window of N frames. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: A counter on Time.deltaTime gets zero-length frames during a pause with Time.timeScale = 0
Two frames of 10 and 30 ms make 50 FPS, not 66.7
The average of instantaneous 1/dt is more accurate than N / the sum of frame times
Every frame the counter allocates memory for the new value
A float sum drifts slowly over millions of additions and subtractions
cards.explain: deltaTime is multiplied by timeScale, so on a pause it is zero — use unscaledDeltaTime. Two frames in 40 ms are 2 / 0.04 = 50 FPS, while the average of 100 and 33.3 is inflated by the fast frame. There are no allocations: the array is allocated once and one slot is overwritten per frame. float rounding error accumulates, which is why the sum is recomputed now and then or kept in a double.

cards.title: Which quantities work this way — and which don’t
cards.body:
The “add the incoming, subtract the leaving” trick works when adding an element can be undone:

— sum and average: subtract;
— the number of matching elements (vowels, enemies in a zone, zeros): −1 if a matching one left;
— letter counters int[26]: count[in]++, count[out]--;
— XOR: XOR-ing again removes the element.

It does not work for the maximum and minimum. Window [9, 4, 7], maximum 9; the 9 leaves — what is the maximum now? A single number “9” cannot tell you; you need to remember who the next candidate is. That is the sliding window maximum problem, and a monotonic deque solves it — lesson 4 of this unit.

A window can also be written as a single loop: an element always enters, one leaves once r ≥ k, and the answer is taken once the window has reached length k.
cards.deep:
Prefix sums as an alternative. prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements, so the sum of window [l..r] is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]. That costs O(n) memory instead of O(1), but answers the sum of any range in O(1): handy when there are many window lengths or the queries arrive after the precomputation. Keep prefixes in long: with n = 10⁵ and |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴ the sum reaches 10⁹, and with larger values it overflows int.

Rolling hash (Rabin–Karp, substring search). The polynomial hash of a window, h = Σ s[i]·B^(k−1−i) mod M, also slides in O(1): subtract the leaving character’s contribution s[l]·B^(k−1), multiply by B, add the incoming one. Searching for a pattern of length m in a text of length n is O(n + m) on average. Equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings, so a match is verified character by character, and in the worst case with collisions it is O(n·m).

Precision. The drift of a float sum is the accumulated rounding error of every +=; float carries about 7 significant digits. The fixes are recomputing every N steps, summing in double, or Kahan compensated summation (a second variable collects the lost low-order bits). Integers do not drift — which is why frame times are sometimes stored as microseconds in a long.

Unity. unscaledDeltaTime is the full interval between frames, including waiting for vsync or the GPU. To see who is slow, the CPU or the GPU, there is FrameTimingManager (CPU and GPU time per frame) and ProfilerRecorder (profiler counters in a build); an averaging window over their numbers is built the same way.

cards.q: You are solving Maximum Average Subarray I out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: length exactly k, can numbers be negative, return a double, n and k up to 10⁵
Name the brute force: (n − k + 1)·k additions, up to 2.5·10⁹ with k ≈ n/2
Idea: neighbouring windows share k − 1 elements — add the incoming, subtract the leaving
Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: sum holds exactly the last k elements
Run the example [1, 12, −5, −6, 50, 3], k = 4 — the answer is 12.75
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: k = n, every number negative, division in double
cards.explain: As with any problem: agree on the statement, name the baseline and its cost, then the idea, the code and a run on an example, and only then the complexity and edge cases. “Every number negative” checks that best starts from the first sum, not from zero.

cards.q: Match each window quantity with how to update it on a slide.
pairs: +1 if a vowel entered; −1 if one left
Keep the sum, divide once at the end
Cannot be undone by subtraction: needs a deque

lessons.title: Variable-size window
lessons.sub: Grow on the right, shrink on the left: why a nested while is still O(n), and when the window breaks

cards.title: The problem and the key property
cards.body:
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LeetCode #3). Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Constraints: 0 ≤ |s| ≤ 5·10⁴; the string contains English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

Examples: "abcabcbb" → 3 (“abc”), "bbbbb" → 1, "pwwkew" → 3 (“wke”). “pwke” does not count: it is a subsequence, the letters are taken with a gap.

The signals are the same as for a fixed-size window — a contiguous piece and the best one — but the length is not given; it is what we are looking for. A variable-size window works when the condition is monotonic:

— if a window is valid, every window inside it is valid too: removing a character cannot add a repeat;
— if a window is invalid, every window containing it is invalid too: the repeat does not go away.

Hence the strategy: once the window breaks, growing it is pointless — shrink from the left. While the window is valid, try to grow it.
cards.code:
int a = LengthOfLongestSubstring("pwwkew"); // 3: "wke"
int b = LengthOfLongestSubstring("");       // 0

cards.q: Substring s[l..r] has no repeats. What can you say about s[l+1..r] and about s[l..r+1]?
options: s[l+1..r] definitely has no repeats; s[l..r+1] depends on the character s[r+1]
Both definitely have no repeats
s[l+1..r] may contain a repeat, while s[l..r+1] cannot
cards.explain: Removing a character on the left cannot create more repeats. Adding one on the right creates a repeat if s[r+1] is already inside. That is monotonicity: a valid window stays valid after shrinking, and an invalid one stays invalid after growing. That is why the left edge only ever moves forward.

wrong.1: Growing can break the window: “abc” has no repeats, but “abca” does.
wrong.2: The other way round: removing a character from a repeat-free window cannot produce a repeat. Adding one can.

cards.title: From brute force to a window
cards.body:
Brute force: from every start i, walk right with a HashSet<char> until a repeat shows up. For an arbitrary alphabet that is O(n²). A fair caveat: a repeat-free substring is no longer than the alphabet size σ, so here brute force is O(n·σ), and on LeetCode with σ ≈ 95 it even passes. But for integers or Unicode it is a square, and the interviewer expects O(n).

What is repeated: brute force hits a repeat at j and restarts from i + 1 — re-checking characters i+1..j−1 that are already known to be distinct. Don’t reset the window: the right edge r only moves forward, and when s[r] is already inside, move the left edge l until the duplicate is gone.

Invariant: after the inner while, the window s[l..r] has no repeats — and that is when the answer is updated.

Why O(n) despite the while. Count not one iteration of the for but all the work in the pass. Each Remove moves l by one, and l only grows and cannot overtake r. So over the whole pass there are at most n removals and exactly n additions — at most 2n set operations. A single iteration can be expensive (four removals in a row), but the total is linear.

cards.q: How many times in total does the while body — window.Remove(s[l++]) — run over a whole pass on a string of length n?
options: At most n: each character is removed from the window at most once
Up to n on every iteration of the for — up to n² in total
Exactly as many times as there are repeated characters in the string
cards.explain: Each removal moves l by one, l only grows and never overtakes r. So over the whole pass there are at most n removals, and at most 2n set operations in total. That is “amortised O(1) per step”: the expensive iterations are rare and paid for by the cheap ones.

wrong.1: That would be the case if l were reset backwards. But l only grows: a removed character never re-enters from the same position.
wrong.2: In “gamedev” one letter repeats, yet there are four removals: g, a, m and the first e. Everything to the left of the duplicate goes.

cards.task: Step through the trace on "gamedev". The rig stops when the second “e” arrives at the window “gamed” and asks what the code does.

options.label: Removes the first “e” from the middle of the window
Restarts the window at the new “e”: l = 5

asks.q: Window “gamed”, an “e” arrives, and an “e” is already inside. What does the code do?
asks.explain: A window is a contiguous piece; you cannot cut out the middle. For the first “e” (index 3) to leave, everything to its left leaves too: g, a, m and the e itself — four iterations of the while. Restarting at l = 5 would lose the “d”: the window “de” has no repeats and must not be thrown away.

cards.title: Jumping by the last index
cards.body:
Four removals one by one can be replaced by one jump. Remember, for every character, where it was seen last. If s[r] was already at position p inside the window, the left edge jumps straight to p + 1.

The subtlety: a character’s last position may be left of the window — the character left long ago. Then l must not move. Hence l = Math.Max(l, …): the left edge never moves backwards.

A handy trick is to store index + 1: a fresh array is all zeros, and zero itself means “not seen”, so there is no need to fill it with −1. 128 slots are enough because the problem guarantees ASCII characters.

The complexity is the same, O(n), but now every step is O(1) with no amortisation and no hashing. Memory is O(σ).
cards.deep:
Why the jump loses nothing. Let s[r] = c with the previous c at p ≥ l. Every window that starts in l..p and ends at r or later contains both cs — it is invalid. So the starts l..p can be discarded at once for all future r. It is the same discard argument as for converging pointers.

Unicode. A .NET char is a UTF-16 code unit from 0 to 65,535. For arbitrary text an int[65536] is 256 KB per call; a Dictionary<char, int> is better then. And what a person calls a character can be two chars: an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is a surrogate pair. If the interviewer says “character” about such text, ask whether to count code units or code points; for the latter .NET Core 3.0+ has System.Text.Rune and string.EnumerateRunes(), which Unity does not have.

No allocations. Span<int> next = stackalloc int[128]; is 512 bytes on the stack instead of an array on the heap. C# zeroes stackalloc memory by default (unless [SkipLocalsInit] is applied), so the “zero means not seen” trick still works. Unity has Span<T> since 2021.2 (.NET Standard 2.1). The HashSet<char> version is several times slower: a hash and a bucket lookup on every operation, plus allocating the set itself.

cards.q: On the string "abba" this code returns 3, but the right answer is 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: At r = 2 the second “b” sets l = 2. At r = 3 an “a” arrives, its previous position is 0, and the code sets l = 1: the left edge jumps back into the window “bba”, which has a repeat, length 3. The earlier “a” is already outside the window and l must not move. The fix is the invariant “l never decreases”: l = Math.Max(l, next[c]).

cards.title: The mirror template: the shortest window
cards.body:
Minimum Size Subarray Sum (LeetCode #209). Given an array of positive integers nums and a number target, find the minimal length of a contiguous subarray with sum ≥ target, or 0 if there is none. Constraints: 1 ≤ target ≤ 10⁹, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴.

The monotonicity is mirrored here: the numbers are positive, so a valid window (sum ≥ target) stays valid when it grows, and shrinking only lowers the sum. Once you find a valid window, growing it further is pointless — anything longer is valid anyway. Record the length and shrink, trying to make it shorter.

Two templates worth telling apart out loud:
— looking for the longest — shrink while the window is bad, take the answer after the while;
— looking for the shortest — shrink while the window is good, take the answer inside the while.

The complexity is the same, O(n): l only grows. The sum is at most 10⁵·10⁴ = 10⁹ and fits in an int. If no window is valid, best stays int.MaxValue — that must be turned into 0.
cards.deep:
The LeetCode follow-up: O(n log n). Prefix sums of positive numbers are strictly increasing. For each start i, binary-search the first j with prefix[j] − prefix[i] ≥ target — Array.BinarySearch over the prefix array (when the value is absent it returns ~index of the insertion point). It is worse than the window, but it shows you see the monotonicity of prefixes. The window is O(n) time and O(1) memory.

Why positivity matters so much. The window proof relies on the fact that for a fixed r the sum of [l..r] decreases as l grows. With zeros it does not increase — the window still works. With negative numbers the property is gone and you need a different tool: prefixes and a monotonic deque (LeetCode #862, lesson 4).

cards.q: Assemble the Minimum Size Subarray Sum solution.
cards.explain: We want the shortest, so shrink while the window is good: while (sum >= target), and record the length r − l + 1 inside. nums[l++] subtracts the current left element and only then moves the edge; nums[++l] would subtract its neighbour. If no window was valid, best is still int.MaxValue, and the problem says to return 0.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 4, 2, 5, 1, 1, 3, 6], target = 8. The rig stops after the first shrink and asks what to do next.

options.label: Shrink again: record length 3 and drop the 4

asks.q: Length 4 was recorded and the 1 dropped on the left: window [4, 2, 5], sum = 11. What next?
asks.explain: 11 ≥ 8 — the window [4, 2, 5] is still good, so the while goes on: record length 3 and drop the 4, sum = 7. Growing a good window is pointless — every extension is good too, just longer. And it is too early to stop: [3, 6] of length 2 is still ahead.

cards.title: When the window does not work
cards.body:
Everything rests on monotonicity. With negative numbers it breaks: shrinking can increase the sum, and growing can decrease it.

Example: nums = [1, −1, 5], target = 5. The window reaches r = 2 with sum 5, records length 3, drops the 1, the sum becomes 4 < 5, and the while stops. The window concludes that nothing shorter exists and returns 3. But the answer is 1: the subarray [5]. Reaching it required dropping the −1 as well, which would have increased the sum — the window never considers that.

What to use instead:
— “sum exactly k, numbers of any sign” (LeetCode #560) — prefix sums in a dictionary: the sum of [l..r] is prefix[r+1] − prefix[l], and at each step you look up how many times the prefix prefix − k has occurred. That is the prefix sums lesson in the hash map unit;
— “shortest with sum ≥ k, numbers of any sign” (LeetCode #862) — prefixes plus a monotonic deque, lesson 4 of this unit.

Zeros don’t break monotonicity: with them the sum does not grow when you shrink, and the window works.

cards.q: Where does a variable-size window give the right answer in O(n)? Select all.
options: The longest subarray with at most two distinct numbers
The shortest subarray with sum ≥ target, all numbers positive
The shortest subarray with sum ≥ target, numbers of any sign
How many subarrays sum to exactly k, numbers of any sign
The longest substring where each letter occurs at most twice
cards.explain: “At most two distinct” and “each letter at most twice” are monotonic: the condition holds inside a valid window, and growing an invalid one does not fix it. Positive numbers are the “shortest” template. With negative numbers shrinking can increase the sum, so there is no monotonicity: “≥ target” needs prefixes and a deque, “exactly k” needs prefixes in a dictionary.

cards.q: You are solving Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: substring, not subsequence; which characters — ASCII or any Unicode; the empty string
Name the brute force: from every start walk to the first repeat — O(n²) for a large alphabet
Idea: a repeat-free window, grow on the right, shrink on the left on a repeat — the left edge never goes back
Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: s[l..r] has no repeats, l only grows
Run "abba": check that l does not jump backwards
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(σ) memory — and why the while does not make it quadratic
Edge cases: empty string, all characters equal, all distinct
cards.explain: Statement, baseline, idea, code with the invariant, a run, complexity, edge cases. “abba” is the best example to run: it breaks the jump without Math.Max. And interviewers often ask separately why the nested while is still O(n).

lessons.title: Window with a counter
lessons.sub: A replacement budget, a maxFreq you never decrease, and Minimum Window Substring with a “how many still needed” counter

cards.title: The problem: a window with a replacement budget
cards.body:
Longest Repeating Character Replacement (LeetCode #424). Given a string s of uppercase English letters and a number k, you may replace at most k characters with any uppercase letters. Find the length of the longest substring of one repeated letter you can get this way. Constraints: 1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10⁵, 0 ≤ k ≤ |s|.

Example: "AABABBA", k = 1 → 4: in “AABA” replace the B with an A.

Rephrase it. Which letter do you keep in a window? The most frequent one — everything else has to be replaced. So a window is valid when

length − maxFreq ≤ k, where maxFreq is how many times the most frequent letter occurs in the window.

The condition is monotonic: remove a character from a valid window and the length drops by 1 while maxFreq drops by at most 1, so “length − maxFreq” does not grow. That means the variable-size window from the previous lesson works, and the letter frequencies of the window live in an int[26] counter: a letter enters — count[c − 'A']++, it leaves — --.
cards.code: int ans = CharacterReplacement("AABABBA", 1); // 4: "AABA" -> "AAAA"

cards.q: k = 2. Which window is valid?
options: “AABBA”
“ABCAB”
“ABCDA”
cards.explain: “AABBA”: length 5, the most frequent is A ×3, replace 5 − 3 = 2 ≤ 2 — valid, it becomes “AAAAA”. In “ABCAB” the most frequent are A and B with 2 each: replace 3 > 2. In “ABCDA” A ×2: replace 3 > 2.

wrong.1: The most frequent letters, A and B, occur twice each. Keep one of them and you replace 5 − 2 = 3 characters, with a budget of 2.
wrong.2: A occurs twice, the others once: replace 5 − 2 = 3 > 2.

cards.title: The honest version: a while and the true maximum
cards.body:
The “longest” template from the previous lesson: add s[r], shrink from the left while the window is bad, then update the answer. Bad means more than k replacements are needed: r − l + 1 − maxFreq > k.

Here maxFreq is recomputed every time over 26 counters. A step costs O(26), the pass — O(26·n), which is O(n) with a constant of 26. Memory is O(26).

Invariant: after the while the window is valid — at most k letters need replacing.

count.Max() is LINQ (using System.Linq). In Unity — on both Mono and IL2CPP — it walks the array through IEnumerable<int> and allocates an enumerator on every call; in .NET 7+ Max over an array takes a Span and allocates nothing. In a hot loop write your own loop over the 26 slots, but in an interview this form reads better. And below is how to get rid of those 26 operations too.

cards.task: Step through the trace on "AABABBA", k = 1. The rig stops twice when the window turns bad and asks what the honest version does.

options.label: Removes the “A” on the left: l = 1
Removes the “B” it has just added

asks.q: Window “AABAB”: length 5, the most frequent is A ×3, 2 replacements needed > 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The window is bad, so the while runs: remove the leftmost “A”, l = 1. The answer is only updated after the while, once the window is valid again — best = 5 cannot be recorded. And the window never shrinks on the right: r only grows.

options.label: Removes another “A” on the left: window “BAB”
Stops shrinking and adds the next “B”

asks.q: The “A” is gone: window “ABAB”, length 4, the most frequent is now ×2, 2 replacements. What next?
asks.explain: 4 − 2 = 2 > 1 — the window is still bad, and the while removes the next “A”: “BAB”, 1 replacement. Notice: the honest version recomputed the maximum from 3 down to 2 and so shrank the window to length 3, below the record of 4. The next card shows a version that does not do that.

cards.title: Why maxFreq never needs to go down
cards.body:
We don’t need every valid window, only a window longer than the record. A window of length L is valid when L − maxFreq ≤ k, that is L ≤ maxFreq + k. So the record can only grow when maxFreq grows — the highest letter frequency we have ever seen in a window.

Hence the classic solution:
— update maxFreq upwards only: maxFreq = Math.Max(maxFreq, ++count[c]) — only the letter that has just entered needs checking;
— if the window turned bad, move l once: if instead of while. The window does not shrink, it slides to the right, keeping the length of the record.

While maxFreq is stale — too high — the window may in fact be invalid. But a window of that length was already found honestly, so the answer is not spoiled. The window can only grow when the counter of the incoming letter exceeds the old maxFreq, and that is a real frequency in the current window.

Invariant: the window length equals the best answer so far, and the window never gets shorter. That is why you can return s.Length − l at the end. The time is an honest O(n), memory O(26).

cards.q: The version with an if and a maxFreq that never decreases. "AABABBA", k = 1. At r = 4 the window “AABAB” is bad: 5 − 3 = 2 > 1. What happens next?
options: l moves by one, and the window “ABAB” of length 4 with the stale maxFreq = 3 counts as valid
l keeps moving until the window is honestly valid: “BAB”
maxFreq is recomputed down to 2, and the window shrinks to “BAB”
cards.explain: The if moves l exactly once, maxFreq stays 3, so 4 − 3 = 1 ≤ 1 — the window “ABAB” counts as valid, even though honestly it needs 2 replacements. The answer is not spoiled: length 4 was already achieved by the honest window “AABA” at r = 3. The window simply slides at length 4 and grows only if some letter reaches frequency 4.

wrong.1: That is what the honest version with a while does. In the if version the window never shrinks below the record; it moves by one.
wrong.2: maxFreq is only updated through Math.Max, that is, only upwards. That is exactly why no recount over 26 counters is needed.

cards.title: Minimum Window Substring: a “how many still needed” counter
cards.body:
Minimum Window Substring (LeetCode #76, hard). Given strings s and t, find the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t including repeats, or the empty string. Constraints: 1 ≤ |s|, |t| ≤ 10⁵, uppercase and lowercase English letters. Follow-up: O(|s| + |t|).

Example: s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" → “BANC”.

We want the shortest, so it is the “shrink while the window is good, answer inside the while” template. The question is how to tell quickly that the window is good. Comparing the window’s dictionary with that of t at every step is O(σ) per step.

Instead, keep two counters: need[c] — how many c are needed, have[c] — how many are in the window. Plus a number formed — how many distinct letters of t are already fully covered. The window covers t ⇔ formed == need.Count, and need.Count − formed is how many letters are still missing.

The key: formed changes only at the moment of crossing. You add c and have[c] becomes exactly need[c] — the letter is covered, formed++. You remove c and have[c] drops below need[c] — it is uncovered, formed--. Extra copies change nothing. The check is O(1), the whole pass is O(|s| + |t|).
cards.deep:
One counter instead of formed. The classic short version: missing = t.Length — how many characters are still missing, repeats included. c enters: if need[c] > 0, then missing--; then need[c]-- (a negative value means surplus). c leaves: need[c]++; if it became > 0, then missing++. The window covers t ⇔ missing == 0. One array instead of two dictionaries.

Arrays instead of dictionaries. The letters are English, so an int[128] indexed by character code is several times faster than a Dictionary<char, int>: no hashing, no TryGetValue. Span<int> need = stackalloc int[128] removes the allocation too. GetValueOrDefault on a dictionary is an extension method from CollectionExtensions: available since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity since 2021.2.

A filtered string. If t is short and s is full of irrelevant letters, you can first collect a list of (index, character) pairs for the letters of t only and run the window over it: fewer steps, and the window length is computed from the original indices. Same asymptotics.

One allocation. Call Substring once, at the end: keep only bestL and bestLen. Allocating a string on every new record is needless garbage.

cards.q: Assemble Minimum Window Substring.
cards.explain: formed counts distinct letters, so compare it with need.Count, not t.Length: for t = "AABC" there are three letters but the length is four. The leaving character is the left one, s[l++]. A letter becomes uncovered when there are fewer than needed: have[gone] < m; with <= an extra copy would wrongly decrease formed. .NET Substring takes a start and a length, not a start and an end.

cards.task: Step through the trace on s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC". The rig stops in the middle of a long shrink and asks what happens when a needed letter is on the left.

options.label: “CODEBA” is no shorter than “ADOBEC”; the “C” is dropped and coverage is lost
“CODEBA” is the new best window; the “C” is dropped
Shrinking stops: the “C” is needed and cannot be dropped

asks.q: The window “CODEBA” covers t, and a “C” is on the left. The best so far is “ADOBEC”. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The lengths are equal, 6 and 6, and the record is only updated when r − l + 1 < bestLen — strictly less. Then the code drops the “C” like any left character: it cannot look ahead. have[C] falls to 0 < 1, formed = 2, and the while ends. Then the window grows to the next “C” and finds “BANC”.

cards.q: On s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" this code returns "BA" instead of "BANC". Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: formed must change only at the moment have[c] crosses need[c]. With >= every extra copy of an already covered letter increases formed again: a second B or A counts as one more covered letter, formed reaches need.Count without a C, and the code declares “BA” a cover. It must be == n: a letter gets covered exactly once.

cards.title: Variations: the same counter in other problems
cards.body:
A permutation inside a string (Permutation in String #567, Find All Anagrams #438). A fixed-size window of length |p| and letter counters: a letter enters — ++, leaves — --. A match is detected not by comparing 26 slots but with the same formed: how many letters of p are fully collected. Once formed == need.Count the window cannot hold any extra letters: its length is exactly |p|, and the needed ones already take all of it.

At most K distinct (Fruit Into Baskets #904 is K = 2). A variable-size window with a Dictionary<int, int> counter; when a value’s count drops to zero, remove the key — then cnt.Count is the number of distinct values. Shrink while there are more than K.

Exactly K distinct (Subarrays with K Different Integers #992, hard). “Exactly” is not monotonic: a valid window breaks both when it shrinks (fewer than K distinct) and when it grows (more than K). The trick: exactly(K) = atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1). And “atMost” counts the number of subarrays: if the window [l..r] is valid, so are all windows that end at r and start no further left than l — there are r − l + 1 of them. Add that number at every step.
cards.deep:
Overflowing the count. There are n(n + 1)/2 subarrays: for n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ — more than int.MaxValue. In #992 n ≤ 2·10⁴ and an int is enough, but in your own problem or a similar one with a larger n count in long — interviewers often check exactly that.

Why the difference is right. The set of subarrays with at most K distinct values is the union of those with exactly K and those with at most K − 1, and the two do not overlap. Both “at most” conditions are monotonic, so each is counted by a window in O(n), and the whole problem is O(n).

Counting by key without a double lookup. cnt[x] = cnt.GetValueOrDefault(x) + 1 looks the key up twice. .NET 6+ has CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(cnt, x, out _)++ — one lookup and a reference to the value. Unity does not have it; if the keys are small numbers, a counter array is faster anyway.

cards.q: Match each problem with its technique.
pairs: Does s contain a permutation of p
A window of length |p| and letter counters
The longest block given k replacements
Length − maxFreq ≤ k, maxFreq upwards only
The shortest window with all letters of t
The number of subarrays with exactly k distinct
The longest subarray with at most 2 distinct
Count distinct, shrink while there are more than 2

cards.q: You are solving Minimum Window Substring out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: repeats in t count, case matters, what to return if there is no window
Name the brute force: from every start grow until t is covered — O(|s|²), too slow for 10⁵
Idea: a “shortest” window — grow until it covers t, then shrink while it still covers
Counters need and have, and formed — how many letters are covered; it changes only when crossing need[c]
Run ADOBECODEBANC / ABC and show where the window loses coverage
State the complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time, O(σ) memory
Edge cases: |t| > |s|, a letter of t missing from s, repeats in t such as "AA"
cards.explain: First agree on repeats and case — they change the solution. Then the baseline, the window idea, the key trick — formed instead of comparing dictionaries — a run, the complexity and edge cases. Repeats in t are the main source of bugs, so check them out loud.

lessons.title: Monotonic deque
lessons.sub: The maximum of every window in O(n): who can be forgotten for good, and what to use instead of the Deque<T> .NET lacks

cards.title: The problem: the maximum of every window
cards.body:
Sliding Window Maximum (LeetCode #239, hard). Given an array nums and a number k, a window of length k slides from left to right one element at a time; return the maximum at every window position — n − k + 1 numbers in total. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴, 1 ≤ k ≤ n.

Example: [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3 → [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

It is a fixed-size window, but the “add the incoming, subtract the leaving” trick fails: you cannot “subtract” a maximum. Window [3, −1, −3], the 3 leaves — who is the maximum now? You need to remember the next candidates, and not all of them, only those that still stand a chance.

Signals: the maximum or minimum at every window position — fixed or variable (for example, “the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit”). In a game: the worst frame over the last N frames, the highest terrain cell within a radius, the peak threat over the last k AI ticks.

cards.q: Where do you need the maximum or minimum over a sliding window? Select all.
options: The worst frame time over the last 120 frames, updated every frame
The longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit
The average frame time over the last 120 frames
The largest number in the whole array
The lowest price over every k consecutive days
cards.explain: The worst frame is a maximum over a fixed-size window, the lowest price over k days is a minimum over a window. max − min ≤ limit is a variable-size window that needs both the maximum and the minimum. The average is a sum with subtraction, no deque needed. The maximum of the whole array is a single pass with no window at all.

cards.title: Brute force and O(n log k) solutions
cards.body:
Brute force: scan k elements for every window — O(n·k). With k ≈ n/2 and n = 10⁵ that is ≈ 2.5·10⁹ comparisons — too slow.

An ordered set. Keep the window’s elements in a SortedSet — a red-black tree: insertion and removal are O(log k), the maximum is the rightmost node. The trap: SortedSet is a set, so equal values collapse into one. Window [3, 1, 3]: the first 3 leaves, you remove 3 — and the second 3, still in the window, is gone too. So store the pair (value, index): the pairs are distinct, and tuples compare by the first field, then the second. The result is O(n log k), memory O(k).

A heap. A max-heap with lazy deletion: push (index, value), and before answering discard everything at the top that has left the window. No removal from the middle of the heap is needed, but stale elements can pile up — O(n log n) and O(n) memory. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> exists since .NET 6; Unity does not have it, but it does have SortedSet.

Either is a fine first answer in an interview. But the interviewer will ask: can you do it in O(n)?

cards.q: Why put the pair (value, index) into the SortedSet rather than just the value?
options: A set collapses equal values: removing the 3 that left would also lose the other 3 still in the window
Without the index, SortedSet cannot compare the elements
The index is needed for Max to run in O(1)
cards.explain: SortedSet stores each value once: Add of the second 3 returns false and adds nothing. When the first 3 leaves, Remove(3) deletes the only entry, and the window [1, 3] is left without its 3. A pair with the index makes every window element unique.

wrong.1: ints are comparable as they are. The problem is not comparison but that equal values are one entry of the set.
wrong.2: SortedSet.Max walks to the rightmost node of the tree, O(log k) with or without the pair.

cards.title: The key idea: who can be forgotten for good
cards.body:
Let j < i and nums[j] ≤ nums[i]. Then j will never be the maximum again: every future window that contains j also contains i — it is further right and leaves later — and its value is no smaller. Such a j can be thrown away immediately.

Who remains? Candidates with nobody greater or equal to their right. Keep their indices in a deque — a queue you can push to and pop from at both ends:

— the indices in the deque increase, and the values strictly decrease;
— nums[i] arrives — pop from the back everyone ≤ it, then push i to the back;
— the index at the front has left the window (≤ i − k) — pop it;
— the window maximum is at the front.

Why O(n): every index enters the deque once and leaves at most once — at most 2n operations in total, just like the left edge of the window in the previous lessons. The deque holds at most k indices — memory O(k).

At most one index leaves from the front per step: only i − k drops out of the window. That is why it is an if there, not a while.

cards.q: Assemble the deque solution. The deque is an array plus two indices: the live part is dq[head..tail−1].
cards.explain: The window is [i − k + 1..i], so index i − k is already outside it: the condition is <=. Pop from the back everyone not greater than the new value: that keeps the deque values strictly decreasing. The maximum is at the front, nums[dq[head]]. At most one index leaves from the front per step, so an if is enough; a while would also be correct. No ring is needed: every index is pushed once, an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [2, 7, 4, 1, 3, 6, 5, 8], k = 3. The rig stops twice before a new number arrives and asks what the deque does first.

asks.q: The deque is [1, 2, 3] — values 7, 4, 1. i = 4, x = 3 arrives. What does the code do first?
asks.explain: The front comes first: index 1 ≤ i − k = 1, the 7 has dropped out of the window [2..4] and leaves. Only then the back: the 1 ≤ 3 is popped, the 4 is greater than 3 and stays. The deque becomes [2, 4], and the window maximum is 4.

options.label: Pushes index 6 (value 5) to the back: deque [5, 6]
Pops index 5 from the front and pushes 6

asks.q: The deque is [5] — value 6. i = 6, x = 5 arrives. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Only those ≤ the new value are popped from the back: 6 > 5, so the 6 stays. Index 5 has not dropped out of the window [4..6]. The 5 goes to the back: it is smaller than the 6 for now, but the 6 drops out of the window earlier (index 5 would leave from the front at i = 8), and then the 5 may become the maximum. The deque values still decrease: 6, 5. This array never gets to i = 8: at i = 7 the 8 pops both from the back.

cards.q: On nums = [5, 1, 1, 1], k = 2 this code returns [5, 5, 1] instead of [5, 1, 1]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: At i = 2 the window is [1..2], and index 0 with the 5 must leave: 0 ≤ 2 − 2. The < condition does not pop it, so the 5 stays the maximum of a window of length k + 1. Index i − k is the first one already outside the window, hence <=.

cards.title: .NET has no deque: what to use instead
cards.body:
The .NET standard library has no Deque<T>. What it has, and why it does not fit:

— Queue<T> is a circular array, but you can only remove from the front: popping the back is impossible;
— Stack<T> — only the top;
— List<T>.RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole array — O(n) per operation;
— LinkedList<T> does everything in O(1): AddLast, RemoveLast, RemoveFirst, First, Last. But every AddLast is a new node object on the heap (about 48 bytes for an int on 64-bit), the nodes are scattered in memory, and they are garbage for the collector. In Unity with the Boehm GC, such code running every frame shows up.

Your own deque on a circular array: an array, a head index and a count. With a power-of-two capacity, “wrapping around” is & (Length − 1) instead of %. Every operation is O(1), growth by doubling is amortised O(1), as with List<T>. After warm-up there are no allocations.

#239 itself does not even need that: every index is pushed once, so an array of length n and two indices are enough — head only grows, no ring required. The price is O(n) memory instead of O(k); a ring of k slots brings it back to O(k), since the deque never holds more than k indices. Your own deque is needed when the number of elements in the stream is not bounded in advance — say, in a game that runs for hours.

cards.q: Deques in .NET and Unity. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: LinkedList<T> gives O(1) at both ends but allocates a node object on every add
Queue<T> works as a deque: it can remove from the back
In a deque on a circular array with capacity 2ᵏ the wrapped index is computed with & (Length − 1)
List<T>.RemoveAt(0) is O(1) because there is an array inside
For #239 an array of length n with two indices is enough, no ring needed
cards.explain: LinkedList is a doubly linked list: operations at the ends are O(1), but every node is a heap object. Queue<T> can only remove from the front. The mask only works for a power-of-two capacity: x & (2ᵏ − 1) is x mod 2ᵏ, and for −1 it also gives the last index. RemoveAt(0) shifts every element — O(n). In #239 every index is pushed once, so an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.

cards.title: Where else a deque works, and when it is not needed
cards.body:
A variable-size window + two deques (LeetCode #1438): the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit. One deque keeps the maximum candidates (values decrease), the other the minimum candidates (values increase). When the window is bad, move l and pop from the fronts any indices that fell below l.

Negative numbers (LeetCode #862): the shortest subarray with sum ≥ k. The window from lesson 2 breaks here; what works is prefix sums (in a long: with n and |nums[i]| up to 10⁵ they reach 10¹⁰) plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes, O(n) — the same principle of “throw away whoever will never be useful again”.

Unity: inflating obstacles on a grid by the agent radius with a square kernel. A cell becomes blocked if the (2r + 1)×(2r + 1) square around it contains an obstacle — that is a maximum over a window: first along rows, then along columns. The deque gives O(W·H) for any radius instead of O(W·H·r²).

When a deque is overkill. The worst frame over the last 120 frames is 120 comparisons per frame — a fraction of a microsecond. A plain scan of the ring buffer is simpler and harder to get wrong. A deque pays off when the window is large and there are many steps: n and k around 10⁵, large grids, server metrics.
cards.deep:
The exact count. In #239 every index is pushed to the back once and popped at most once — from the back or the front. So there are at most 2n deque operations in total, even though a single step may pop k − 1 elements. It is the same amortised argument as for the left edge of the window and for the monotonic stack (the stacks unit): a deque is a monotonic stack whose “bottom” also leaves the window.

Heap versus deque in memory. With lazy deletion the heap keeps elements that have left the window until they surface at the top. On a decreasing array the top is always the oldest element, and it leaves on time. On an increasing array the new element is always on top while the old ones pile up below — up to n elements, though the window holds k. The deque holds at most k.

Cache and Burst. A deque on an array is sequential memory, with no pointers and no GC. In a Burst job the same solution is written on a NativeArray<int> with two indices — managed collections are not available there. Inflating obstacles row by row parallelises naturally: every row is an independent task (IJobParallelFor over rows, then over columns).

Why a tuple works in SortedSet. ValueTuple<int, int> implements IComparable: compare by the first field, then by the second on a tie. The default comparer uses it, with no boxing.

cards.q: Match each approach to the window maximum with its cost.
pairs: O(n log n) and up to O(n) memory
O(n), but a node object per element

cards.q: You are solving Sliding Window Maximum out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: k ≤ n, how many numbers to return, whether there are repeats
Name the O(n·k) brute force and why a sum with subtraction does not work here
Offer O(n log k): a SortedSet of (value, index) pairs — and the trap with repeats
The O(n) idea: a left element no greater than a right one is never the maximum again — a deque of decreasing values
Write the code: front left the window — pop; back ≤ x — keep popping; push i; answer from the front
Run [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3, showing the deque at every step
Complexity O(n): every index enters and leaves once; .NET has no Deque<T> — an array with two indices
cards.explain: The O(n log k) solution is an honest stepping stone: the interviewer sees you know the cost of collections and will ask for better. Then the domination idea, the code, a run and the complexity with the “enters and leaves once” argument. Mention the missing Deque<T> in .NET yourself — it is a platform-knowledge question.

lessons.title: Unit finale: window and deque
lessons.sub: New problems, a Minimum Window Substring trace with repeats in t, a trap and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match each statement with its technique.
pairs: The longest run of ones if you may flip at most k zeros
Variable-size window: zeros in the window ≤ k
Every position in s where a permutation of p starts
A window of length |p| and letter counters
How many subarrays sum to exactly k, numbers of any sign
The minimum of every window of k elements
The largest sum of k consecutive numbers
Fixed-size window: + the incoming, − the leaving

cards.q: Max Consecutive Ones III (LeetCode #1004): an array of 0s and 1s, you may flip at most k zeros; find the longest run of ones. What do you keep in the window and when do you shrink?
options: A count of zeros in the window; shrink from the left while there are more than k zeros
A count of ones in the window; shrink while there are fewer than k ones
A window does not fit: you need prefix sums
cards.explain: A window is valid if its zeros can be flipped: zeros ≤ k. The condition is monotonic — a valid window’s sub-windows have no more zeros — so the “longest” template works: grow on the right, shrink while the window is bad, take the answer after the while. It is #424 with budget k, except the “extra” letters are always zeros. O(n), O(1) memory.

wrong.1: Ones cost nothing — the budget is spent on zeros. The window is bad when there are more than k zeros.
wrong.2: There are no negative numbers here, and “zeros ≤ k” is monotonic. Prefixes are needed when monotonicity breaks.

cards.q: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ k, numbers from −10⁵ to 10⁵, n ≤ 10⁵. What do you choose?
options: Prefix sums and a monotonic deque of indices
A variable-size window: shrink while the sum is ≥ k
A fixed-size window for every length from 1 to n
cards.explain: Negative numbers break monotonicity: shrinking can increase the sum, and the window misses the answer — as on [1, −1, 5] with target 5. This is LeetCode #862: prefixes plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes, O(n). Trying every length is O(n²): about n²/2 = 5·10⁹ operations for n = 10⁵.

wrong.1: On [1, −1, 5], target 5, the window returns 3, but the answer is 1: reaching [5] requires dropping the −1, which would increase the sum.
wrong.2: It works, but it is O(n²): n lengths, a pass over the array for each. For n = 10⁵ that is about 5·10⁹ operations.

cards.task: Step through the Minimum Window Substring trace on s = "BAXAYBAA", t = "AAB" — t has two As. The rig asks twice what happens to the formed counter.

options: formed = 1
formed = 2
asks.q: need = {A: 2, B: 1}, need.Count = 2. The window is “B”, formed = 1. The first “A” arrives. What does formed become?
asks.explain: have[A] = 1, but 2 are needed: the letter A is not covered yet, so formed stays 1. formed grows only at the moment have[c] becomes exactly need[c] — for A that happens on the second “A”.

options.label: Drops the “A” — coverage is lost, formed = 1
Drops the “A”, coverage holds: there is another A in the window
Records “AYBA” as the new best window

asks.q: The window “AYBA” covers t, and an “A” is on the left. The best so far is “BAXA”. What does the code do?
asks.explain: “AYBA” has length 4 — no shorter than “BAXA”, so the record stays (it must be strictly less). The “A” leaves: have[A] drops from 2 to 1 < 2, the letter A becomes uncovered, formed = 1. One A is still in the window, but two are needed. Then another “A” arrives, and the window shrinks to the answer “BAA”.

cards.q: On the string "abcbd" this code returns 4, but the right answer is 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: At r = 3 a “b” arrives at the window “abc”. The if removes only the “a”, l = 1, while the first “b” stays; Add of the second “b” returns false. The window “bcb”, which has a repeat, counts as valid, and at r = 4 “bcbd” gives 4. Shrink while the duplicate is inside: a while, not an if.

cards.q: Window maximum, k = 3, nums = [6, 2, 5, 3, 4]. After i = 3 the deque holds indices [2, 3] — values 5, 3. i = 4, x = 4 arrives. What is in the deque after the step, and what is the window maximum?
options: [2, 4] — values 5, 4; maximum 5
[4] — value 4; maximum 4
[2, 3, 4] — values 5, 3, 4; maximum 5
[3, 4] — values 3, 4; maximum 4
cards.explain: The front: index 2 ≤ 4 − 3 = 1? No — the 5 is still in the window [2..4]. The back: 3 ≤ 4 — pop it; 5 ≤ 4 — no, stop. Push 4. The deque is [2, 4], the values decrease, and the maximum is the front, 5.

wrong.1: The 5 at index 2 is still in the window [2..4]: only an index ≤ i − k = 1 leaves from the front. And only those ≤ x leave from the back.
wrong.2: The 3 is ≤ 4 and to its left — it will never be the maximum again, so it is popped. Otherwise the deque values would stop decreasing.
wrong.3: The 5 is greater than the 4 — it is not popped from the back, and it has not left the window.

cards.q: The complexity of this unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: A variable-size window with a while inside a for is O(n) because l only grows
Minimum Window Substring is O(|s|·|t|)
A monotonic deque for the window maximum is O(n): every index enters and leaves once
The honest #424 that recomputes the maximum over 26 counters is O(26·n)
A SortedSet for the window maximum is O(n) because Max takes O(1)
cards.explain: A nested while does not make the window quadratic: l moves at most n times per pass. Minimum Window is O(|s| + |t|): t is counted once and formed is checked in O(1). The deque is ≤ 2n operations. The honest #424 is 26 operations per step. A SortedSet is O(n log k): insertion and removal in the tree are O(log k), and Max also walks to the rightmost node.

cards.q: Unity: the HUD needs the worst frame over the last 120 frames. What is the sensible choice?
options: Scan the ring buffer of 120 values every frame: 120 comparisons take a fraction of a microsecond
A monotonic deque only: otherwise it is O(n·k) and the game will stutter
A SortedSet of frame times with removal of the leaving one
cards.explain: k = 120 and one window per frame: a plain scan costs a fraction of a microsecond, with no allocations and no chance of a bug. “O(n·k)” here means 120 operations per frame, not per game. A deque pays off when the window and the stream are large. A SortedSet allocates a tree node on every insertion — garbage every frame.

wrong.1: There is one window per frame, and scanning it is 120 comparisons. Asymptotics matter when k and n are large; here the constant is tiny.
wrong.2: It works, but every insertion into a SortedSet is a new heap node, which is GC garbage every frame. And it is more complex than a plain scan.

cards.q: You are solving Max Consecutive Ones III out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: the array holds only 0s and 1s, k can be 0, n up to 10⁵
Name the brute force: every subarray with a count of zeros — O(n²)
Recognise the pattern: the longest subarray with the monotonic condition “zeros ≤ k” — a variable-size window
Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: after the while there are at most k zeros in the window
Run [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1], k = 2 and show where the window shrinks
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory — l only grows
Edge cases: k = 0, all zeros, all ones, k ≥ the number of zeros
cards.explain: The same script as in every lesson of the unit: the statement, the baseline, the pattern from its signals (a contiguous piece, “the longest”, a monotonic condition), code with the invariant, a run, the complexity, edge cases. With k ≥ the number of zeros the answer is n, and the code should produce it on its own, with no special case.

units.title: Stacks and linked lists
units.blurb: Matching brackets and a min stack, the monotonic stack, reversing and merging lists, fast and slow pointers, reversing in groups. LinkedList<T> from the inside and an allocation-free list on indices.

units.title: Binary search
units.blurb: Boundary invariants without off-by-one errors, the rotated array, searching on the answer, the median of two arrays. For games: a weighted loot table and a fair Fisher–Yates shuffle.

units.title: Sorting, intervals and greedy
units.blurb: How .NET sorts and when you do not need to, merging and inserting intervals, one-pass greedy, Kadane, and how to prove a greedy solution is correct.

units.title: Heaps and top-K

units.title: Trees

units.title: Graphs: traversal, connectivity, order

units.blurb: Decision trees, pruning, from recursion to a table, the unbounded knapsack, DP on two strings and LIS in O(n log n). How to spot DP in a problem and name the state and the transition.
